title: StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion
abstract: Voice style conversion (VSC) aims to transform a source utterance to match the timbre, accent, and emotion of a target voice while preserving linguistic content. StyleStream 1.0 introduced the first streamable zero-shot VSC system with state-of-the-art conversion quality, but remained limited in two ways: approximately 1s end-to-end latency on consumer hardware, and the lack of a text-based interface for designing or editing target voices. We present StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses these limitations. To reduce latency, we train a few-step pixel MeanFlow model and further fine-tune it with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing, improving robustness under streaming inference. This reduces end-to-end latency to 520~ms on a consumer GPU, a 2x speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality. To enable controllable style manipulation, we remove the mel-spectrogram context and instead route target style information through a compact style embedding. In this embedding space, we train a unified text-conditioned flow matching model that supports both text-based voice design, which maps natural language prompts to voice styles, and instruction-based voice editing, which modifies a specific attribute of a source utterance while preserving the rest. Experiments show that StyleStream 2.0 achieves the strongest target style fidelity on VSC, voice design, and voice editing, while remaining competitive on intelligibility and non-edited attribute preservation.

## StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion

headings: StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion
3.3 Voice Controller: Unified Voice Design and Editing
body_start:
Abstract

Voice style conversion (VSC) aims to transform a source utterance to match the timbre, accent, and emotion of a target voice while preserving linguistic content.
StyleStream 1.0 introduced the first streamable zero-shot VSC system with state-of-the-art conversion quality, but remained limited in two ways: approximately 1s end-to-end latency on consumer hardware, and the lack of a text-based interface for designing or editing target voices.
We present StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses these limitations.
To reduce latency, we train a few-step pixel MeanFlow model and further fine-tune it with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing, improving robustness under streaming inference.
This reduces end-to-end latency to 520 ms on a consumer GPU, a 2x speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality.
To enable controllable style manipulation, we remove the mel-spectrogram context and instead route target style information through a compact style embedding.
In this embedding space, we train a unified text-conditioned flow matching model that supports both text-based voice design, which maps natural language prompts to voice styles, and instruction-based voice editing, which modifies a specific attribute of a source utterance while preserving the rest.
Experiments show that StyleStream 2.0 achieves the strongest target style fidelity on VSC, voice design, and voice editing, while remaining competitive on intelligibility and non-edited attribute preservation. Samples can be found here: https://berkeley-speech-group.github.io/StyleStream2.0.

## 1 Introduction

Voice style conversion (VSC) modifies how an utterance is spoken while preserving what is said.
Following StyleStream 1.0 [41], we define voice style as the joint combination of timbre, accent, and emotion.
A large body of voice conversion work focuses on timbre conversion, aiming to change speaker identity while preserving content and other paralinguistic factors [52, 37, 61, 9, 4, 42, 65].
Separate lines of work address accent conversion [30, 5, 29] and emotional voice conversion [72, 48, 10] as standalone tasks.
More recent systems have begun to address holistic style transfer, jointly converting timbre, accent, and emotion from a single reference utterance [69, 36, 68, 3, 41].
Among them, StyleStream 1.0 [41] is the first to demonstrate high-quality zero-shot VSC in a streaming setting.
However, its approximately one-second end-to-end latency on consumer hardware remains high for latency-sensitive interaction.
Reducing this latency while preserving holistic conversion quality is therefore a key challenge for making streaming VSC practical.

A second limitation is that existing VSC systems largely require a target reference utterance.
This makes voice specification indirect: users must provide an example voice rather than describe the desired attributes.
In contrast, text-prompted control has become increasingly common in text-to-speech, where natural-language prompts can specify accent, emotion, and fine-grained vocal qualities such as a soft, warm, breathy, or singing-like voice [21, 34, 64, 59, 25, 26, 6, 12].
However, these systems synthesize speech from text rather than converting an input utterance, and therefore do not directly solve streaming speech-to-speech VSC.
Recent speech-to-speech conversion work also explores text-guided editing [54, 22, 66, 51], but typically over a single axis such as timbre or emotion.
To our knowledge, no prior system provides text-based voice design and editing for holistic VSC, let alone in a streaming setting.

We present StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses both limitations.
StyleStream 2.0 inherits the two-stage architecture of StyleStream 1.0: a Destylizer that extracts content features disentangled from style, and a Stylizer that reconstructs target speech from those content features and a target style.
Because StyleStream 1.0 already established the Destylizer as a strong content-style disentangler, we reuse it without modification and focus our changes on the Stylizer.

To reduce latency, we train a few-step pixel MeanFlow [18] Stylizer to replace the multi-step diffusion Stylizer used in StyleStream 1.0.
We further fine-tune this Stylizer with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing [27] to improve robustness under chunk-by-chunk inference.
This reduces end-to-end latency to 520 ms on a consumer GPU, a 2 $\times$ speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality.

To enable text-based control, we change how style enters the Stylizer.
StyleStream 1.0 conditions the Stylizer on both an unmasked mel-spectrogram context and a style embedding extracted from the target utterance, which leaves style information partially distributed across two conditioning channels.
We remove the mel-spectrogram context so that target style is represented through a single style embedding.
This makes text-based design and editing a problem of predicting or modifying this embedding.
Inspired by the unified image generation and editing model FLUX Kontext [33], we train a unified text-conditioned DiT in the style-embedding space: given a natural-language prompt, the model predicts a target style embedding for voice design; given an existing utterance embedding and a text instruction, the same model modifies the embedding along the requested attribute for voice editing.

For text-based control, we focus on age, gender, accent, and emotion.
These attributes provide a structured and measurable interface for specifying target voices, while covering the major perceptual factors needed for holistic VSC.
This structured interface supports both prompt-based voice design and attribute-targeted voice editing, and remains largely unexplored for holistic VSC, especially under streaming constraints.

We evaluate StyleStream 2.0 in two settings.
First, for standard target-speech-conditioned VSC, we compare against existing reference-based conversion systems and measure conversion quality, intelligibility, and target style fidelity.
Second, for text-based control, no native holistic VSC baseline exists.
We therefore construct strong cascaded baselines: for voice design, we combine ASR with prompt-controlled TTS; for voice editing, we combine prompt-controlled TTS with reference-based VSC.
These cascades benefit from powerful ASR and TTS systems, yet StyleStream 2.0 achieves stronger results on many metrics while remaining a pure speech-to-speech system that also supports streaming inference.

In summary, our contributions are:

• 

We introduce a faster streaming VSC model by training a few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer and fine-tuning it with autoregressive feedback, reducing end-to-end latency to approximately 520 ms on consumer hardware while preserving conversion quality.

• 

We propose a unified text-conditioned style-embedding model for natural-language voice design and attribute-targeted editing over age, gender, accent, and emotion in holistic VSC.

• 

We evaluate StyleStream 2.0 across standard target-speech-conditioned VSC and text-based voice design / editing, showing strong target-style fidelity while remaining competitive in intelligibility, non-edited attribute preservation, and audio quality against both reference-based and cascaded baselines.

## 2 Related Work

Prior speech-to-speech conversion work spans several directions, including voice conversion that primarily changes speaker identity while preserving content and other style factors [52, 37, 61, 9, 4, 40, 32], streaming or real-time voice conversion [42, 65, 45, 63], and separate lines on accent conversion and emotional voice conversion [30, 5, 29, 72, 48, 10]. More recent systems have begun to model richer, holistic voice style across timbre, accent, and emotion, including the Vevo family [69, 36, 68] and StyleStream 1.0 [41]. In parallel, prompt-controlled TTS systems enable natural-language specification of target voice characteristics [21, 34, 64, 59, 25, 26, 6, 12], with only a few open-source systems explicitly supporting holistic control over timbre, accent, and emotion [60, 25]. Closer to our setting, a smaller body of work explores text-guided speech-to-speech conversion [54, 22, 66, 51], but these methods typically focus on a single attribute and are evaluated offline. Thus, while prior work shows that speech-to-speech conversion, prompt-based control, and limited text-guided editing are all feasible, no prior system simultaneously provides fast streaming holistic VSC together with unified text-based voice design and editing.

Separately, diffusion and flow-matching models have become strong acoustic generators for speech synthesis and conversion [14, 13, 8, 15, 35, 40], but their iterative sampling cost is a bottleneck for streaming applications. Recent few-step generative models reduce this cost by producing high-quality samples in only a few steps, or even one step [17, 56, 57, 18, 19, 44]. However, fast sampling alone does not guarantee high-quality streaming inference, since short chunks provide limited context and can lead to degraded quality at chunk boundaries. Inspired by Self Forcing for autoregressive video diffusion [27], StyleStream 2.0 combines a few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer with autoregressive fine-tuning to improve streaming robustness while also enabling controllable holistic voice design and editing.

## 3 Method

StyleStream 2.0 follows the Destylizer-Stylizer framework of StyleStream 1.0 [41].
The Destylizer extracts source content features while suppressing speaker timbre, accent, and emotion.
The Stylizer maps these content features and a target style embedding to a mel-spectrogram, which is converted to waveform by a causal Vocos-based vocoder [55].
The style embedding can be obtained from a reference utterance or from a text-conditioned Voice Controller, allowing the same Stylizer to support reference-based conversion, text-based design, and text-guided editing.

We first recap the Destylizer, then introduce the redesigned Stylizer with pixel MeanFlow training and autoregressive feedback fine-tuning, and finally present the Voice Controller for unified voice design and editing.

## 3.1 Destylizer

We use the Destylizer from StyleStream 1.0.
The Destylizer consists of a frozen HuBERT-Large [24] encoder followed by six conformer [20] blocks.
During training, the Destylizer output is passed through a finite scalar quantization (FSQ) [47] module and then a transformer ASR decoder.
The conformer blocks and the ASR decoder are jointly optimized with a sequence-to-sequence ASR loss.
This training setup encourages the representation to preserve linguistic content, while the compact FSQ bottleneck, with a codebook size of 45, discourages encoding style cues that are not needed for character prediction.
At inference, we discard the FSQ module and ASR decoder, and use the continuous output features immediately before the FSQ layer as content features $f_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{c}\times T}$ at 50 Hz.

## 3.2 Stylizer

## 3.2.1 Preliminary: Pixel MeanFlow (pMF)

Pixel MeanFlow (pMF) [44] combines JiT-style [39] $x$ -prediction with MeanFlow [18, 19] objective for few-step guided generation.
Let $x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}$ be a clean sample and $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ be Gaussian noise.
We use the linear interpolation path

 $z_{t}=(1-t)x+t\epsilon,\qquad t\in[0,1],$ 

(1)

whose instantaneous Flow Matching velocity is

 $v(z_{t},t)=\frac{dz_{t}}{dt}=\epsilon-x.$ 

(2)

JiT motivates predicting the clean sample $x$ rather than noisy or velocity-space quantities, since $x$ lies closer to the data manifold and can be easier for a Transformer to model in high-dimensional spaces.
MeanFlow instead improves sampling efficiency by learning an average velocity over an interval $[r,t]$ :

 $u(z_{t},r,t)=\frac{1}{t-r}\int_{r}^{t}v(z_{\tau},\tau)\,d\tau,$ 

(3)

which is related to the instantaneous velocity by the MeanFlow identity

 $v(z_{t},t)=u(z_{t},r,t)+(t-r)\frac{d}{dt}u(z_{t},r,t).$ 

(4)

pMF combines these two ideas by having the network predict an $x$ -like quantity rather than a velocity.
Because pMF uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) distillation, the guidance scale $\omega$ is also provided as an input to the network.
Given condition $c$ , the model prediction $\hat{x}_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)$ is converted to an average velocity by

 $u_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)=\frac{z_{t}-\hat{x}_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)}{t}.$ 

(5)

Let $\varnothing$ denote the null condition.
The conditional and unconditional instantaneous fields are obtained from the degenerate interval $r=t$ :

 $v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c,\omega)=u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,t,c,\omega),\qquad v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,\varnothing,\omega)=u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,t,\varnothing,\omega).$ 

(6)

Following the pMF CFG distillation formulation, the guided velocity target is

 $v_{\mathrm{cfg}}(z_{t},t,c,\omega)=(\epsilon-x)+\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c,\omega)-v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,\varnothing,\omega)\right).$ 

(7)

When $\omega=1$ , the guidance vanishes and the target reduces to the standard Flow Matching velocity.

Using the MeanFlow identity, the instantaneous velocity implied by the predicted average velocity is

 $V_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)=u_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)+(t-r)\frac{d}{dt}u_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega),$ 

(8)

where the total derivative is computed with a Jacobian-vector product (JVP).
The final pMF objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pMF}}=\mathbb{E}_{x,\epsilon,c,r,t,\omega}\left[\left\|V_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)-v_{\mathrm{cfg}}(z_{t},t,c,\omega)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].$ 

(9)

pMF keeps the network prediction in an $x$ -like space while applying supervision in the MeanFlow velocity space needed for few-step guided generation. With CFG distillation, guided sampling requires only one model evaluation per sampling step, further reducing inference cost.

## 3.2.2 Stylizer Architecture and Training

Architecture.

An overview of the Stylizer is in Figure 1. Our Stylizer is a DiT-based model that follows the overall design of StyleStream 1.0, with two main modifications.
First, we remove the reference mel-spectrogram context used for mel-inpainting in StyleStream 1.0, so target style must be represented entirely by the style embedding.
This makes the style space directly usable for voice design and editing.
Second, because the style embedding is now the only source of target-style information, we replace the original TDNN-based style encoder [31] with a stronger perceiver-resampler encoder [28, 2, 38].

The new style encoder first extracts SSL features from a frozen WavLM [7] model11
 1

 https://huggingface.co/microsoft/wavlm-base-plus.
Let the WavLM hidden states be $H\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times L\times D}$ , where $B$ is the batch size, $T$ is the number of frames, $L=12$ is the number of WavLM layers, and $D$ is the hidden dimension.
Instead of reducing $H$ by layer-weighted summation and temporal pooling as in StyleStream 1.0, we concatenate all layer outputs along time to obtain $\tilde{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(TL)\times D}$ .
A perceiver resampler with $N_{q}$ learnable queries compresses $\tilde{H}$ into a fixed-size representation $S\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N_{q}\times D_{q}}$ , through cross-attention to $\tilde{H}$ and self-attention among the queries.
We flatten $S$ and apply an MLP to obtain the style embedding $e_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C}$ , where $C$ is the final style embedding dimension.
The style encoder is trained jointly with the Stylizer under the pMF objective, and we compare it with the StyleStream 1.0 style encoder in Section 5.4.

Training.

We train the Stylizer using the pMF objective introduced in Section 3.2.1.
Here, $x$ is the target mel-spectrogram, $z_{t}=(1-t)x+t\epsilon$ , and the condition is $c=(f_{c},e_{s})$ , where $f_{c}$ is the Destylizer content representation and $e_{s}$ is the style embedding.
During training, $f_{c}$ and $e_{s}$ are extracted from the same utterance. At inference, $e_{s}$ may instead come from a different reference utterance or from the Voice Controller (see Section 3.3).

At the DiT input, we concatenate $z_{t}$ , $f_{c}$ , and a past-output channel along the channel dimension.
This past-output channel is zero during offline pretraining and is filled with generated history during autoregressive fine-tuning (Section 3.2.3).
The flow times $r$ and $t$ , style embedding $e_{s}$ , and guidance scale $\omega$ are embedded as vectors, summed, and injected into the DiT through adaLN-zero [49].
The model predicts an $x$ -like mel estimate, which is converted into the average velocity $u_{\theta}(z_{t},r,t,c,\omega)$ by Eq. (5) and the implied instantaneous velocity $V_{\theta}$ by Eq. (8).

For CFG distillation, we randomly sample the guidance scale $\omega$ and replace $c=(f_{c},e_{s})$ with null condition $\varnothing$ with probability $p_{\mathrm{drop}}$ .
When constructing the CFG target velocity, we stop gradients on $v_{\mathrm{cfg}}$ (Eq. (7)), so the model is updated only through the predicted compound velocity $V_{\theta}$ .
At inference, we provide the desired $\omega$ directly and require only one model evaluation per sampling step.
Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

## 3.2.3 Autoregressive Fine-Tuning

Figure 1: Left: Stylizer architecture. $[r,t]$ is the MeanFlow interval, $\omega$ is the CFG strength. Right: Voice Controller architecture. When used for voice design, the auxiliary input is null $\varnothing$ ; for voice editing, source style embedding is also part of the input.

conclusion: We introduced StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC system. By combining a few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer with autoregressive fine-tuning, it reduces streaming latency while preserving holistic style conversion quality. A unified text-conditioned controller further enables natural-language voice design and single-attribute voice editing in the same style-embedding space. Across reference-conditioned VSC, voice design, and editing, StyleStream 2.0 improves target-style fidelity while remaining competitive in intelligibility and preservation.

title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Abstract.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers.
Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times.
The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits.
Here we address the second limitation.
We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between $75\times$ and $724\times$ faster than the reference implementation), and scales to $200{,}000$ independent learning households.
We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month.
We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Keywords: 
multi-agent reinforcement learning, JAX, heterogeneous macroeconomics, Krusell–Smith model, GPU-accelerated simulation

††footnotetext: The views expressed in this paper are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of Banca d’Italia.††footnotetext: This paper has been accepted at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF’26), Milan, Italy, https://icaif2026.org/.

## 1. Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto, 1998) and multi-agent RL (MARL) (Albrecht et al., 2024) have gradually become the basis of a new modelling paradigm for simulating the behaviour of agents in economics and finance.
In RL, agents learn to maximise their rewards through repeated interaction with the economy they inhabit, so that MARL becomes a principled way of populating a simulated economy with many diverse decision makers, each optimising a reasonable objective.

The adoption of this approach was pioneered in finance, where RL and MARL are now commonly used to represent trading, hedging or market-making agents across a range of markets (Karpe et al., 2020; Ardon et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023; Mascioli et al., 2024; Evans and Ganesh, 2024; Bacaloni et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), or within multi-agent market simulators supported by a growing ecosystem of open-source platforms (Amrouni et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Ardon et al., 2023; Frey et al., 2023).
In macroeconomics and structural macro-financial modelling, adoption has been comparatively slower.
Indeed, in spite of a growing body of specialised research in the field, from stylised economies (Zheng et al., 2022; Cook and Palmer, 2025; Brusatin et al., 2024), to proofs of concept in monetary policy (Chen et al., 2025; Hinterlang and Tänzer, 2021), and tax design (Curry et al., 2023; Mi et al., 2024; Dwarakanath et al., 2024a; Agrawal et al., 2025), the methodology has not entered the toolkit of policymakers and practitioners.

In our view, the reason is twofold.
On the one hand, this is due to scepticism and resistance towards alternative modelling methodologies, from a community that is long accustomed to a specific way of building models based on the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) approach.
This resistance is understandable, as the DSGE approach provides a shared frame of reference that keeps modelling out of the “wilderness of bounded rationality” (Farmer, 2024),
where infinitely many deviations from optimality become available.
On the other hand, this is due to the considerably higher computational cost of training RL or MARL systems, whereas a typical DSGE model can be specified and solved in seconds.
A shared framework and fast solvers, in turn, make these models practical to use, and explain the remarkable success of specialised modelling software such as Dynare (Adjemian et al., 2011; Villemot, 2011).

The first limitation of MARL approaches has been convincingly addressed in a recently introduced framework, the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC) (Gabriele et al., 2026).
MARL-BC places deep RL households inside a real business cycle (RBC) economy, so that the MARL system reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits, recovering the representative-agent RBC and the mean-field Krusell–Smith economy.
Hence, MARL-BC extends the classic models rather than replacing them, and it does so in a way that can be checked against results the profession already trusts.
However, MARL-BC does not address the second limitation we mentioned, since training requires multiple hours per run (Gabriele et al., 2026).

In this work, we leverage JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018), a library for just-in-time compilation of numerical code to hardware accelerators, to reduce MARL-BC training time from hours to seconds, thereby addressing the second adoption bottleneck described above, and fostering a wider usage of the methodology by economists and practitioners.
JAX has often been proposed as a viable way to lower RL training times by allowing environment, policy and optimiser to live inside a single compiled program directly on the accelerator (Lu et al., 2022; Rutherford et al., 2024; Pretorius et al., 2021).
The financial community has already extensively explored this route, with the JAX-LOB simulator for limit order book RL trading agents (Frey et al., 2023), and the JaxMARL-HFT simulator extending it to large-scale multi-agent high-frequency trading (Mohl et al., 2025).
EconoJax (Ponse et al., 2024) applies the same strategy to a stylised economic simulation, but no equivalent exists for structural MARL-driven macroeconomic modelling, a gap this paper fills.

More specifically, our contributions are as follows:

• 

We propose JaxMARL-BC, an end-to-end JAX simulator which trains MARL-BC economies in seconds rather than hours, and scales easily to hundreds of thousands of independent learning agents.

• 

We verify the correctness of our simulator against the known DSGE limits of the MARL-BC, reproducing the results at ten times the population size and at a small fraction of the cost.

• 

We extensively measure the scalability to large populations of agents and to large numbers of parallel environments, which we characterise via a simple cost law that we verify empirically.

• 

We showcase the capability of the simulator by performing a realistic calibration exercise of a large model with heterogeneous returns on capital, with $110$ training runs sweeping different degrees of ex-ante heterogeneity in a two-hour computation that would have previously taken over a month.

We release JaxMARL-BC as open source11
 1

 https://github.com/danmonuni/jax-marl-bc., together with a prototype LLM-augmented dashboard that turns natural-language requests into simulation configurations, so that non-technical users can experiment without touching the command line.
Removing the computational barrier to MARL in macroeconomics can let the methodology spread beyond toy demonstrations and become common practice for structural macro and macro-financial modelling.

We structure the rest of this work as follows.
In Sec. 2 we review related work.
In Sec. 3 we describe the JaxMARL-BC simulator.
In Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 we report the experimental setup and the results of our experiments.
Finally, in Sec. 6 we conclude.

## 2. Related work

Training RL and MARL systems typically requires substantial time and computational resources, which can limit their adoption.
The creation of simulation environments in JAX has therefore become an active line of work.
The design pattern was popularised for single-agent RL by PureJaxRL (Lu et al., 2022) and is now packaged in multi-agent libraries such as JaxMARL (Rutherford et al., 2024) and Mava (Pretorius et al., 2021), which report speedups of one to four orders of magnitude over comparable CPU runs.
Among application domains, finance has been the most active adopter of this pattern.
JAX-LOB (Frey et al., 2023) was the first GPU-accelerated limit order book simulator, processing thousands of books in parallel and delivering at least a $7\times$ speedup over comparable CPU implementations.
JaxMARL-HFT (Mohl et al., 2025) builds on JAX-LOB and extends it to a heterogeneous set of agents with distinct observations, actions and rewards, reporting up to a $240\times$ reduction in training time.
EconoJax (Ponse et al., 2024) ports the AI-Economist environment (Zheng et al., 2022) to JAX and trains populations of $100$ agents in fifteen minutes, down from the several days required by the original implementation.
JaxMARL-BC follows the same design philosophy, but targets a
domain none of these packages cover, namely structural heterogeneous macroeconomic modelling.
Our work is also close to the ABIDES-Economist (Dwarakanath et al., 2024b), which populates agent-based economies with RL agents, but which is not implemented in JAX and does not specifically target established macroeconomic benchmarks.

A different line of work uses deep learning, without RL, to solve heterogeneous-agent models (Maliar et al., 2021; Azinovic et al., 2022; Han et al., 2026), and certain fast conventional methods, such as the sequence-space Jacobian (Auclert et al., 2021), can also be used for the same task.
JaxMARL-BC does not aim to compete with these methods on the classes of models they already solve well.
Rather, it aims to facilitate the growth and adoption of a new modelling paradigm based on independent learning agents, which these methods do not represent.

## 3. The JaxMARL-BC simulator

We describe JaxMARL-BC in two parts.
In the first part (Sec. 3.1) we provide an overview of the MARL-BC model that forms the basis of the simulator, and in the second part (Sec. 3.2) we describe the architectural choices that allow for drastically lower training time, and we outline a simple cost model for training time.
Finally, in Sec. 3.3 we briefly describe the LLM-augmented dashboard which allows non-technical users to experiment with the simulator.

## 3.1. The underlying model

The underlying model is based on the MARL-BC economy of (Gabriele et al., 2026).

One period.
Household $i$ enters period $t$ with capital $k^{i}_{t}$ , a labour endowment $\ell^{i}_{t}$ , and fixed productivities of capital $\kappa^{i}$ and of labour $\lambda^{i}$ .
Effective aggregates are productivity-weighted population means,

(1)

 $K_{t}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa^{i}k^{i}_{t},\qquad L_{t}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{i}\ell^{i}_{t},$ 

which are turned into output through a Cobb–Douglas function

(2)

 $Y_{t}=A_{t}K_{t}^{\alpha}L_{t}^{1-\alpha},$ 

with capital elasticity $\alpha$ and aggregate technology $A_{t}$ .
The returns on capital and wages of the households depend on their productivity of capital and labour via

(3)

 $r^{i}_{t}=\alpha\frac{Y_{t}}{K_{t}}\kappa^{i},\qquad w^{i}_{t}=(1-\alpha)\frac{Y_{t}}{L_{t}}\lambda^{i},$ 

and the cash-on-hand at time $t$ is given by

(4)

 $a^{i}_{t}=w^{i}_{t}\ell^{i}_{t}+r^{i}_{t}k^{i}_{t}+(1-\delta)k^{i}_{t},$ 

where $\delta$ is the capital depreciation rate.

The household’s problem.
The households choose their consumption fraction $\hat{c}^{i}_{t}$ , from which consumption and next-period capital follow as

(5)

 $c^{i}_{t}=\hat{c}^{i}_{t}\,a^{i}_{t},\qquad k^{i}_{t+1}=(1-\hat{c}^{i}_{t})\,a^{i}_{t}.$ 

The households can also choose next-period labour endowment $\ell^{i}_{t+1}$ .
Consumption and labour enter the reward as

(6)

 $R^{i}_{t}=\log c^{i}_{t}+b\log\!\left(1-\ell^{i}_{t}\right),$ 

where the weight $b\geq 0$ prices leisure relative to consumption.
Each household thus learns a policy that maps its own observations to an action $(\hat{c}^{i}_{t},\ell^{i}_{t+1})$ in order to maximise $\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\beta^{t}R^{i}_{t}]$ , where $\beta$ is the household’s discount factor.

Learning.
Households are trained by deep RL, and specifically by Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017).
PPO is a standard algorithm for RL, and also for MARL where typically, as in our case, all agents are treated as independent learners in the same environment (De Witt et al., 2020).
With $n>1$ learners in one economy, the transitions and rewards any household observes depend on what the others are currently doing, so each faces a non-stationary problem and the single-agent convergence guarantees no longer apply (Albrecht et al., 2024).
For symmetric agents, a standard remedy is parameter sharing, in which a single policy network serves the entire population and is evaluated on each agent’s private observations.
This stabilises training without forcing identical behaviour, since household characteristics enter through the observation (Yu et al., 2022).
MARL-BC interprets this configuration as a stylised form of “social learning” (Whalen et al., 2018; Ndousse et al., 2021), and we adopt the same approach here.

Known limits of the model.
The MARL-BC paper shows that the model reproduces standard DSGE models in two limit cases.
Specifically, with a single agent ( $n=1$ ), individual and aggregate quantities coincide and the framework reduces to the textbook representative-agent RBC, while with many ex-ante identical agents ( $n\gg 1$ and $\kappa^{i}=\lambda^{i}=1\;\forall i$ ), the framework reproduces the well-known mean-field Krusell–Smith model.
These two limits make the present work easily testable, since the target behaviour is known from a well-established literature, and they also address the first of the adoption obstacles discussed in the introduction, by anchoring the framework to model classes widely recognised by the community.

## 3.2. The JAX speedup

We now describe the JAX design that enables the speedup of our simulator.
The left panel of Figure 1 shows the three axes upon which a single rollout of the simulator is parallelised and executed.
These axes differ in the kind of dependence that holds among their elements, and each kind calls for a different JAX construct.
Along the first axis are the $n$ households of one economy, which are not independent of one another, as they are coupled through the aggregates of Eq. (1) that determine the prices they all face.
The agent axis is therefore a reduction axis, and we represent it as a plain array dimension so that $n=10$ and $n=10{,}000$ execute the very same program, only on wider arrays.
By contrast, the second axis represents $E$ copies of the economy, which are fully independent of one another.
This is the kind of parallelism jax.vmap is designed for, as it takes a function written for a
single instance and lifts it to a batch of independent ones.
Here, a single jax.vmap over the environment’s ‘reset’ and ‘step’ functions produces the $E$ parallel economies.
The policy forward pass flattens these two axes into one batch dimension, so the policy network only ever sees their product, the batch width $W=E\times n$ .
The third axis, the $T$ periods of a rollout, is instead irreducibly sequential and is carried by a lax.scan.
All of these computations happen inside one jit boundary, enclosing the optimiser, the environment reset and every update.

The computational design just described suggests a simple model of run time, which we will later use to organise and understand our measurements.
To write it down, we first define the sequential depth $D$ as the number of irreducible stages that must run one after another.
In practice, these are the environment periods and the gradient steps, since period $t+1$ depends on period $t$ and gradient step $j+1$ depends on step $j$ .
Two hardware-related properties also need to be defined.
The latency $\tau$ is the fixed overhead of launching a one-stage computation, and hence it does not depend on the width $W$ , while the effective maximum throughput $P$ is the number of agent-transitions per second the device can sustain once it is fully occupied.
Given these definitions, we can model the total training time $T_{\mathrm{train}}$ as

(7)

 $T_{\mathrm{train}}\;\approx\;D\left(\tau+\frac{W}{P}\right),$ 

since a training run performs $D$ stages, and each stage costs a fixed $\tau$ for launching the batch computation and then roughly $W/P$ for performing it.
The above equation clearly identifies two regimes meeting at $W\approx\tau P$ , i.e. the batch width whose execution costs roughly as much as one launch overhead.
For $W\ll\tau P$ the fixed cost $D\tau$ dominates and enlarging the batch width is close to free, while for $W\gg\tau P$ the cost becomes linear in $W$ with slope $D/P$ .
In practice, stages are of two kinds, rollout periods and gradient steps, each with different overheads
conclusion:
We presented JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator for MARL-driven macroeconomic modelling.
Training a MARL-BC economy takes tens of seconds rather than hours, and populations of $2\times 10^{5}$ independent learning households come within reach of a single run, a regime never touched previously.
Speedups of this size change what can be attempted, as large-scale runs and parameter calibration can become an integral part of model development.

Several directions follow naturally.
Wider model coverage is the most immediate extension.
The RBC and Krusell–Smith economies studied here are natural entry points, but the same machinery should accommodate Huggett economies, New Keynesian economies and their heterogeneous-agent (HANK) versions.
At the same time, the rational-expectations counterpart of the economies studied here remains within reach of classical solution methods, and it will be important to address economies with richer heterogeneity and with less stringent rational expectations or general equilibrium assumptions, where classical methods cannot be used.
On the algorithmic side, while PPO was adequate for everything we ran, richer environments may benefit from advanced off-policy learners such as SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018).
A JAX simulator is also largely differentiable end-to-end, so gradients with respect to structural parameters come for free.
These could make gradient-based calibration available in place of grid search, in the spirit of recent work on differentiable agent-based models (Dyer et al., 2023; Quera-Bofarull et al., 2025), and also pave the way for the development of targeted gradient-based RL solvers.

JaxMARL-BC is released as open source, together with an LLM-augmented dashboard.
The framework is anchored to model classes the profession already trusts, and it is fast enough to quickly iterate on model specifications.
We expect these two properties to facilitate the transition of MARL from proof-of-concept demonstration to standard practice in macroeconomic modelling.

title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

body_start:
Abstract

LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and
training.11
 1

 The authors used large language model tools for manuscript editing
and software implementation. The authors reviewed and take responsibility for all text, code,
analyses, claims, and citations. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to
changes affecting its
scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs
with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine
human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe
ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and
pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce Sane, an agent-based framework
that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent
instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline
first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and
expected score relations for each. Sane also defines a scorer-independent
validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe
agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its
expected relation. Because Sane generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of
aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, Sane produces 3.7 times as many
validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (Jrh) at comparable end-to-end validity
and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain,
including professionalism and toxicity, where Jrh detects none.
On faithfulness, Sane achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11
judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman $\rho=0.852$ ), while
Jrh does not ( $\rho=0.100$ ).

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: End-to-end comparison of native test-case generation and validation
pipelines. Both SANE and JRH receive a scorer definition, implementation, and
representative examples. Sane begins with a fixed set of behavioral
requirements. It identifies capabilities per scorer, derives recipes per capability, then
generates cases per recipe. Both harnesses instantiate cases and apply LLM validation. Sane separates
recipe alignment from case realization and expected-relation applicability before assembling
the validated test suite. Jrh uses a validator LLM with retries.
Automating capability identification and recipe ideation makes Sane’s aligned recipe
inventory adapt to new
scorers. Dashed boxes mark automated operations.
Figure 3 defines the oracle decisions and validity accounting.

LLM judges now assign benchmark scores, curate supervised fine-tuning data, provide preference and
reward signals for post-training, and inform deployment gates for models and prompts
(Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024). Their decisions are useful only when a scoring
implementation measures its stated criterion reliably. Agreement with human annotations on a
held-out benchmark provides important evidence, but an aggregate agreement score does not
characterize how a judge responds to input variations that should preserve or alter that criterion.
Behavioral testing applies controlled changes to characterize these responses before comparable
input variation occurs in deployment.

Behavioral testing evaluates whether a model satisfies focused, task-relevant
behavioral properties rather than only summarizing its average performance on held-out data. It
treats the model as a black box and evaluates its responses to targeted examples and controlled
input changes. These tests primarily
use two categories: minimum functionality tests, and metamorphic tests with invariance or
directional expectations. Minimum functionality tests evaluate
individual capabilities on targeted examples.
Invariance and directional tests state whether outputs should remain unchanged or move in an
expected direction after controlled input transformations (Ribeiro et al., 2020).
In a reference-free setting, metamorphic
testing specifies the relation that should hold between scorer outputs before and after a controlled
input transformation (Chen et al., 1998; Segura et al., 2016).

Many metamorphic testing methods begin from fixed, human-authored recipes, which constrain
the available perturbations and the scoring criteria to which they apply.
CheckList established a fixed, reusable testing inventory for
NLP (Ribeiro et al., 2020). Humans

specify capabilities and tests, then use the framework’s

templates, lexicons, and perturbations to generate concrete test cases. FBI adapts this approach to evaluator
LLMs. Doddapaneni et al. (2024) generate
perturbations for 22 human-designed categories and manually validate every generated perturbation,
producing a 2,400-case benchmark. Jrh instead provides an open-source harness that automatically
generates and executes judge-reliability tests from a
fixed, human-authored recipe library, with optional human review
(Dev et al., 2026). Across these systems, automation begins only after
humans define the testing inventory. Jrh, the closest prior system, draws from fixed tests for label
changes, formatting, paraphrase, verbosity, repeatability, and ordinal calibration.

A fixed recipe library works when each selected transformation has the same interpretation for
every scorer to which it is applied. This condition does not hold in general. Formatting changes may
be irrelevant to a faithfulness scorer but directly relevant to a professionalism scorer. Adding
relevant detail should reduce a concision score, but increase a coverage score when the detail
supplies missing salient information. A generic verbosity recipe cannot assign one expected relation
to both. The required perturbation and score relation therefore depend on the scorer specification,
its output contract, and the data being evaluated.

We introduce Sane, a reference-free agent-based framework that automates capability
identification, scorer-specific recipe ideation, test-case generation, and validation.

Sane organizes testing around six fixed behavioral requirements: monotonicity, subadditivity,
repeatability, robustness, dynamic range, and calibration. It encodes these requirements as reusable
agent instructions. The requirements remain fixed across scorers, while the capabilities,
perturbations, and expected relations that operationalize them depend on scorer intent. For each
scorer, the agent reads the specification, implementation, and representative inputs, identifies
capabilities pertinent to the scoring criterion, and ideates recipes and expected relations for each
capability. Sane next instantiates test cases for each recipe and validates the complete
progression from design to execution: whether the recipe agrees with scorer intent, whether the
generated text realizes the requested perturbation, and whether the expected relation applies to the
realized instance. Behavioral testing and metamorphic testing are well-explored foundations of
Sane. We do not claim novelty in their behavioral requirements or relation types. Our
contribution replaces human-authored recipe design with an agent that
determines how general behavioral requirements apply
to each scorer and derives the corresponding perturbations and expected relations to target its
specific scoring domain. Since our
framework makes no assumptions about scorer type, the same procedure could be applied to multi-agent evaluators
and statistical metrics in addition to single-model LLM judges; we do not evaluate these
scorer types here.

We compare Sane against Jrh, a recent open-source harness
for judge reliability and the most directly comparable prior system (Dev et al., 2026), across
faithfulness, fluency, coherence, professionalism, and toxicity.
Figure 1 compares the two harness architectures and their
automation boundaries. Both methods use Claude Opus 5 and the same balanced 1,200-example
generation dataset, composed of 300 examples each from AggreFact-CNN, AggreFact-XSum,
TofuEval-MediaS, and TofuEval-MeetB.
To isolate the fully automated pipelines, neither method uses human review during generation. We
pass every generated recipe and test case to automated validation without manual editing, rejection,
or selection. Sane identifies each scorer’s capabilities and uses the six requirements
to derive scorer-specific perturbations and expected relations. Its aligned recipe
inventory therefore expands with the scorer set. Jrh continues to draw from its fixed human-authored
library. Across five domains, Sane accumulates 108 unique aligned recipes, while Jrh yields
seven. After test-case validation, Sane produces 3.7 times as many validated test families and
detects scorer
deficiencies in all five domains,
including professionalism and toxicity, where Jrh fails to detect
any under the evaluated configuration.

We make four contributions. First, we automate the scorer-specific reasoning required
to translate fixed general behavioral requirements into capabilities, perturbations, and expected
relations. This design expands the aligned recipe inventory as scorers are added. Second, we define a
formal, scorer-independent validation framework that separates recipe alignment, perturbation
realization, and instance-level relation applicability. Third, we show that Sane detects scorer deficiencies
with tests adapted to faithfulness, fluency, coherence, professionalism, and toxicity, including
scorer-dependent expected relations that Jrh’s fixed recipes did not express. Fourth, we evaluate
human alignment at the judge-ranking level and find that
Sane’s faithfulness test suite ranks 11 judge
models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance. Model-level rank concordance is
the relevant unit because we evaluate LLM judges themselves, not individual model outputs.

## 2 Related work

## Behavioral testing in NLP and LLMs.

Behavioral testing evaluates focused, task-relevant properties through targeted examples
and controlled input changes rather than relying only on aggregate held-out performance.
CheckList adapted this approach to NLP through a fixed, human-authored matrix of linguistic capabilities and three test
types: minimum functionality, invariance, and directional expectation
(Ribeiro et al., 2020). AdaTest later used language models to propose tests within a
user-guided topic tree. Users select valid suggestions and organize the tree to direct subsequent
generation (Ribeiro and Lundberg, 2022). Recent systems automate more aspects of test-case
construction. Ferrando et al. (2023) generate source sentences and candidate
translations for predefined machine-translation capabilities. SynthEval uses controlled language-model
generation to find difficult cases, after which experts identify recurring failures and manually
design test templates (Zhao et al., 2024). These methods reduce the cost of
instantiating and expanding tests, but retain human selection of capabilities, topics, or templates.
SANE automates the preceding scorer-specific decisions: it identifies pertinent capabilities and
derives recipes from the scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs.

## Metamorphic testing and automated relation design.

Metamorphic testing addresses the oracle problem by specifying relations that should hold between
source and follow-up executions (Chen et al., 1998; Segura et al., 2016).
Relation identification, input transformation, follow-up generation, and relation checking
are separate parts of this process. LLM-based systems now automate several of them. MR-Adopt
recovers a reusable input transformation from a developer-written test that already contains a
source input, follow-up input, and output assertion (Xu et al., 2024).
Cho et al. (2025) collect 191 relations from prior NLP research and execute 38 of
them across four LLMs, demonstrating the breadth of applicable relations while retaining a curated
relation inventory. Cañizares et al. (2026) propose a domain-independent assistant
that infers new relations and generates follow-up cases, with validation and repair stages, for three
software domains. Their system operationalizes relations within a metamorphic-testing environment
and accepts domain context through a conversational interface. These results establish LLM assistance
for relation inference and follow-up validation outside judge testing. SANE instead defines and
evaluates a judge-specific entry point: given an arbitrary scorer, it derives the capabilities,
recipes, perturbations, and expected score relations required to test that scorer.

## LLM judges as measurement instruments.

LLM judges can agree well with human preferences on summarization, dialogue, and pairwise model
comparison (Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023). Agreement with human annotations does
not, by itself, establish that a judge measures its stated criterion consistently. Measurement
theory separates validity, which concerns whether scores represent the intended construct, from
reliability, which concerns variation under repeated application of the measurement procedure
(Chehbouni et al., 2025). Empirical work confirms that these questions require
separate tests. Lee et al. (2025) measure self-consistency and agreement across
scoring scales, while Rating Roulette measures intra-rater reliability across repeated calls
(Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025). Recent work on contemporary proprietary judges shows that
an overconfidence advisory and single-call self-debate improve the calibration and score-distribution
spread of verbalized confidence (Hsiao, 2026). Thakur et al. (2025) show that percent agreement can conceal
large score differences and report sensitivity to prompt complexity and lenient scoring. This line
of work establishes repeated execution, prompt variation, scale choice, and criterion validity as
distinct properties of a judge as a measurement instrument.

## Behavioral testing of LLM judges.

Judge-specific test suites convert these reliability questions into controlled
evaluations. FBI defines 22 human-designed perturbation categories across factuality, instruction
following, long-form coherence, and reasoning. It generates 2,400 cases and manually validates
every perturbation (Doddapaneni et al., 2024). CALM defines 12 judge biases and automates
principle-guided response modifications for each category (Ye et al., 2025). Jrh generates and validates cases for a fixed suite covering label changes, formatting invariance,
semantic paraphrase, verbosity, stochastic stability, and ordinal calibration
(Dev et al., 2026). It also supports human review before judge execution and is the closest
engineering comparison to SANE. CheckList, FBI, CALM, and JRH
demonstrate the value of targeted tests and automatic perturbation generation. In each system, the
test inventory remains fixed after its authors define the capabilities, test types, bias categories,
or recipes.

SANE automates scorer-specific metamorphic test design. Its reusable behavioral
requirements remain constant. The agent then determines how they apply to each scorer and produces a
new recipe inventory. SANE then separates three validity questions: whether a recipe agrees with
scorer intent, whether a generated case realizes the recipe, and whether the expected relation
applies to that realized case. Our contribution is an agent pipeline that reasons from general behavioral requirements
to derive scorer-specific capabilities, metamorphic recipes, and expected relations, then explicitly
accounts for validity from candidate recipe to validated test family.

## 3 SANE

Given a scorer specification and representative examples, Sane performs two
generation steps, as shown in Figure 1. First, the agent identifies key
capabilities implied by the scorer and derives perturbation
recipes that target them. Each recipe states a perturbation and its expected effect on
scorer outputs. Second, the agent instantiates test cases intended to realize each recipe’s
perturbation. A recipe together with its generated test cases is a
candidate test family. The collection of a scorer’s
candidate test families is its candidate test suite.

Generation alone does not establish that a candidate test family measures its intended
claim. First, the recipe and expected relation must agree with scorer intent. The recipe-alignment
oracle shown in Figure 1 and detailed in
Figure 4(a) predicts this condition, denoted by $A_{r}$ . Second, an
effective test case must realize the recipe from which it was generated, and the expected relation
must apply for the test case. These two conditions, denoted by $Z_{t,r}$ and
 $I_{t,r}$ , are independently predicted by the case-realization oracle in
Figure 1 and detailed in Figure 4(b).
Equations 4–6 formalize the three
decisions. A test case is valid exactly when it is joint-valid, meaning that all three are true,
as formally defined in Section 3.2.

For each aligned recipe, Sane samples $n$ test cases. Depending on computational budget
and feasibility, this may be a partial sample or the full generated set. If a majority of them are
joint-valid, we consider the recipe and the sampled joint-valid cases a
validated test family.
Collecting a scorer’s validated test families yields its
validated test suite. Given this generation
and joint validation, the suite measures whether a scorer behaves reliably on capabilities
specific to its scoring domain.

## 3.1 Scorer-specific test-suite generation

Let scorer $s$ consist of a natural-language specification $p_{s}$ , an implementation and output
contract $c_{s}$ , and representative examples $D_{s}$ . Let $B$ denote the fixed general
behavioral requirements encoded in the harness. Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the agent model

Both harnesses are regenerated with the same model, so the comparison controls for generator
capability. What remains open is whether the absolute generation and realization rates transfer to
weaker agent models. While GPT-5.2 panels validate recipes and test cases at scale, human annotation
would provide an independent estimate of oracle error, which may influence reported
scorer-deficiency counts. Judge-ranking alignment is evaluated for

Extending this analysis requires comparable benchmarks for other scorer criteria.

Future work should test additional generator models and human validation panels. A
retrieval library of validated scorer problems, capabilities, and recipes could reuse successful
designs across related scorer domains while preserving scorer-specific reasoning.
conclusion:
Sane automates scorer-specific metamorphic recipe ideation from general behavioral requirements
and validates both recipes and generated cases before test execution. Across five scorers, this
procedure produces more aligned, validated, and fault-detecting test families than Jrh,
the leading open-source harness for judge reliability. On faithfulness, Sane test-suite scores provide human-aligned differentiation of judge models, supporting automated
scorer-specific testing as a practical method for LLM-judge reliability.

Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone.
