body_start:
Abstract

Online reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks, but modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience. Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone. Building on this observation, we develop RINSE, a practical data filtering method for online RL. Experiments on standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting show that RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance over standard PPO and local attribution baselines. These results suggest that RL-IF provides a practical and principled framework for understanding and improving online RL.

## 1 Introduction

Online reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central paradigm for learning decision-making policies through repeated interaction with an environment, from robotic control (Todorov et al., 2012; Andrychowicz et al., 2020) to the alignment and enhancement of large language models (LLMs) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). Despite this success, modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience: training often requires millions of interactions, while the quality of collected experience can vary substantially across time and trajectories, leading to well-known challenges such as sample inefficiency, high variance, and training instability (Yu, 2018; Henderson et al., 2018; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2019). Hence, understanding the contribution of individual training instances from these experiences is fundamental to data-centric studies of RL and has broad implications for applications such as data selection (Hu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026), experience replay (Schaul et al., 2016), or interpretation (Hu et al., 2025).

Data attribution offers a natural lens for understanding the role of individual training instances. In supervised learning, data attribution aims to identify the training examples that most strongly drive model behavior (Koh and Liang, 2017; Deng et al., 2025), with applications in model debugging (Koh and Liang, 2017), mislabeled data detection (Pruthi et al., 2020), data valuation (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Jia et al., 2019), and data selection (Xia et al., 2024). Recently, Hu et al. (2025) introduce data attribution to online RL, and develop a local attribution framework for PPO. The proposed framework measures the influence of rollout records on a local policy update within a round, and shows that such local scores can identify harmful training time steps and improve sample efficiency through data filtering.

However, the existing attribution methods are not yet principled and capture only a partial notion of data influence in online RL. First, they mainly rely on heuristic influence estimation, such as gradient dot products, which are intuitive and scalable, but do not fully account for the training dynamics or correspond to a clear counterfactual notion of data value (Koh and Liang, 2017). Second, the scope of existing attribution methods is restricted to a single training round, leaving the influence of training data across rounds largely unexplored. Characterizing such inter-round influence is more challenging in online RL because the effect of a single training occurrence can propagate across future rounds through subsequent optimization updates and, in principle, through changes in the policy-induced distribution of future rollout data.

This motivates the development of a framework that directly estimates counterfactual influence beyond the local scope of individual RL training rounds. To address this, we formulate data attribution in online RL through a principled leave-one-out objective defined over multiple training rounds, and use it to study the non-local value of rollout data. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

A non-local attribution framework for online RL (Section 3.1). Prior online-RL attribution methods are local and heuristic; we formulate non-local data attribution in online RL through an RL leave-one-out objective, RL-LOO, defined over the training trajectory.

• 

A first-order estimator with optimization and sampling effects (Section 3.2). We derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator of RL-LOO, and show that online-RL data influence decomposes into optimization effect and sampling effect. This yields both a conceptual lens for understanding long-horizon influence and a computationally efficient approximation, RL-IF-opt, that is well supported by our theory and experiments.

• 

A practical data-selection algorithm with downstream gains (Section 4). Building on an efficient approximation to RL-IF, we develop RINSE, a non-local attribution-based filtering method for online RL. Across standard benchmark environments and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting, RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance relative to standard PPO and local filtering baselines.

## 2 Preliminaries

## 2.1 Background

Online RL algorithms.

We consider an online reinforcement learning (RL) process indexed by rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$ . At round $t$ , the current policy $\pi_{\theta_{t}}$ interacts with the environment to collect a rollout buffer $D_{t}$ , after which the policy is updated for $M$ gradient steps. In this work, we focus on a specific RL algorithm, proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017). Given the state action pair $(s,a)$ , the standard clipped PPO objective maximizes

 $L^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim D_{t}}\Big[\min\big(r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A},\mathrm{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}\big)\Big],\quad r_{t}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\theta_{t}}(a\mid s)}.$ 

(1)

Here, $r_{t}(\theta)$ is the policy ratio, $\hat{A}$ is an advantage estimate, $\pi_{\theta_{t}}$ is the behavior policy used to collect the rollout, and $\epsilon$ is the clipping threshold. Schulman et al. (2017) also introduced an alternative formulation of the PPO objective, in which the clipping mechanism is replaced by KL regularization. Specifically, let $\beta$ be the coefficient of the KL penalty, and the KL-regularized form of PPO maximizes

 $L^{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim D_{t}}\big[r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\big)\big].$ 

Let $P_{t}(\cdot\mid\theta_{t})$ denote the distribution over rollout buffers induced by $\pi_{\theta_{t}}$ , where a rollout buffer $D_{t}$ is the collection of trajectories sampled in round $t$ . Write $D_{t}^{(j)}\subseteq D_{t}$ for the $j$ -th minibatch in round $t$ , and $\theta_{t}^{(j)}$ for the parameter at the $j$ -th gradient step, with $\theta_{t}=\theta_{t}^{(0)}=\theta_{t-1}^{(M)}$ . For simplicity, we assume that the policy is updated with stochastic gradient descent, and each update takes the form:

 $\theta_{t}^{(j)}=\theta_{t}^{(j-1)}-\frac{\eta_{t}}{b}\sum_{x\in D_{t}^{(j)}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{t}^{(j-1)},x),\qquad D_{t}\sim P_{t}(\cdot\mid\theta_{t}),$ 

(2)

where $\eta_{t}$ is the learning rate, $b$ is the minibatch size, and $\ell$ denotes the PPO loss.

Figure 1: Two-fold data influence in RL. A training occurrence $z^{*}\in D_{k}^{(l)}$ affects learning through (i) the optimization path (blue): propagating via parameter updates to $\theta_{T}^{(M)}$ , and (ii) the sampling path (orange): altering future rollout buffers $D_{k+1},D_{k+2},\dots$ . These effects are coupled through the policy-induced data distribution.

Local data attribution in online RL.

Hu et al. (2025) propose a local data attribution framework for online RL, which measures how much a training sample contributes to a downstream target function $f$ . In this setting, the training samples are scored by gradient inner products between the per-sample gradient and gradient on an attribution target $f$ . The local attribution score is estimated as

 $I^{(k,l)}(z^{*};f):=-\eta_{k}\,\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta,z^{*}),\nabla_{\theta}f(\theta)\right\rangle,$ 

(3)

A key design choice is the attribution target $f$ . Hu et al. (2025) propose to leverage a policy-gradient surrogate for downstream return, defined on a reference validation distribution. Given a reference policy $\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}$ and a reference advantage estimator $\hat{A}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ , Hu et al. (2025) define

 $f^{\mathrm{return}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi^{\mathrm{ref}},\,(s,a)\sim\tau}\big[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\,\hat{A}^{\mathrm{ref}}(s,a)\big].$ 

(4)

The target gives the attribution score a direct behavioral interpretation: a positive score means the sample pushes the policy toward higher surrogate return, whereas a negative score suggests that removing the sample may help.

Discrepancy between short-term and long-term influence.

A major limitation of local data attribution is its myopic view of data influence. To illustrate this point, we empirically estimate the data influence11
 1

 We estimate data influence by removing the sample from the training trajectory and measuring the resulting change in the final attribution target, as formally defined in Section 3.1. in LunarLander (Brockman et al., 2016), and track how the influence of the same sample changes as the horizon $H$ grows, where horizon means the number of training rounds over which the sample’s effect is propagated and evaluated. As shown in Figure 2, a good sample that stabilizes the lander may appear harmful from a short-term viewpoint even though it improves downstream behavior and is beneficial in the long run, and vice versa. Systematically, we also observed a bias induced by the local viewpoint. In particular, local attribution tends to overestimate the long-term value of late-episode samples, those from late time steps in an episode.

Figure 2: Left: two LunarLander samples that appear harmful locally but are beneficial in the long run. Right: fraction of late-episode samples labeled harmful vs. attribution horizon $H$ . 

Two-fold data influence in online RL.

In online RL, the influence of a training sample is not limited to its direct effect on a parameter update. A rollout affects learning through two coupled channels, as demonstrated in Figure 1. First, it influences the checkpoint by contributing to the gradient update that produces the next parameter. This is the usual optimization effect of data: removing one sample perturbs the parameter trajectory and therefore the final checkpoint. Second, the same rollout influences future data sampling. Since subsequent rollout buffers are collected by policies obtained from earlier checkpoints, perturbing one training sample changes not only the next iterate but also the state-action distribution from which later data are drawn. This is referred to as the sampling effect: a sample influences future learning by altering the distribution of later data. Hence, in on-policy RL, data influence is inherently two-fold: it acts on both the optimization path and the sampling path. Moreover, the two effects are generally entangled rather than separable: a perturbation to one sample changes the data distribution of future rollouts, and this distributional shift in turn alters the subsequent optimization trajectory.

## 3 Measuring Data Influence in Online RL

In this section, we systematically formulate and approximate data influence in online reinforcement learning. We first introduce a leave-one-out counterfactual objective, RL-LOO, which measures the long-term effect of removing a training occurrence. Then, we derive a first-order influence estimator, RL-IF, that approximates this counterfactual without retraining by propagating perturbations through the training trajectory. The resulting recursion naturally decomposes data influence into the aforementioned optimization effect and sampling effect, and admits theoretical guarantees under suitable smoothness assumptions. Finally, we analyze both the effectiveness of RL-IF and the relative contributions of these two effects through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation.

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

Following prior work, we study data attribution in an online PPO-style training pipeline, and extend it beyond individual RL training rounds. Let $\theta_{T}^{(M)}$ denote the final policy parameter after all rounds of training. Our goal is to systematically measure how one training sample would affect a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place.

We formalize this through a leave-one-out (LOO) (Koh and Liang, 2017) counterfactual specific to RL, or RL-LOO, following a similar setup in supervised learning literature (Hara et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). The unit of attribution is a particular occurrence of a sample in a training minibatch, written as $z^{*}\in D_{k}^{(l)}$ , which specifies both the sample identity and the minibatch in which it is used. Let $\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{(M;-z^{*})}$ denote the final parameter obtained by removing this occurrence from the training trajectory and replaying the remaining optimization process, including the induced changes in future sampling. For a downstream target function $f$ , RL-LOO is defined as

 $\mathrm{RL}\text{-}\mathrm{LOO}^{(k,l)}(z^{*};f):=f(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{(M;-z^{*})})-f(\theta_{T}^{(M)}).$ 

This quantity measures the effect of removing one training occurrence on a downstream target after subsequent training. As for the attribution target, we adopt the negative of the target defined in (4), so that negative scores identify occurrences whose removal improves the surrogate objective. In the non-local setting, the reference policy is naturally chosen as the final policy $\pi_{\theta_{T}}^{(M)}$ , so that the target measures how removing one training occurrence changes the surrogate return of the final policy on its own induced distribution. $\hat{A}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ can be approximated using the corresponding critic and the same GAE procedure and hyperparameters as PPO. When exact advantages are used, we show that RL-LOO with this target serves as a local proxy for the change in final expected return in Appendix A.4.

## 3.2 Approximating Leave-One-Out in RL

We now derive a first-order estimator, RL-IF (RL InFluence), for approximating RL-LOO. At a high level, RL-LOO asks how the final policy would change if a training sample were removed from a rollout-based training trajectory. Rather than explicitly retraining the policy, RL-IF approximates this counterfactual effect through first-order perturbation analysis.

Consider the RL training process in (2). Let $z^{*}\in D_{k}^{(l)}$ be a sample removed from update $(k,l)$ , and let $\theta_{t}^{(j)}(\varepsilon)$ denote the perturbed training trajectory obtained by continuously downweighting $z^{*}$ by a scalar $\varepsilon$ . A first-order Taylor expansion gives

 $\mathrm{RL}\text{-}\mathrm{LOO}^{(k,l)}(z^{*};f)\approx\nabla_{\theta}f(\theta_{T}^{(M)})^{\top}\Delta_{T}^{(M)},\qquad\Delta_{t}^{(j)}:=\left.\frac{\partial\theta_{t}^{(j)}(\varepsilon)}{\partial\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0},$ 

(5)

which motivates the first-order estimator

 $\mathrm{RL}\text{-}\mathrm{IF}^{(k,l)}(z^{*};f):=\nabla_{\theta}f(\theta_{T}^{(M)})^{\top}\Delta_{T}^{(M)}.$ 

The key step is to characterize the perturbation trajectory $\Delta_{t}^{(j)}$ . In online RL, perturbations propagate through two distinct channels, the optimization effect and the sampling effect, respectively. To unify the effects from both channels, we define the stage update operator

 $F_{t}^{(j)}(\vartheta,\beta):=\vartheta-\frac{\eta_{t}}{b}\sum_{x\sim S_{t}^{(j)}(\beta)}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\vartheta,x),\quad S_{t}^{(j)}(\beta):=\begin{cases}D_{t}^{(j)},&\text{if }t=k\text{ and }j>l,\\
P_{t}(\cdot\mid\beta),&\text{if }t\geq k+1.\end{cases}$ 

(6)

where $\vartheta$ denotes the parameter being updated and $\beta$ denotes the policy parameter controlling data collection. Differentiating the update recursion with respect to $\varepsilon$ yields

 $\Delta_{t}^{(j)}=\frac{\partial F_{t}^{(j)}}{\partial\vartheta}\Delta_{t}^{(j-1)}+\frac{\partial F_{t}^{(j)}}{\partial\beta}\Delta_{t}^{(0)},$ 

where the resulting recursion naturally distinguishes the two channels: the first term associated with the current parameters $\vartheta$ captures the optimization effect, and the second term related to the sampling parameters $\beta$ captures the sampling effect. With further simplification, the resulting first-order perturbation recursion is summarized below.

Proposition 3.1: First-order perturbation recursion for RL-IF

Let $\Delta_{t}^{(j)}$ denote the perturbation induced by downweighting sample $z^{*}\in D_{k}^{(l)}$ . The perturbation is initialized as

 $\Delta_{k}^{(l)}=\frac{\eta_{k}}{b}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{k}^{(l-1)},z^{*}),$ 

and evolves according to

 $\Delta_{t}^{(j)}=\begin{cases}A_{t}^{(j)}\Delta_{t}^{(j-1)},&\text{if }t=k,\ j>l,\\[4.0pt]
A_{t}^{(j)}\Delta_{t}^{(j-1)}+B_{t}^{(j)}\Delta_{t}^{(0)},&\text{if }t\geq k+1,\end{c
limitations:
We study data attribution in online reinforcement learning, where the training data are generated by the evolving policy rather than drawn from a fixed distribution. To capture this setting, we formulate a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, and derive a first-order estimator, RL-IF, that propagates the effect of one training occurrence through both later optimization and future sampling. This yields a counterfactual perspective on data value in online RL that goes beyond local attribution. Empirically, the resulting optimization-only approximation, RL-IF-opt, is already effective enough to support a practical filtering method, RINSE, which improves efficiency and final performance on standard benchmarks and in an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting.

Our work also has several limitations. First, the current development is specialized to PPO-style on-policy training (Schulman et al., 2017) and to a first-order approximation of the leave-one-out trajectory. Extending the framework to other online RL algorithms, including closely related trust-region methods such as TRPO (Schulman et al., 2015) and other settings with substantially different sampling or update structures, remains an important direction. Second, our derivation is based on SGD-style (Amari, 1993) updates, whereas modern deep RL and RLHF pipelines often rely on adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). Although the method works empirically in our Adam-based experiments, a derivation that explicitly accounts for adaptive preconditioning would make the estimator more principled (Deng et al., 2026). Finally, our analysis and experiments suggest that the sampling term is often smaller than the optimization term in the regimes we study, but this need not hold universally; understanding when sampling effects become dominant is an open question.
conclusion:
We study data attribution in online reinforcement learning, where the training data are generated by the evolving policy rather than drawn from a fixed distribution. To capture this setting, we formulate a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, and derive a first-order estimator, RL-IF, that propagates the effect of one training occurrence through both later optimization and future sampling. This yields a counterfactual perspective on data value in online RL that goes beyond local attribution. Empirically, the resulting optimization-only approximation, RL-IF-opt, is already effective enough to support a practical filtering method, RINSE, which improves efficiency and final performance on standard benchmarks and in an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting.

Our work also has several limitations. First, the current development is specialized to PPO-style on-policy training (Schulman et al., 2017) and to a first-order approximation of the leave-one-out trajectory. Extending the framework to other online RL algorithms, including closely related trust-region methods such as TRPO (Schulman et al., 2015) and other settings with substantially different sampling or update structures, remains an important direction. Second, our derivation is based on SGD-style (Amari, 1993) updates, whereas modern deep RL and RLHF pipelines often rely on adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). Although the method works empirically in our Adam-based experiments, a derivation that explicitly accounts for adaptive preconditioning would make the estimator more principled (Deng et al., 2026). Finally, our analysis and experiments suggest that the sampling term is often smaller than the optimization term in the regimes we study, but this need not hold universally; understanding when sampling effects become dominant is an open question.

title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.

body_start:
Abstract

Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^{2}$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.

## I Introduction

Fig. 1: The overall system using weights as memory. An episode is encoded by fitting an INR from a meta-learned initialization $\theta$ ; the weight delta $\Delta$ is the memory and reconstructs the frames. With no frame access, the same $\Delta$ is decoded into the next joint command and a natural-language answer.

Robots that operate over extended horizons must remember what they have observed.
When the information that determines the correct action has already left the field of view, a robot without memory can only guess.
In robotic manipulation, the evidence that resolves such a decision can lie seconds, minutes, or in long-horizon deployments hours in the past, and by then the scene itself may no longer show it: a quantity that accumulated over time, a property visible only before it was occluded, a reference fixed at the outset of the episode.
Feeding the entire observation stream back into the policy is not a general answer, as its cost scales with how long the robot has been running rather than with how much of what it saw actually needs to be remembered.
We consider such settings non-Markovian, as the information needed at time $t$ is distributed across the episode rather than contained in any single frame, a gap that recent benchmarks make explicit [1].
Throughout, memory refers to a persistent representation of information that can be accessed independently of the original input that produced it.

Existing sequence models hold information in one of three places.
The first is transient activations: an LSTM’s hidden state [2] or a transformer’s key-value cache [3] compresses observed history, but the stored information is bound to the current computation, and once the forward pass ends or the context window closes it cannot be queried on its own terms.
The second is explicit external storage, from differentiable memory matrices [4] to retrieval over document collections [5], which decouples storage capacity from model capacity at the cost of memory becoming a record that must be retrieved before reasoning can proceed.
A third and more recent paradigm encodes memory directly into parameters: Titans [6] updates a dedicated memory module’s weights during inference, and GradMem [7] performs test-time gradient descent on learnable memory tokens, both showing that gradient-based optimization at inference time can construct persistent memory for a model.
These methods, however, have been developed primarily for language sequences, and they continually update a single running memory over an incoming stream rather than representing individual experiences as separable memories.

In this work, each robot episode is encoded as its own parameter-space memory: a neural implicit representation (INR) fitted to the episode from a shared meta-learned initialization, whose weights constitute the memory.
A learned projector maps these weights into token embeddings for a language model, which answers natural-language questions about the episode, and the same tokens condition an action decoder that predicts the robot’s next joint command.
No frame is stored, reconstructed, or retrieved at query time.
We evaluate on RoboMME [1], a benchmark of 16 non-Markovian manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory, and show that a memory encoded in this way is legible to a downstream model without frame re-access.
The contributions of this work are:

• 

A formulation of episodic memory for robotics as INR weights, and a tensor-wise projector mapping them into the token space of pre-trained language backbones, yielding, to our knowledge, the first system to answer natural-language questions about a video episode from INR weights alone.

• 

An action decoder of the same weight-tokens that regresses the robot’s optimal next joint command, extending weight-space memory from recall to action.

• 

Matched noise and within-task controls, together with an initialization ablation, attributing both question answering and action decoding to episode content and establishing the shared meta-learned origin as the condition that renders the weights decodable.

## II Related work

## II-A Neural Implicit Networks

A neural implicit representation (INR) is a neural network trained to encode a signal as a continuous function, $f(x)\to y$ , mapping input coordinates directly to signal values rather than storing data on a discrete grid. Once trained, the network can then reconstruct the original signal through forward passes over the learned parameters. SIREN [8] established the basic feasibility of representing perceptual signals this way: its periodic sine activations counteract the spectral bias of ReLU networks, which limits the fine detail they can represent, and yield high-fidelity reconstructions of images, objects, and audio.

Subsequent work extended what fitted parameters can hold.
NeRF [9] extended implicit representations from two dimensions into three, so that scene geometry and appearance could be recovered directly from learned parameters.
LeRF [10] built on this by distilling CLIP and DINO feature embeddings into a NeRF’s weight space, allowing open-vocabulary semantic queries over the encoded scene.

Video, being a substantially larger signal than a static image or scene, makes fitting speed a practical bottleneck for these pixel-wise architectures. NeRV [11] represents video as a function of time $t$ , predicting a full RGB frame from a single temporal coordinate rather than querying spatial locations one at a time, which is considerably faster to fit and reconstruct than pixel-wise INRs [12].

Fitting cost has itself been a target, falling from hours to seconds through alternative parameterizations [13, 14], amortized prediction of weights in a single forward pass [15], or meta-learned initializations that converge in a handful of gradient steps [16], making per-instance fitting practical online rather than offline.
This literature establishes that perceptual detail, geometry, semantics, and temporal evolution can all be stored in INR parameters, but it largely treats fitted weights as a route to reconstruction and compression rather than as representations to be queried in their own right.

## II-B Weight Space Learning

Weight space learning treats the parameters of trained networks as a data modality in their own right [17].
Functa [18] (data as a function) introduced this framing for INRs, treating each fitted function as a data point in a learned representation space, with classifiers trained directly on these resulting modulation vectors generalizing to unseen instances.
This effect depends on all fitted functions sharing a common origin, an observation grounded via the Implicit Function Theorem [19].

A shared initialization is the standard means of supplying such an origin.
MAML [20] learns an initialization from which a few gradient updates produce task-specific parameters, which offers a way to produce fitted weights that remain comparable across instances.
COIN++ [21] applies this combination of shared initialization and fast per-instance fitting to INRs specifically by meta-learning a shared base network and representing each new signal through low-dimensional modulations fitted at inference time.
It is a close precedent for treating adaptation from a common origin as an encoding mechanism.
Gielisse et al. [22] show that meta-learned SIREN initializations combined with a transformer over the resulting weights can outperform permutation-equivariant alternatives on classification.

Once fitted weights sit in a shared coordinate system, standard learning algorithms can exploit that structure directly.
De Luigi et al. [23] show that an encoder trained over fitted INR weights for 3D shapes yields embeddings that support retrieval, clustering, and classification.
Weight-space representations have more recently begun serving as direct inputs to foundation models: LLaNA [24] projects fitted NeRF weights into the embedding space of a large language model, following the training scheme of LLaVA [25], so that the model answers natural-language queries about a 3D scene while conditioning on weights rather than on pixels, image features, or rendered views.

Fig. 2: Overall System Pipeline. (1) Each episode is fitted as an INR from the shared meta-learned initialization $\theta$ , yielding a weight delta $\Delta$ . (2) Each tensor of $\Delta$ is projected independently and pooled into 8 tokens, giving 56 weight-tokens. (3) The tokens condition either the recall head (TinyLlama-1.1B) or the action head (Pythia-400M), with no access to frames.

## II-C Memory in Robotic Manipulation

Robot manipulation systems store interaction history in the same three places identified in Section I: as an external record, in activations, or, far more rarely, in parameters. The first is the most common and takes two forms. Symbolic approaches derive non-differentiable abstractions from the interaction history, tracking object-centric states [26] or appending past actions to the input prompt [27], with recent systems using large vision-language models to write language-based subgoals or memory summaries [28, 29, 30]. Offloading memory and reasoning externally in this way is costly at inference and makes end-to-end optimization difficult. Perceptual approaches instead retain differentiable visual or multimodal features, either appended directly to the model input as context tokens [31] or cached in memory banks for later retrieval [32, 33]. Recurrent approaches compress history into a fixed-size latent state through iterative updates, from recurrent behavior-cloning policies [34] to recent state-space models [35, 36]. Each of these retains observations, derived features, or activation states.

## III Methods

## III-A Task definition

Given a video episode $\epsilon$ consisting of a sequence of frames $x_{1},\dots,x_{T}$ and a natural-language query about the episode, the system produces an output by factorizing this mapping through a weight-space memory representation. Each episode $\epsilon$ is mapped to its own parameter vector $\phi$ and, through the delta defined below, to its own memory representation $\Delta$ .

An episode is first encoded into the parameters of an INR by fitting it to reconstruct the video. Let $\phi$ denote the resulting parameter vector and $\theta$ a shared and task-agnostic initialization common to all episodes. The episode’s memory representation is the delta

 $\Delta=\phi-\theta,$ 

(1)

which isolates the change induced by that specific episode ( $\phi$ ) from the initialization shared across the dataset ( $\theta$ ). A learned projector $f_{\psi}$ maps $\Delta$ into a sequence of token embeddings compatible with a language model $g$ . We consider two ways of querying this representation (see Figure 2). For question answering, given a natural-language question $q$ ,

 $\hat{y}=g(f_{\psi}(\Delta),q),$ 

(2)

where the language model conditions on both the projected weight-tokens and the question. For action decoding, the linguistic decoding of $g$ ’s output is replaced by a regression head $h_{\omega}$ applied to its final hidden state,

 $\hat{a}=h_{\omega}\big(g(f_{\psi}(\Delta),\,q)\big)\approx a\in\mathbb{R}^{d},$ 

(3)

with $q$ given by the episode’s task instruction, $g$ instantiated separately per output head, and $a$ the absolute joint-space command at the point where the episode’s observation ends.

## III-B Dataset generation

All experiments use RoboMME [1], a benchmark of question-answering videos built on the ManiSkill simulator [37] with a 7-DOF Franka Panda arm. Each video shows the arm performing a tabletop manipulation task, and the accompanying questions probe aspects of the episode that no isolated frame can resolve. The 16 task types form four suites, each targeting a distinct form of memory: Counting (temporal), Permanence (spatial), Reference (object), and Imitation (procedural).

Each task type contributes 100 source episodes, giving a base corpus of 1,600 episodes split 70/15/15 into train, validation, and test partitions, with frames rendered at $64\times 64$  px. A single episode does not produce a single INR: for each episode, 10 random truncation points $T_{\text{cut}}$ are drawn from its timeline, and an INR is fit independently to the frames up to $T_{\text{cut}}$ . The label fields are extracted at that last frame, so each source episode supplies multiple temporally distinct memories, for 16,000 fitted INRs per configuration (Figure 3). Four label types are read out at each cut, ordered by increasing dependence on memory: gripper, whether the gripper is closed at the cut frame, resolvable from that frame alone. choice_action is the atomic action being performed. subgoal is a fine-grained sub-step the robot is currently executing, such as picking up a given cube for the third time, and task_goal, the instruction governing the episode, whose instances within a task are near-duplicates differing in a single attribute such as a color or a repetition count.

Every INR is fit from a common initialization $\theta$ , learned via MAML [20], which optimizes $\theta$ so that a small number of gradient steps produces a good per-episode fit on any episode from the training distribution. Per-episode fitting then adapts $\theta$ through 500 steps of full-batch Adam on the reconstruction objective of Section III-C. Because adapted and initialization weights are typically close in magnitude, with the initialization dominating the raw parameter values, we follow [22] in taking the difference $\Delta$ (Eq. 1) as the representation rather than the raw fitted weights, isolating the change induced by the specific episode. Fitting from a shared origin is also what makes deltas comparable across instances, per the shared-coordinate-system arguments of Section II-B.

Fig. 3: RoboMME ground truth at a single frame, illustrated on an example PickXtimes episode. Each frame is paired with the label fields read out when it serves as the cut frame $T_{\text{cut}}$ : the gripper state (gripper), the atomic action in progress (choice_action), the current sub-step (subgoal), the instruction governing the episode (task_goal), and the commanded joint vector (joint_action).

To verify that this construction yields organized weight representations, t-SNE embeddings were computed over the fitted deltas (Figure 4). No suite or task label was used in fitting the INRs or computing the embedding. Under the meta-learned initialization, Permanence and Imitation task-type weights form tight, well-separated clusters, while Counting and Reference weights interleave with one another but remain distinct from the other two suites. Coherent clusters form even for tasks that never appeared in meta-training, which uses only five of the 16 task types. Randomly initialized weights show no visible separation by suite. This is consistent with adaptation from the shared initialization inducing an organized common weight space, and it is the delta that the downstream experiments operate on.

Fig. 4: t-SNE of INR weight space, meta (Flavor 2) versus random initialization (Flavor 1), colored by memory suite. Both embeddings (PCA-100, perplexity 30) use the same 8 tasks, 2 per suite, 100 samples each. Axes are arbitrary.

## III-C System architecture

The system comprises three components, following Figure 2: the INR encoder producing each episode’s delta, the projector mapping the delta into weight-tokens, and two output heads (decoders) over the resulting token sequence.

## III-C1 INR Encoder

Each episode’s INR follows NeRV [11]: a positional encoding lifts the normalized timestep into a high-frequency sinusoidal embedding, a three-layer MLP stem maps it to a spatial feature map, a series of NeRV blocks progressively upsample it through a $3\times 3$ convolution, a PixelShuffle layer [38], and a GELU activation, and a final $1\times 1$ convolution produces the RGB frame (full architectural specifications follow Appendix A.1 of [11]). Each INR is fit by minimizing a weighted combination of $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ reconstruction and structural dissimilarity,

 $\mathcal{L}_{\text{NeRV}}=\lambda\|\hat{x}-x\|_{1}+(1-\lambda)(1-\text{SSIM}(\hat{x},x)),$ 

(4)

with $\lambda=0.7$ : the $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ term encourages pixel-accurate reconstruction, while the SSIM term preserves local structural patterns that $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ alone can blur. During meta-training, the inner-loop learning rate is a per-parameter vector learned jointly with $\theta$ over $K=3$ inner steps, following the MetaSDF formulation of [16].

## III-C2 Weight-Token Projector

conclusion:
Experimental results establish projected INR weight-delta tokens as a queryable episode representation: a language model answers memory-dependent questions from the weight-tokens alone, an action decoder predicts the robot’s next joint command from the same tokens, and meta-learned parameter origins are shown to be necessary for such information to be decodable. The weight delta $\Delta$ thereby functions as a persistent and individually addressable memory object, a property no activation-bound representation offers, and one that complements continually overwritten parametric memories such as Titans [6] wherever individual episodes must remain separable. For robotics, where RoboMME identifies memory as a binding constraint on generalist policies [1], our results suggest memory representations, rather than frame retention alone, as a design axis for vision-language-action systems [42].

There are several limitations. All accuracies rest on two training seeds and a limited corpus of source episodes, so differences of one to three points between adjacent configurations should not be over-read. Scoring a closed candidate set by likelihood establishes discrimination, not free-form generation, and the memory construction is offline, with no external baseline such as a vision-language model given the frames directly. Scaling INR capacity and resolution, evaluating open-ended generation, and moving the INR fit and language model updates online as test-time training in the sense of Titans [6] are delegated to future work.

body_start:
Abstract.

A systematic understanding of the global structure of neural-network loss landscapes remains challenging due to their high dimensionality. Symmetries arising from network architectures and learning objectives provide a way to investigate aspects of this structure. Although a growing number of studies have drawn attention to these symmetries, a systematic characterization of them, as well as of the critical orbits they give rise to, remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this work we establish a topological symmetry index, based on the methodologies from the family of equivariant degree theories, to decode these symmetries. The frameworks apply to arbitrary network architectures and include methods applicable to degenerate critical orbits. The index detects the isotropy of the critical points and quantifies the corresponding net topological contributions. Several examples, including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks, are presented to illustrate the computations.

Keywords:
Symmetries, Topological Index, Equivariant Degree Theory, Neural Network, Loss Landscape.

## 1. Introduction

Symmetries in neural network give rise to a rich variety of phenomena in its high-dimensional loss landscapes. One line of research, developed by Arjevani and Field, studies the spurious minima and their symmetries in shallow networks, as well as their bifurcations as network width $k$ varies. For two-layer ReLU networks in a specific teacher–student setting, they observed in [3] that critical points obtained by SGD have symmetries conjugate to maximal subgroups of $S_{k}$ of intransitive type. In [6], they analytically constructed these families of critical points and expressed them as convergent power series in $k^{-1/2}.$ The corresponding Hessian spectra were further analyzed in [4]. They further extended analogous results to symmetric tensor decomposition in [1], and studied the optimization landscape of networks with polynomial activations [2]. In [5], they identified width thresholds in a shallow ReLU network at which saddles turn into local minima and rigorously established in [7] that over-parameterization (adding neurons) introduces negative Hessian eigenvalues and thereby turns local minima into saddles. Using equivariant bifurcation theory, they further showed in [8] that the local minima emerge through steady-state bifurcations along the standard representation of $S_{k}$ rather than through spontaneous symmetry breaking of global minima. Correspondingly, Liu [30] studied bifurcations from global minima in leaky ReLU networks of arbitrary width, using the negative-slope parameter as the bifurcation parameter, and obtained unified results on the bifurcating branches and their symmetries.

Beyond the structure of critical points, other work connects network symmetries to the broader geometry of loss landscapes, training dynamics, and optimization. Zhao et al. [39] identified flat low-loss valleys with continuous symmetry-induced critical orbits, and derived initialization-fixed conserved quantities that constrain gradient-flow reachability. In [37], they further studied the connectivity of minima and identified loss barriers along linear mode connectivity. Zamir et al. [36] improved the learning-to-optimize (L2O) framework by enabling the optimizer to select, along group orbits, parameters that are more favorable for subsequent descent prior to local updates. The discovery of the symmetry actions themselves is addressed in [38], which proposes a method for automatically discovering data-dependent symmetries through infinitesimal characterizations of Lie group and expressing loss invariance as differential constraints.

The use of symmetry extends further to network design, where equivariant architectures incorporate prescribed symmetries to improve data efficiency and physical consistency. Kondor and Trivedi [29] established, under appropriate assumptions, the equivalence between compact-group equivariance and generalized convolutional structure. Tensor field networks [33] combine spherical harmonics and Clebsch–Gordan coupling to construct equivariant layers for three-dimensional point clouds, while [28] use tensor products and irreducible decompositions to implement equivariant nonlinearities entirely in Fourier space. [18] developed concentric spherical networks combining intra-sphere graph convolutions with inter-sphere radial convolutions, with equivariance established for the icosahedral rotation group. The e3nn framework [25] provides a unified set of composable operations for constructing $E(3)$ -equivariant architectures. For physical dynamical systems, Wang et al. [34] designed forecasting networks incorporating different physical symmetries, and demonstrated improvements in prediction and generalization. They subsequently introduced relaxed group and steerable convolutions with symmetry regularization to accommodate imperfectly symmetric dynamics [35], and established an approximation-error lower bound for strictly equivariant models applied to non-equivariant targets.

These studies demonstrate the importance of symmetry for understanding loss landscapes and training dynamics, as well as its value for optimizer and network design. However, when it comes to the symmetric structure of the loss landscape, most of the above analyses either focus on a specific network architecture or presuppose a priori knowledge of the critical points. These considerations motivate a complementary question:

Can a unified, computable criterion certify the presence of critical orbits and characterize their symmetries
across different network architectures without explicitly constructing the
critical points?

In this work, we address this question by introducing a topological symmetry index based on the methodology of Equivariant Degree Theory. Under suitable hypotheses, the index provides criteria for the existence of critical orbits with specified symmetries within a prescribed region.

To formulate the problem precisely, let $G$ be a symmetry group inherent in a neural network and acting on its parameter space. The interplay among architectural structure, learning setting, data distribution, activation functions, and loss specification can endow the resulting loss function $\mathscr{L}$ with $G$ -invariance, i.e. $\mathscr{L}(g\cdot\theta)=\mathscr{L}(\theta),g\in G.$ 
When the group action is isometric, this invariance implies the $G$ -equivariance of its gradient:

(1)

 $\nabla\mathscr{L}(g\cdot\theta)=g\cdot\nabla\mathscr{L}(\theta),\;\;g\in G.$ 

We therefore seek the zeros of $\nabla\mathscr{L}$ , which are precisely the critical points of $\mathscr{L}$ . The equivariance allows us to obtain integer-valued topological weights associated with orbit types. We define the symmetry index

(2)

 $\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega)=\Big\{\big((K_{j_{1}}),n_{j_{1}}\big),\big((K_{j_{2}}),n_{j_{2}}\big),\cdots,\big((K_{j_{s}}),n_{j_{s}}\big)\Big\}$ 

by extracting the maximal orbit types among those with nonzero coefficients associated with $\nabla\mathscr{L}$ on $\Omega$ , written as

(3)

 $\mathbf{a}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}n_{j}(K_{j})\in U(G).$ 

Here, $U(G)$ is the Euler ring (see appendix A for definition and properties of Euler ring), and each integer coefficient $n_{j},\;j=1,\cdots,m$ is associated with the conjugacy class $(K_{j}),$ where $K_{j}$ is a subgroup of $G$ . A nonzero coefficient certifies the existence of a critical orbit whose isotropy type is at least $(K_{j}).$ The selected maximal orbit types are denoted by $(K_{j_{1}}),\ldots,(K_{j_{s}})$ . The underlying degree theories and computational methods are introduced in Sections 3 and 4. One is also refered to [11, 13, 12, 17, 16, 22, 24, 23, 21, 32] and the reference therein for more comprehensive details about the constructions of equivariant degrees, as well as their applications [20, 9, 14, 10, 19, 30].

Theorem 1 (Topological symmetry index of a neural-network).

Suppose that the parameter space $V$ is a finite-dimensional orthogonal representation of a compact Lie group $G$ , and that
the loss function $\mathscr{L}$ is twice continuously
differentiable and $G$ -invariant. Let $\Omega\subset V$ be an open bounded and $G$ -invariant parameter subset such that $\nabla\mathscr{L}$ is nonzero on $\partial\Omega$ . Then the symmetry index $\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega)$ defined in (2) is well defined. Moreover, for every

 $\bigl((K_{j_{r}}),n_{j_{r}}\bigr)\in\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega),\;\;r=1,\cdots,s,$ 

there exists $\theta_{*}\in\Omega$ such that

 $\nabla\mathscr{L}(\theta_{*})=0,$ 

and its symmetry is at least $(K_{j_{r}}).$ 

The same conclusion holds when $V$ is replaced by a $G$ -manifold equipped with a $G$ -invariant Riemannian metric (see Section 4).

The subsequent sections are arranged as follows. For the readers convenience, Section 2 collects the notations and definitions used throughout the paper. Given that the loss function in (1) is of gradient type, Sections 3 and 4 present two gradient-related Equivariant Degree methods, together with the algorithms to determine $(K)$ and the corresponding $n_{K}$ . More precisely, in sections 3.1-3.2, one can find construction of gradient degree based on recursive formula and the method of reducing to slice. In section 3.3, we focus on the linear isomorphism in which the ambient space $V$ is an orthogonal $G$ -representation, and the degree is constructed through the basic degree induced by irreducible decomposition of $V.$ On the other hand, Section 4 treats the general setting of a $G$ -manifold $V$ . Without an underlying linear structure, the construction proceeds instead through orbit-type stratification and an inductive summation over the resulting strata. Section 5 then applies the resulting index to several concrete examples: a softplus teacher–student model (Section 5.1), an $O(3)$ -equivariant network (Section 5.2), and a transformer architecture (Section 5.3), using the linear isomorphism method, the slice principle, and the recursive formula, respectively. Appendix B recalls the construction and computational algorithm of the Equivariant Brouwer Degree, since, as the paper unfolds, one may quickly observe that the computation of the gradient-related Equivariant Degree methods ultimately can reduce to their Brouwer counterpart. Moreover, Appendices A and C present the properties of the Euler and Burnside rings, and the definition of amalgamated groups, respectively.

## 2. Some Equivariant Terminology

We first emphasize that the degree theories considered in this work require $G$ to be a compact Lie group. Accordingly, the present analysis does not cover noncompact groups such as the positive scaling symmetries associated with ReLU activation.

To construct the symmetry index $\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega)$ , one must first specify the following several ingredients:

• 

The loss function $\mathscr{L}$ should be $G$ -invariant, with $G$ -equivariant gradient $\nabla\mathscr{L}$ .

• 

The parameter space $V$ and the $G$ action on $V$ must be identified.

• 

A suitable domain $\Omega\subset V$ must be specified:
 $\Omega$ is required to be an open bounded $G$ -invariant subset of $V$ . Most importantly, $\Omega$ must be chosen so that

 $\nabla\mathscr{L}(\theta)\neq 0,\;\;\theta\in\partial\Omega,$ 

a condition on which the equivariant degree theory, and hence our approach, rests.

These constitute the basic ingredients needed for the construction of
 $\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega)$ . Each arises naturally from the construction of equivariant degree, and its significance will become apparent as the
framework is developed below. The resulting $G$ -equivariant gradient degree is an element of the Euler ring $U(G)$ of the form

 $\nabla_{G}\text{-}\deg(\nabla\mathscr{L},\Omega)=n_{1}(K_{1})+n_{2}(K_{2})+\cdots+n_{m}(K_{m}),$ 

from which the symmetry index $\mathcal{I}_{G}(\mathscr{L},\Omega)$ is read off directly. The precise definition of the degree, the term $(K_{j})$ and $n_{j}$ , and the techniques appropriate to the different settings to derive this degree will be developed in detail in Sections 3 and 4.

We next introduce the notation and preliminary
concepts that will be used throughout the work:
Unless
otherwise stated, every subgroup $K\leq G$ is assumed to be closed. Let $V$ be a $G$ -space and let $\theta\in V$ . The following notations will be used throughout:

Notation

Description

 $N(K)$ 

Normalizer of $K$ in $G$ 

 $W(K)=N(K)/K$ 

Weyl group of $K$ 

 $(K)=\{gKg^{-1}:g\in G\}$

 $\Phi(G)=\{(K):K\leq G\}$

 $\Phi_{0}(G)=\{(K)\in\Phi(G):W(K)\text{ finite}\}$

 $G_{\theta}=\{g\in G:g{\theta}={\theta}\}$

 $\Phi(G,V)=\{(K)\in\Phi(G):(K)=(G_{\theta})\text{ for some }\theta\in V\}$

 $\{(G_{\theta}):\theta\in V\}$

Table 1. Notations

An orbit whose isotropy group belongs to the conjugacy class $(K)$ is called a $(K)$ -orbit. The set $\Phi(G)$ is partially ordered by

 $(K)\leq(H)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gKg^{-1}\subseteq H\text{ for some }g\in G.$ 

For classes in $\Phi_{0}(G)$ , let $n(K,H)$ count the conjugates of $H$ that contain $K$ , i.e.

(4)

 $n(K,H):=\left|\left\{H^{\prime}\in(H):K\subseteq H^{\prime}\right\}\right|.$ 

Notice that $W(K)$ acts naturally on $V^{K}$ , and its action on $V_{K}$ is free. Finally, a smooth manifold equipped with a smooth $G$ -action will be called a $G$ -manifold.

We next collect several notions common to the degree constructions in the subsequent sections. For uniformity, we formulate them for a smooth $n$ -dimensional $G$ -manifold, an $n$ -dimensional orthogonal $G$ -representation constitutes a special case.

Equip the smooth $n$ -dimensional $G$ -manifold $V$ with a $G$ -invariant Riemannian metric, and choose a relatively compact invariant open subset $\Omega$ . We write $C_{G}^{2}(V,\mathbb{R})$ for the twice continuously differentiable $G$ -invariant functions on $V$ . For $\varphi\in C_{G}^{2}(V,\mathbb{R})$ , its gradient is an equivariant section of the tangent bundle:

 $\nabla\varphi:V\longrightarrow TV,\qquad\nabla\varphi(\theta)\in T_{\theta}V.$ 

Definition 2 ( $G$ -Equivariant Gradient Admissible Pair).

We call the pair $(\nabla\varphi,\Omega)$ a
 $G$ -equivariant gradient admissible pair if $\nabla\varphi(\theta)\neq 0,\;\theta\in\partial\Omega,$ i.e. $\nabla\varphi$ doesn’t vanish on the boundary of $\Omega.$ 

Denote by $\mathcal{M}_{G}^{\nabla}(V,TV)$ all the admissible pairs in $V$ . Allowing $V$ to range over finite-dimensional smooth $G$ -manifolds, we define

 $\mathcal{M}_{G}^{\nabla}:=\bigcup_{V}\mathcal{M}_{G}^{\nabla}(V,TV).$ 

Definition 3 ( $G$ -Gradient $\Omega$ -Admissible Homotopy).

We call a homotopy $\nabla\Phi:[0,1]\times V\longrightarrow TV$ $G$ -gradient $\Omega$ -admissible if, for every $t\in[0,1]$ ,

 $\nabla\Phi_{t}:=\nabla\Phi(t,\cdot):V\longrightarrow TV$ 

is a $G$ -equivariant gradient vector field and $\nabla\Phi(\theta)\neq 0,\theta\in\partial\Omega.$ 

We now introduce the two algebraic structures in which the equivariant
degrees considered below take their values.

Definition 4 (Euler ring).

The Euler ring of $G$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}$ -module

 $U(G):=\bigoplus_{(K)\in\Phi(G)}\mathbb{Z}(K),$ 

so that each $a\in U(G)$ has a unique representation

 $a=\sum_{(K)\in\Phi(G)}n_{K}(K),\qquad n_{K}\in\mathbb{Z},$ 

with only finitely many $n_{K}$ nonzero. Multiplication on $U(G)$ is defined on generators by

 $(K)*(H):=\sum_{(S)\in\Phi(G)}c_{S}(S),\qquad(K),(H)\in\Phi(G),$ 

where

(5)

 $c_{S}:=\chi_{c}\bigl((G/K\times G/H)_{S}/N(S)\bigr),$ 

and extended bilinearly to all of $U(G)$ . Here $\chi_{c}$ denotes the Euler characteristic with respect to Alexander–Spanier cohomology with compact support.

Definition 5 (Burnside ring).

The Burnside ring of $G$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}$ -module generated by the classes with finite Weyl group,

 $A(G):=\bigoplus_{(K)\in\Phi_{0}(G)}\mathbb{Z}(K),$ 

whose elements are written as

 $b=\sum_{(K)\in\Phi_{0}(G)}n_{K}(K)$ 

with $n_{K}\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Multiplication on $A(G)$ is defined by

 $(K)\cdot(H):=\sum_{(S)\in\Phi_{0}(G)}n_{S}(S),\qquad(K),(H)\in\Phi_{0}(G),$ 

where $n_{S}$ is the number of $(S)$ -orbits in $G/K\times G/H$ , and extended bilinearly to all of $A(G)$ .

Notice that $n_{S}$ can be determined recursively from

(6)

 $n_{S}=\frac{n(S,K)|W(K)|\,n(S,H)|W(H)|-\displaystyle\sum_{(\widetilde{S})>(S)}n_{\widetilde{S}}\,n(S,\widetilde{S})\,|W(\widetilde{S})|}{|W(S)|}.$ 

The two rings are related by the ring homomorphism $\pi_{0}\colon U(G)\to A(G),$ 

(7)

 $\pi_{0}((K))=\begin{cases}(K),&(K)\in\Phi_{0}(G),\\
0,&(K)\notin\Phi_{0}(G).\end{cases}$ 

As will be seen in the subsequent sections, the homomorphism $\pi_{0}$ 
provides the key reduction from the Euler-ring-valued equivariant gradient
degree to its Burnside-ring-valued counterpart, and will play an essential
role in the computation of the corresponding basic degrees. For more details regarding Burnside ring and Euler ring, including some of their properties and corresponding proofs, one is referred to Appendix A.

## 3. Equivariant Gradient Degree on Orthogonal $G$ -representations

Having established the common notations and algebraic framework, we now introduce the equivariant gradient degree, beginning with orthogonal $G$ -representations

body_start:
Abstract: 
One of the main challenges associated with the implementation of an Open RAN User-Centric Cell-Free network is the appropriate formulation of serving clusters. This problem can be effectively solved using a proposed AI Agent, based on a large language model. Simulation results have shown that the proposed solution allows for over a 2-fold increase in the median of the user throughput distribution compared to the state-of-the-art network-centric architecture.

Słowa kluczowe: AI, 6G, architektura zorientowana na użytkownika, Massive MIMO, Duże Modele Językowe

Keywords: AI, 6G, User-Centric Cell-Free Architecture, Massive MIMO, Large Language Models.

## 1. Wstęp

Jedną z kluczowych technik pozwalających znacznie poprawić efektywność widmową sieci mobilnych szóstej generacji (6G) jest zastosowanie tzw. architektury zorientowanej na użytkownika (ang. User-Centric Cell-Free) [2]. W ramach nowej architektury użytkownik może być jednocześnie obsługiwany przez wiele zsynchronizowanych stacji bazowych (nazywanych też często punktami dostępowymi), najczęściej wyposażonych w macierze antenowe M-MIMO (ang. Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output). Nowa architektura pozwala na zmniejszenie dysproporcji w mocy odbieranej w różnych punktach sieci. Jest to szczególnie istotne w przypadku użytkowników znajdujących się w podobnej odległości od kilku stacji bazowych [6]. Ponadto możliwe jest skoordynowane sterowanie wiązką w celu zmniejszenia interferencji. Z punktu widzenia praktycznego wdrożenia architektury zorientowanej na użytkownika duży potencjał ma koncepcja otwartej sieci dostępowej Open RAN (ang. Open Radio Access Network) [7, 4]. Zakłada ona tzw. podział 7.2, pozwalający na rozdzielenie funkcjonalności stacji bazowej na zwirtualizowaną jednostkę O-CU (Open RAN Centralized Unit) odpowiedzialną m.in. za zarządzanie zasobami radiowymi, zwirtualizowaną jednostkę O-DU (Open RAN Distributed Unit), realizującą funkcje warstwy fizycznej wyższego poziomu i warstwy dostępu do łącza, oraz fizyczny O-RU (Open RAN Radio Unit), odpowiedzialny np. za funkcje warstwy fizycznej niższego poziomu i realizujący transmisję radiową. Z perspektywy sieci zorientowanej na użytkownika jedno O-CU i jedno O-DU zaimplementowane w wirtualnym środowisku mogą koordynować transmisję z wielu O-RU, pełniąc funkcję CPU (ang. Central Processing Unit). Dodatkowo koncepcja Open RAN poprzez zastosowanie otwartych interfejsów i jednostki RIC (ang. RAN Intelligent Controller) pozwala na implementację dedykowanych algorytmów optymalizujących sieć, np. z wykorzystaniem metod AI (ang. Artificial Intelligence), w tym agentów AI bazujących na modelach językowych [8].

Ze względu na ograniczone zasoby obliczeniowe po stronie O-CU/O-DU oraz O-RU, jednym z głównych wyzwań związanych z zarządzaniem siecią zorientowaną na użytkownika jest tzw. formowanie klastrów obsługujących [1]. Procedura ta ma na celu określenie zbioru O-RU, które powinny obsługiwać konkretnego użytkownika. Ze względu na dużą liczbę możliwych kombinacji jest to zadanie nietrywialne. Ponadto wykonane niewłaściwie może wręcz pogorszyć wydajność sieci, np. w przypadku gdy zbyt duża liczba O-RU obsługuje użytkownika, część znacząco oddalonych O-RU będzie miała marginalny wpływ na poprawę jego przepływności, "marnując" w ten sposób cenne zasoby radiowe. Z drugiej strony, zbyt mała liczba O-RU nie zapewni wzrostu odbieranej mocy i koordynacji interferencji. Z tej perspektywy rozsądne wydaje się zastosowanie wspomnianych metod AI, ze szczególnym uwzględnieniem modeli językowych, które pozwolą na interakcję ze środowiskiem i interpretację wyników podobną do procesu konfiguracji parametrów sieci dokonywanego przez człowieka, jednak odbywająca się w sposób ciągły i automatyczny.

W tej pracy proponuję Agenta AI zarządzającego siecią Open RAN zorientowaną na użytkownika. W związku z bardzo dużą liczbą możliwych kombinacji przypisania użytkowników do O-RU proponuję podejście hierarchiczne, w którym Agent AI zaimplementowany jako rApp modyfikuje parametry algorytmu formowania klastrów obsługujących zaimplementowanego bezpośrednio w O-CU/O-DU w zależności od lokalizacji użytkowników w sieci. Zaproponowany Agent AI maksymalizuje medianę rozkładu przepływności użytkowników. Dodatkowo w odróżnieniu od metod MAB (ang. Multi-Arm Bandit) wykorzystuje historyczną wiedzę, zmniejszając czas potrzebny na odkrywanie nowych rozwiązań. Zaproponowany Agent AI jest zweryfikowany z użyciem zaawansowanego symulatora sieci zorientowanej na użytkownika wykorzystującego trójwymiarowe śledzenie promieni (ang. Ray-Tracing), przydział zasobów radiowych w czasie-częstotliwości-przestrzeni, schematy modulacji i kodowania MCS (ang. Modulation and Coding Schemes) i prekoder ZF (Zero-Forcing) [5]. W dalszej części tej pracy w rozdziale 2 opisany jest zaproponowany Agent AI. W Rozdziale 3 przedstawione są wyniki, a wnioski są sformułowane w Rozdziale 4.

## 2. Agent AI Zarządzający Siecią Zorientowaną na Użytkownika

Figure 1: Agenta AI zarządzający formowaniem klastrów obsługujących w sieci zorientowanej na użytkownika.

W tej pracy proponuję Agenta AI odpowiedzialnego za formowanie klastrów obsługujących w łączu w dół w sieci Open RAN zorientowanej na użytkownika, jak przedstawiono na Rys. 1. W tej sieci wiele O-RU wyposażonych w macierze M-MIMO jest podłączonych do zwirtualizowanego O-CU/O-DU pełniącego rolę CPU. Poza przydziałem zasobów radiowych oraz koordynacją transmisji do użytkowników z fizycznych jednostek radiowych O-RU, jednym z najistotniejszych zadań O-CU/O-DU jest zestawienie klastrów obsługujących. Wymaga ono odpowiedniej konfiguracji O-RU tworzących ten klaster w celu zapewnienia m.in. wymiany danych użytkownika, synchronizacji transmisji oraz wymiany informacji o współczynnikach kanałów radiowych poszczególnych użytkowników. W szczególności potencjalnym wyzwaniem jest formowanie klastrów obsługujących wymagających koordynacji pomiędzy dwoma O-CU/O-DU, tj. fragmentami sieci obsługiwanymi przez różne CPU. Zanim jednak to nastąpi należy wskazać którzy użytkownicy powinni być obsługiwani przez które O-RU - dokonać formowania klastrów obsługujących. W ramach zaproponowanego schematu zarządzania założono, że O-CU/O-DU posiada wbudowany algorytm formowania klastrów obsługujących o niskiej złożoności tj., odpowiedni do zastosowań wymagających czasu reakcji na poziomie pojedynczych milisekund.
Taki algorytm został zaproponowany w [9]. Klaster obsługujący $k$ -tego użytkownika (oznaczony symbolem $\mathcal{M}_{k}$ ) tworzony jest przez minimalną liczbę O-RU $N_{k}$ , wybranych spośród wszystkich $L$ O-RU (indeksowanych przez zmienną $l$ ), o największej mocy nadawanej do użytkownika $p_{k,l}$ spełniających warunek:

 $\frac{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{M}_{k}}p_{k,l}}{\sum_{l=1}^{\mathrm{L}}p_{k,l}}\geq\Delta,$ 

(1)

gdzie $\Delta$ jest parametrem algorytmu w zakresie od $0$ do $1$ . Wartości $\Delta$ bliskie $0$ odpowiadają architekturze zorientowanej na sieć (jeden użytkownik obsługiwany przez 1 O-RU o największej mocy odbieranej), a wartość $\Delta=1$ oznacza, że użytkownik jest obsługiwany przez wszystkie O-RU w swoim zasięgu. Z tej perspektywy, głównym wyzwaniem jest odpowiednie dobranie parametru $\Delta$ w zależności od aktualnego rozmieszczenia użytkowników w sieci.

W tym celu zaproponowałem Agenta AI, który w związku z relatywnie długim czasem odpowiedzi (rzędu kilku sekund) i dużymi wymaganiami na zasoby obliczeniowe jest zaimplementowany jako rApp w Non-RT RIC (patrz Rys. 1). Interakcja Agenta AI ze środowiskiem bazuje na cyklu uczenia ze wzmocnieniem i wykorzystuje interfejs O1 do pobierania danych o sieci oraz zmiany parametru $\Delta$ , tzn. Agent AI uczy się poprzez interakcję ze środowiskiem, tzn. cyklicznie rozpoznaje stan, wykonuje akcję, korzystając z historycznej wiedzy zapisanej w bazie danych, i obserwuje nagrodę. Poszczególne elementy cyklu zdefiniowane są w sposób następujący:

• 

Stan reprezentowany jest przez macierz pozycji użytkowników wyrażonych jako współrzędne X,Y.

• 

Akcja polega na wyborze przez agenta wartości parametru $\Delta$ z zakresu od 0 do 1.

• 

Nagroda jest zdefiniowana jako mediana rozkładu przepływności użytkowników.

Zaproponowany Agent AI bazuje na modelu językowym, a sposób w jaki wybiera akcję na bazie aktualnego stanu i danych historycznych zdefiniowany jest w sposób tekstowy w ramach tzw.

• 

System Prompt, który określa kontekst sytuacyjny oraz ogólny sposób zachowania Agenta AI. W zaproponowanym przeze mnie system prompt informuję agenta, że jest odpowiedzialny za zarządzanie siecią zorientowaną na użytkownika składającą się z $L$ O-RU. Następnie podaję definicję parametru $\Delta$ tzn. jego zakres i interpretację. W końcu informuję agenta, że będą mu podawane jako dane wejściowe położenia użytkowników (stan) oraz dane historyczne zawierające informację o medianie z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników zaobserwowanej dla danych położeń i parametru $\Delta$ . Na tej podstawie agent powinien zwrócić wartość parametru $\Delta$ (akcję), która zapewni największą wartość mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników (nagrodę).

• 

User Prompt, to bezpośrednie zapytanie kierowane do Agenta AI, zawierające dane wejściowe. Dla zaproponowanego Agenta AI user prompt zawiera informację o aktualnych położeniach użytkowników w sieci (stan), oraz dane historyczne, które pozwalają agentowi wnioskować o tym jaki parametr $\Delta$ (akcję) wybrać w aktualnym stanie na podstawie otrzymanych poprzednio nagród. Ponadto, agent używając danych historycznych może wnioskować o tym jak zachować się w nowym do tej pory nie odwiedzonym stanie, bez konieczności potarzania procesu uczenia niezależnie dla różnych położeń użytkowników: stanów.

## 3. Wyniki Symulacji

Zaproponowany Agent AI zarządzający formowaniem klastrów obsługujących w sieci Open RAN zorientowanej na użytkownika został zbadany za pomocą zaawansowanego symulatora zaproponowanego przez autora w poprzedniej pracy [5]. Symulator modeluje sieć M-MIMO o architekturze zorientowanej na użytkownika i wykorzystującej OFDMA. Zastosowano w nim realistyczny model kanału radiowego oparty na trójwymiarowym śledzeniu promieni firmy Wireless InSite, jak również podział na wiele bloków funkcjonalnych, takich jak: formowanie klastrów obsługujących, dedykowany algorytm przydziału zasobów radiowych, prekoder ZF (ang. Zero-Forcing) działający niezależnie dla każdej jednostki radiowej O-RU i 15 schematów modulacji i kodowania. W ramach jednej jednostki radiowej O-RU, podział mocy w obrębie pojedynczego bloku zasobów odbywa się równo pomiędzy wszystkich użytkowników, którym został on przydzielony w rezultacie multipleksacji przestrzennej. Na potrzeby eksperymentów symulacyjnych zaproponowany Agent AI wykorzystuje model językowy Qwen 3.5-32b zainstalowany na lokalnej stacji roboczej z wykorzystaniem oprogramowania Ollama. Pozostałe parametry przeprowadzonych symulacji zostały zestawione w Tabeli 1.

W eksperymencie symulacyjnym porównałem zaproponowanego Agent AI z architekturą zorientowaną na sieć (oznaczenie 1 O-RU na wykresach), architekturą zorientowaną na użytkownika, gdzie wszystkie O-RU obsługują wszystkich użytkowników (oznaczenie 6 O-RU), oraz wyborem parametru $\Delta$ na bazie algorytmu kontekstowego wielorękiego bandyty (oznaczenie MAB - ang. Multi-Arm Bandit) [3]. Algorytmy zostały porównane dla 5 niezależnych stanów, tzn. niezależnie wylosowanych rozkładów położeń użytkowników. Dodatkowo, w związku z tym, że modele językowe bazują na prawdopodobieństwie i ich odpowiedzi mogą różnić się pomiędzy wywołaniami, dla zaproponowanego Agenta AI wykonałem 10 niezależnych przebiegów symulacyjnych, używając tej samej sekwencji stanów. Wynikowy wykres mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników w czasie przedstawiony jest na Rys. 2. Pierwszą obserwacją jest to, że w rozważanych stanach architektura zorientowana na sieć (1 O-RU) osiąga najniższe wartości mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników w każdym stanie: od około 20 do około 30 Mbit/s. Z drugiej strony, skrajna konfiguracja sieci zorientowanej na użytkownika, gdzie każdy użytkownik jest obsługiwany przez wszystkie O-RU, pozwala tylko nieznacznie poprawić medianę przepływności do zakresu około 35–25 Mbit/s. Znaczący wzrost mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników może być osiągnięty poprzez dobór parametru $\Delta$ pomiędzy 0 a 1. W przypadku MAB dobór parametru $\Delta$ odbywa się niezależnie w obrębie każdego stanu i pozwala osiągnąć wartości mediany z rozkładu przepustowości użytkowników z zakresu od 35 Mbit/s do nawet około 70 Mbit/s w Stanie 2. Z jednej strony, niezależny dobór w każdym stanie pozwala w pojedynczych przypadkach (np. Stan 2 i 3) znaleźć minimalnie lepszą wartość niż proponowany Agent AI; z drugiej strony, wymaga to poświęcenia około 1/3 czasu na sprawdzenie wszystkich wartości parametru $\Delta$ , również takich, które pogarszają medianę przepływności. Wreszcie, widać, że zaproponowany Agent AI wykonuje pełny proces uczenia tylko w Stanie 1, a następnie korzysta z zebranej wiedzy i dokonuje tylko drobnych korekt. W większości stanów średnia mediana przepływności osiągana przez Agenta AI jest podobna do wartości osiąganych przez MAB, jednak odbywa się to (poza Stanem 1) bez konieczności każdorazowego powtarzania procesu uczenia. Oczywiście, w zależności od realizacji mediana rozkładu przepływności użytkowników oscyluje w ramach odchylenia standardowego rzędu kilku Mbit/s.

Figure 2: Mediana przepływności użytkowników w funkcji czasu. Dla Agenta AI uwzględniono średnią i odchylenie standardowe z 10 niezależnych przebiegów symulacyjnych.

Z perspektywy porównania Agenta AI z MAB istotne jest porównanie mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników dla całego eksperymentu symulacyjnego. Takie wyniki przedstawione są na Rys. 3, dodatkowo uwzględniając kwantyle rzędu 10 i 90, reprezentujące odpowiednio przepływność użytkowników mających najgorsze i najlepsze warunki propagacyjne. Za punkt odniesienia przy analizie służy wynik dla architektury zorientowanej na sieć (1 O-RU). Dla architektury zorientowanej na użytkownika, gdzie wszyscy użytkownicy są obsługiwani przez wszystkie O-RU, obserwujemy 1,34-krotny zysk w medianie przepływności oraz 2,35-krotny zysk dla użytkowników charakteryzujących się najgorszymi warunkami propagacyjnymi. Dla tych użytkowników koordynacja interferencji i zwiększenie mocy odbieranej są kluczowe. Niestety, odbywa się to kosztem użytkowników o najlepszych warunkach propagacyjnych, dla których osiągane przepływności to tylko 64% referencyjnych. Może to być spowodowane koniecznością podziału mocy nadawanej na bardzo wielu, często odległych użytkowników. Z drugiej strony wyniki pokazują zalety z dynamicznego dostosowywania parametru $\Delta$ , widoczne zarówno dla zaproponowanego Agenta AI, jak i MAB. W przypadku mediany z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników zaproponowany Agent AI poprawia wynik dla architektury zorientowanej na sieć 2,18 raza, a MAB tylko 1,95: zysk około 12% na korzyść Agenta AI. Wynika to głównie ze zdolności Agenta AI do wnioskowania co do wartości parametru $\Delta$ w Stanach 2, 3, 4, 5 na podstawie szczątkowych danych historycznych, np. ze Stanu 1 bez konieczności przechodzenia każdorazowo niezależnego procesu uczenia, jak to ma miejsce w przypadku MAB. Podobne zależności widoczne są dla użytkowników o najmniej korzystnych warunkach radiowych: Agent AI zapewnia zysk 2,25-krotny, a MAB 2,13-krotny. W końcu dla użytkowników charakteryzujących się najlepszymi warunkami propagacyjnymi Agent AI zapewnia poprawę przepływności o około 20%, w stosunku do MAB zapewniającego tylko około 4%.

Figure 3: Porównanie kwantyli rzędu 10, 50, i 90 z rozkładu przepływności użytkowników z całej symulacji.

## 4. Wnioski

Formowanie klastrów obsługujących jest jednym z kluczowych wyzwań dla sieci 6G zorientowanych na użytkownika. W tej pracy zaproponowałem wykorzystanie do tego celu Agenta AI bazującego na modelu językowym. W odróżnieniu od metod MAB Agent AI może wykorzystywać wnioskowanie zbliżone do ludzkiego na podstawie danych historycznych, co pozwala utrzymywać wysoką medianę rozkładu przepływności użytkowników, dokonując jedynie drobnych korekt dla zmieniających się położeń użytkowników. W rezultacie zaproponowany Agent AI poprawi medianę przepływności użytkowników o około 12% w stosunku do rozwiązania MAB. Jednym z dalszych kierunków rozwoju jest porównanie wyników osiąganych przez zaproponowanego Agenta AI dla różnych modeli językowych, zarówno mniejszych jak i dużych komercyjnych modeli ulokowanych w chmurze np. ChatGPT lub Gemini.

title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
abstract: Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.
