headings: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
Two heads on one frozen backbone.
Warming up the reward head buys speed, not quality.
Choice of data source for the reference pool.
body_start:
Abstract

Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.

Figure 1: Four-step samples from DualHeads. Z-Image-Turbo (Jiang et al., 2026) fine-tuned with DualHeads using the HPSv3 reward (Ma et al., 2025).

## 1 Introduction

Diffusion distillation (Song et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024b; Sauer et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2024) turns powerful diffusion models (Song et al., 2021; Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Lipman et al., 2023) into few-step generators that produce high-quality samples in a handful of network evaluations, bringing applications such as real-time interactive video generation within reach (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025).

Speed alone, however, does not make a sample correct: a distilled student inherits the teacher’s failures, and may still misspell the prompted text, miscount objects, or ignore the requested style. Such failures are readily caught by external evaluators, such as text recognizers, object detectors, or preference models. Using these external evaluators as rewards to post-train a generator is now standard practice for diffusion models (Lee et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Prabhudesai et al., 2024).

Existing methods fall into two families, each typically addressing only one side of this setting. First, reinforcement learning (RL) with black-box rewards has succeeded for multi-step diffusion models, through policy gradients that reinforce high-reward denoising steps (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025) or forward-process objectives (Zheng et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026a; Lee et al., 2026). These, however, rely on what distillation removes: policy gradients
estimate updates from stochastic multi-step rollouts, which become high-variance with only a few steps, and forward-process objectives need a score or velocity field that a distilled generator need not preserve.
Second, methods designed for few-step generators pay for the step constraint elsewhere: they backpropagate through a differentiable reward (Luo, 2025) which may not always be feasible, match the generator to the original multi-step model (the teacher) using its score and a second diffusion model fitted to the generator’s samples (Luo et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a, e.g.,), or adapt multi-step RL specifically to flow-map generators such as consistency models and MeanFlow (Li et al., 2026c; Huang et al., 2026b).
Methods from both families rely on something beyond samples and black-box scores: trajectory likelihoods, a score field, reward gradients, or the teacher’s score.

In practice, however, the only thing any few-step generator is guaranteed to provide is samples. This leads to our central question: given only its own samples, black-box reward evaluations, and examples of high-quality images from a reference model, can we tilt a few-step generator toward higher reward regions while keeping it close to those images?

We show that this can be done with
only one backbone network and two binary classifiers. We begin with the standard reference-regularized RL objective (Levine, 2018),
which maximizes the expected reward while penalizing the reverse KL divergence to the reference distribution to prevent reward hacking. Its optimum is the reference distribution reweighted by the exponentiated reward.
The two terms are, however, hard to optimize directly in our setting, since we treat the reward as a black box and the KL term depends on the density ratio between the generator and the reference. Our key observation is that both can be replaced by quantities learned through classification.

This leads to DualHeads, a simple framework consisting of two identical lightweight heads on a shared frozen diffusion backbone.
A reward head learns which samples are better from their black-box rewards: for multiple generations of the same prompt, rewards are normalized within the group and converted into soft optimality labels.
A reference head distinguishes noised reference images from noised generator predictions.
Both heads are trained with the same binary cross-entropy objective and updated online as the generator updates.
To update the generator, we evaluate the two heads on a noised generator prediction and maximize a weighted sum of their logits. Gradients pass through both heads and a single generator forward pass; the sampled trajectory and the head parameters remain fixed.
The heads are discarded at inference. We note that at the optimum of the reference head, maximizing this weighted sum is equivalent to the reference-regularized objective from above, with the reward-head logit in place of the reward and the ratio of head weights setting the regularization strength.

We evaluate DualHeads at a four-step setup on complementary modern reward functions, including visual text rendering (OCR), compositional generation (GenEval), and human preference (HPS, PickScore, etc.).
Compared with existing methods, DualHeads achieves on-par performance in the few-step regime while preserving generation quality. It raises OCR accuracy from $0.59$ to $0.92$ and GenEval from $0.63$ to $0.90$ over the base model, and gives the best HPSv3 on Z-Image (Fig. 1).

Our contributions are:

• 

We introduce DualHeads, a simple framework that adapts few-step generators from reward evaluations and reference samples alone, using two classifier heads on a frozen backbone.

• 

We show that, with optimal heads, the weighted-logit generator objective is a reverse-KL-regularized reward objective whose temperature is set by the head-weight ratio.

• 

We provide
empirical results with both rule-based and model-based rewards, showing that a four-step student reaches task rewards close to 40-step RL methods while preserving quality.

## 2 Related Work

## Step distillation of diffusion models.

Progressive and consistency distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022; Song et al., 2023) turn a pretrained diffusion model into a few-step generator that covers the sampling trajectory in a small number of large jumps. Latent consistency models (Luo et al., 2023) extend this to text-to-image latent diffusion.
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) (Yin et al., 2024b) instead matches the student’s output distribution to the teacher’s by following the gradient from a score difference, which requires an auxiliary network that tracks the student’s score online. DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a) stabilizes this estimator and adds an adversarial term on real data, and TDM (Luo et al., 2025) extends the matching to every step of the sampling trajectory.
Parallel work relies on adversarial supervision. ADD (Sauer et al., 2024b) distills with a discriminator on pretrained image features, and LADD (Sauer et al., 2024a) moves the discriminator onto frozen features of the teacher diffusion model itself.
DualHeads is built on top of a few-step distilled diffusion model. Our reference head follows LADD’s design of heads on frozen diffusion features.

## Reward optimization of diffusion models.

Methods for optimizing a reward differ mainly in how the reward signal reaches the generator. Differentiable rewards can be backpropagated through directly (Xu et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Prabhudesai et al., 2023), but black-box rewards cannot. Reinforcement learning (RL) removes this requirement: DDPO (Black et al., 2024) and DPOK (Fan et al., 2023) use policy gradients, and Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and DanceGRPO (Xue et al., 2025) adapt group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024) to flow models.
These methods need transition likelihoods along stochastic multi-step rollouts, which recent work avoids by training on the forward process.
DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026) contrasts positive and negative samples under clipped group-relative optimality labels, CRD (Zhu et al., 2026) matches prompt-centered rewards to cancel an intractable normalizer, and AWM (Xue et al., 2026), RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026), RVM (Choi et al., 2026a), and DGPO (Luo et al., 2026b) use related advantage- or reward-weighted targets. In all of them, the reward serves only as a sample weight or a regression target, and no explicit reward model is learned.
DualHeads uses labels of the same form as
DiffusionNFT, but fits them with an explicit classifier and guides the student
through that classifier’s input gradient.

## Reward optimization coupled with distillation.

Other methods optimize the reward inside a distillation pipeline and differ mainly in what keeps the generator close to good images while the reward is optimized.
Most rely on a teacher. Some combine a reward objective with distribution matching (Jiang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026); for example, RTDMD (Huang et al., 2026a) minimizes a KL divergence to a reward-tilted teacher.
Closest to our setting, TDM-R1 (Luo et al., 2026a) post-trains a few-step student with non-differentiable rewards by learning a diffusion-model surrogate reward, and regularizes it with trajectory distribution matching, which requires the teacher and an online fake score.
Flow-OPD (Fang et al., 2026) and DiffusionOPD (Li et al., 2026a) first train task-specific teachers with RL and then distill them into one student, without reducing the step count. REST (Li et al., 2026b) co-trains an eight-step student with an evolving teacher.
Others do without a teacher. MeanFlowNFT (Huang et al., 2026b) applies forward-process RL to a distilled four-step generator, anchored to a frozen EMA of itself, and Self-OPD (Zhang et al., 2026) scores branched student rollouts against the student’s own deterministic trajectory.
Reward Lightning (Cheng et al., 2026) is closest in architecture: it jointly distills a video teacher into a few-step generator with discriminator and reward heads on one frozen backbone, but its reward head is pretrained on preference pairs and kept frozen.
DualHeads instead post-trains a distilled generator and refits its reward head online, on pointwise group-relative labels from black-box rewards, while its reference head keeps the generator close to the reference pool.

Generator update of DualHeads. The generator $f_{\theta}$ first rolls out $N$ steps from noise without gradient; the endpoint $x_{1}$ is re-noised to $x_{t_{i}}$ , from which $f_{\theta}$ predicts $\hat{x}_{1}$ in one differentiable step. The prediction is noised to $x_{t}$ and sent to a frozen feature extractor $F$ followed by a reference head $D_{\phi}$ and a reward head $R_{\psi}$ ; the generator ascends the utility $s=\lambda_{D}D_{\phi}+\lambda_{R}R_{\psi}$ through $\hat{x}_{1}$ , while the backbone and both heads stay fixed during its update.

## 3 Method

DualHeads adapts a few-step generator so that its samples score higher under an external reward while staying close to a reference distribution. For this, we use two binary classifiers on a shared frozen backbone: one learns reference fidelity, the other reward optimality.
Section 3.1 describes the few-step generation setting and the corresponding reward-tilted target.
Section 3.2 defines the two classifier objectives and Section 3.3 gives the single utility the generator maximizes.

## 3.1 Background

## Setup of few-step generator.

Let $\theta$ denote the parameters of a neural network few-step generator $f_{\theta}$ ; $c$ the frozen prompt embeddings and $x$ an image sample.
We write time in the flow-matching convention, with data at $t=1$ . For a clean sample $x_{1}$ 
and noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ , the interpolant at time $t\in[0,1]$ and the
generator’s clean-data prediction are:

 $x_{t}\;=\;\mathcal{N}_{t}(x_{1};\epsilon)=t\,x_{1}+(1-t)\,\epsilon,\qquad f_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t)\;=\;x_{t}+(1-t)\,v_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t),$ 

(1)

where $v_{\theta}$ is the velocity representation of the model output.
Starting from Gaussian noise $x_{t_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ , the $N$ -step stochastic
sampler follows a timestep grid $0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}=1$ .
At each step, the model predicts the clean endpoint and re-noises it to the next timestep:

 $x_{t_{i+1}}=\mathcal{N}_{t_{i+1}}\!\left(f_{\theta}(x_{t_{i}},c,t_{i});\epsilon_{i+1}\right),\qquad i=0,\ldots,N-1,$ 

(2)

where $\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{N}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ are independent Gaussian noise.
The noising operator satisfies $\mathcal{N}_{1}(x;\epsilon)=x$ ,
so the final step adds no noise and returns $x_{t_{N}}=f_{\theta}(x_{t_{N-1}},c,t_{N-1})$ .
We write $p_{\theta}(x|c)$ for the distribution of the sampler’s output $x=x_{t_{N}}$ .

## Goal: a reward-tilted reference distribution.

We are given a black-box image reward $r(x,c)\in[0,1]$ and prompt-paired reference samples from a conditional distribution $p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x|c)$ .
Our goal is to train a few-step generator whose output distribution $p_{\theta}(x|c)$ achieves high expected reward while remaining close to the reference distribution.
For a fixed prompt $c$ , a standard formulation for KL-regularized RL training is:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{c}(\theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot|c)\,\middle\|\,p_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|c)\right)-\frac{1}{\beta}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot|c)}\big[r(x,c)\big],$ 

(3)

 $\displaystyle p^{*}(x|c)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z(c)}p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x|c)\exp\!\left(\frac{r(x,c)}{\beta}\right),$ 

(4)

where $\beta>0$ controls the strength of reference regularization relative to reward, $p^{*}(x|c)$ is the optimal solution to Eq. 3, and $Z(c)$ is the normalizing constant.
Indeed, $\mathcal{J}_{c}(\theta)=\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\|p^{*})-\log Z(c)$ , so minimizing $\mathcal{J}_{c}$ is equivalent to fitting the reward-tilted target in reverse KL.

## 3.2 DualHeads

Since the KL term requires unavailable density ratios and the black-box reward can be non-differentiable, neither term in Eq. 3 is directly tractable. To address this, we propose to learn a classifier surrogate for each: a reference head and a reward head on a shared frozen backbone.

## Two heads on one frozen backbone.

A pretrained frozen network serves as a feature extractor $F(x_{t},c,t)$ for two lightweight heads with identical architecture: 
The reference head $D_{\phi}$ distinguishes reference images $x_{\mathrm{ref}}\sim p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ from online generator
predictions.
The reward head $R_{\psi}$ instead predicts how good a sample is based on some external evaluation score. Its target is a soft label $y\in[0,1]$ , computed from the reward of the rollout endpoint.
Both heads are trained with the same binary cross-entropy loss, $\operatorname{BCE}(\ell;y)=-y\,\log\sigma(\ell)\!-(1\!-\!y)\log\bigl(1\!-\!\sigma(\ell)\bigr)$ . For brevity, we use $D_{\phi}(x_{t},c,t)$ for $D_{\phi}(F(x_{t},c,t),c,t)$ and likewise for $R_{\psi}$ .

The generator prediction $\hat{x}_{1}$ is formed in two steps: a rollout endpoint $x_{1}$ , sampled using Eq. 2, is re-noised to a rollout grid timestep $t_{i}$ , yielding $x_{t_{i}}=\mathcal{N}_{t_{i}}(x_{1};\epsilon^{\prime})$ , and the generator is then applied in one differentiable step, yielding $\hat{x}_{1}=f_{\theta}(x_{t_{i}},c,t_{i})$ .

The reference head uses hard targets: $1$ for noised reference images, $0$ for noised generator predictions, and its training objective is (Goodfellow et al., 2014):

 $\mathcal{L}_{D}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon,x_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[\operatorname{BCE}\!\left(D_{\phi}(\mathcal{N}_{t}(x_{\mathrm{ref}};\epsilon),c,t);1\right)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon,\hat{x}_{1}}\!\left[\operatorname{BCE}\!\left(D_{\phi}(\mathcal{N}_{t}(\hat{x}_{1};\epsilon),c,t);0\right)\right].$ 

(5)

conclusion: We presented DualHeads, a simple method for adapting few-step diffusion generators using only external reward evaluations and reference samples. It turns KL-regularized reward maximization into two binary classification problems, solved by lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. With four steps, it reaches OCR and GenEval scores of $0.92$ and $0.90$ , comparable to RL methods with 40–80 NFE, while improving all quality and preference scores over the base model, and gives the best HPSv3 on Z-Image-Turbo. The two heads divide the work: the reward head sets what the reward measures, and the reference pool largely sets the rest, such as style. Appendix A discusses limitations and future directions.

title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
abstract: Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

body_start:
Abstract

Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior
 $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ on the VAE latent space. For base generation this
default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning,
however, it carries a structural limitation. We show that the standard
VAE’s KL term does not merely ignore mode structure — it actively
taxes separation and tightness. When the data are multimodal, the ELBO
optimum therefore compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent
envelope. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is
under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, the
dynamic-to-variational error amplification rises sharply, and the
collapse boundary $\beta_{c}$ — the minimum KL strength that preserves
mode coverage — is pushed far above its variational scale. The effect
is large and reproducible: on the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann
distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at $\beta_{c}=0.224$ , while
a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior on the same data collapses at
 $3.16\times 10^{-3}$ — a $71\times$ gap produced by the same pipeline.

We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator,
 $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})$ , and verify the causal chain through controlled
interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at
matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient $0.995\times$ ,
95% CI $[0.79,1.25]$ ). A three-source decomposition localises the
amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution,
bounded and non-systematic anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau, by
contrast, is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no
amount of RL capacity recovers. We state the remedy conditionally: a
non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry
would fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is
coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton (Lean 4)
supports the KL pricing structure — a divergent compactness tax under
a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture — and
the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource
from what requires changing the prior.

## 1 Introduction

Diffusion models are now the dominant paradigm in generative modelling:
denoising diffusion probabilistic models (Ho et al., 2020) and
their score-based SDE generalisation (Song et al., 2021) reach
state-of-the-art sample quality through iterative denoising. Latent
diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) made the paradigm scalable by running
the diffusion process in the compressed latent space of a VAE
(Kingma and Welling, 2013) rather
than in pixel space — the step that turned high-resolution and
text-to-image synthesis into practical technology — and the
latent-diffusion recipe now extends to video
(Blattmann et al., 2023), while diffusion models more broadly have
become standard tools in scientific design, from image scaffolds to de
novo protein structure generation (Watson et al., 2023). In all of these deployed systems the
VAE latent space carries a Gaussian prior $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ by default.
A third layer is being installed on top of this stack:
reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. DDPO (Black et al., 2024) recasts
denoising as a Markov decision process and maximises a downstream
reward by policy gradient; DPOK (Wallace et al., 2023) adds a KL
regulariser anchoring the fine-tuned policy to the pretrained prior —
the same alignment recipe that is mature on large language models
(Ouyang et al., 2022) and is spreading rapidly across diffusion
deployments.

Latent diffusion pipelines thus almost universally place a Gaussian
prior on the VAE latent space, and this default — unproblematic for
base generation — carries a structural limitation that emerges
precisely when the three layers above are combined: multimodal data, a
tight VAE latent space, and RL fine-tuning. This paper asks when that
limitation bites, why, and what to do about it. One clarification
before the contribution: this is not yet another account of
reward-overoptimisation. The RLHF literature already documents
diversity loss from over-optimised rewards
(Gao et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023); our concern is a different,
upstream mechanism — the collapse boundary is set by prior
geometry even when the reward is well designed and the KL strength is
generous. The Gaussian prior issue is the precondition that determines
where the boundary sits, not a pathology of the reward signal.

Figure 1: Overview. (a) The data are multimodal: several separated
modes in data space. (b) The VAE prior sets the latent
separation-to-width ratio $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})$ : under a Gaussian
prior the modes can overlap, while a mixture prior keeps them
separated. (c) Under KL-anchored RL fine-tuning, the collapse boundary
 $\beta_{c}$ and the recovery plateau depend on that geometry
(schematic; measured curves in §5).

## 1. The limitation: a Gaussian prior packs multimodal data
into an overlapping latent.

The KL term of the standard VAE objective pulls every encoder posterior
toward the unit Gaussian, forcing $\sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}\approx 1$ . When
the data are multimodal, the encoder must therefore pack distinct modes
into a single broad envelope: the latent modes overlap, and the
separation-to-width ratio $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})$ — the smallest
inter-mode distance measured in units of the mode diameter — drops
below $1$ . This compression is not a training failure but the optimum
of the Gaussian-ELBO objective itself: the KL term does not merely
ignore mode structure — separation and tightness are exactly what it
charges for (the KL pricing structure is quantified by
Propositions 2 and 3 in §3;
Figure 2 shows the compression forming during training).

## 2. When the limitation bites: RL fine-tuning amplifies
overlap.

Overlap alone is not fatal: a base model still samples every mode from
an overlapped latent. The damage appears when the frozen model is
fine-tuned with a KL-anchored RL objective. Once
 $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})<1$ , the score network is under-resolved on the
saddle region between modes, the dynamic-to-variational amplification
 $\mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var}$ rises sharply, and fine-tuning piles mass
onto the reward-target mode, pushing the collapse boundary $\beta_{c}$ —
the minimum KL strength that preserves coverage — far above its
variational scale. The effect is not subtle: on the real
alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution (Exp7), a Gaussian-prior VAE
lands at $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})=0.81$ and collapses at $\beta_{c}=0.224$ ,
while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior on the same data holds
 $1.03$ and collapses only at $3.16\times 10^{-3}$ — a $71\times$ gap
produced by the same score/ODE/fine-tune pipeline.

## 3. When a non-Gaussian prior is needed.

The answer is conditional, and the conditions are checkable before
training: a non-Gaussian prior is needed when the latent geometry would
fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is
coverage-sensitive.

multimodality creates the overlap and RL fine-tuning amplifies it.
Neither factor alone requires changing the prior.

## 4. The remedy: a mode-preserving prior keeps the geometry
out of the amplifier’s reach.

A Gaussian-mixture prior
(Dilokthanakul et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2017; Tomczak and Welling, 2018; Lee et al., 2021)
permits each component to remain tight
( $\sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}\ll 1$ ), and the ELBO then pushes the encoder to
preserve the data’s mode separation rather than average over it.
The downstream chain follows immediately: separated geometry
( $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})>1$ ) keeps $\mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var}$ small,
which keeps $\beta_{c}$ at its variational scale and the coverage plateau
full — $0.70\!\to\!1.00$ in the controlled 1D comparison (Exp5A,
 $K{=}10$ ), $0.58\!\to\!0.73$ decoded coverage in the crowded 2D pack
(Exp6, $K{=}30$ , 3-seed mean), and $\approx 0.67\!\to\!1.0$ latent
coverage on alanine dipeptide (Exp7). The prior change is therefore not
a cosmetic improvement but, in the overlap regime, a necessary
one: the latent geometry is not independently tunable at fixed prior,
so switching the prior is the only lever that moves the geometry out of
the amplifier’s reach (Appendices G, K).

The remedy has an explicit boundary condition. At the exact reverse-KL
optimum, with unlimited policy capacity and complete optimisation, the
collapse boundary is set by geometry alone and the variational
prediction already gives an order-1 prior gap in Exp7 ( $0.69\times$ ,
versus the measured $71\times$ ): nearly everything measured is the
finite-resource pipeline’s amplification, which geometric
separation sidesteps rather than repairs. Under the pipelines we
study — a 2-layer score MLP, $1000$ guidance steps, $150$ ODE
steps — the advantage is real, reproducible over seeds and MD
sampling length (20 ns and 60 ns give identical $\beta_{c}$ for matched
priors), and architecture-independent within the tested family ( $K{=}30$ 
pack and the 2-layer score MLP); whether it persists with a much larger
policy and much longer optimisation is a testable limit we state rather
than conceal.

## The mechanism analyses are the quantitative description of
the limitation, not independent stories.

Four controlled experiments pin down where the amplification lives and
how much overlap it takes to trigger it: a three-source decomposition
localises the amplification to the learned policy — the ODE
solver contributes exactly zero at the boundary from $25$ to $400$ 
steps, KL-anchor mismatch is bounded and moves the boundary
non-systematically, and the residual $15$ – $78\%$ shortfall is
policy-side (Appendix F); saddle-corridor routing is
separately rejected, so the limitation is a static representational
shortfall, not trajectory re-routing (Section 5.1,
Appendix E); the $\alpha(g)=\beta_{c}/\beta_{\rm cross}$ 
scan quantifies how deep into overlap the geometry must fall before the
limitation bites (Appendix I); and the bidirectional
reachability test shows that the tight GMM geometry is unattainable
from the Gaussian ELBO, closing the loop on why the prior — not its
hyperparameters — must change (Appendices G,
K).

The paper’s causal chain is therefore

 $\boxed{\text{prior type}}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\text{ELBO }\Rightarrow\;d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\text{policy-side amplification}}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\beta_{c}\text{ and coverage plateau}},$ 

(causal-chain)

and the core conclusion is conditional rather than comparative: not
“a mixture prior is better than a Gaussian”, but when the latent
geometry would fall into the overlap regime, a non-Gaussian prior is
necessary, because it preserves mode separation and thereby sidesteps
the error amplification of the current pipeline. The remainder
develops the variational theory and its crossover scale (§4), the
experiments and the three-source decomposition (§5), and supporting
appendices: the four-prior family comparison (H),
fixed-prior and matched-geometry interventions
(G, K), separation and rare-basin scans
(I, J), and the machine-checked theory
skeleton (L).

## 2 Related Work

This work intersects four active research threads.

## 2.1 VAE prior choice and downstream impact

The standard VAE uses a Gaussian prior (Kingma and Welling, 2013), but
numerous alternatives have been proposed to better capture multi-modal
data. Jiang et al. (2017) introduced VaDE, which replaces the
Gaussian prior with a GMM and shows improvements in clustering quality.
Tomczak and Welling (2018) proposed VampPriors (learnable mixture priors
parameterised by a decoder network), and Lee et al. (2021) introduced
GMVAE, which combines a GMM prior with a structured inference network.
These works all report that richer priors improve disentanglement and
reconstruction quality, but none has studied the interaction
between prior width and the critical RL fine-tune boundary that is
our focus. The posterior-collapse literature
(Bowman et al., 2016; Alemi et al., 2018) diagnosed how a Gaussian prior lets the
aggregated posterior match it by construction
(Hoffman and Johnson, 2016; Moyer et al., 2018); on real multimodal structure data
the mismatch is concrete — cryo-EM heterogeneous reconstruction with
Gaussian-prior VAEs shows the aggregate posterior spilling past the
prior’s support (Zhong et al., 2021).
Propositions 2 and 3 give that
intuition its quantitative, boundary-facing form — the KL term
actively taxes separation and tightness rather than merely ignoring
them — and connect it to $\beta_{c}$ rather than to base-model
quality.

## 2.2 Latent diffusion models

The stable-diffusion family (Rombach et al., 2022) demonstrated that
VAE priors are practically interchangeable with a Gaussian, and most
subsequent work on latent diffusion (Ho et al., 2020; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2021)
continues to use Gaussian priors by default. The recipe is deployed
infrastructure rather than a toy setting — latent video diffusion
scales it to large video corpora (Blattmann et al., 2023), and
diffusion-based design tools inherit the same generative stack for
scientific applications (Watson et al., 2023) — so a design
choice inside the latent space has practical consequences. Our work
shows that prior choice matters dramatically for fine-tuning
robustness, even if it matters little for base-model quality.

## 2.3 RL fine-tuning of generative models

RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023) and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023)
have become standard tools for aligning large language models, and the
recipe is now spreading to diffusion: DDPO (Black et al., 2024) treats
denoising as an MDP for policy-gradient reward maximisation, DPOK
(Wallace et al., 2023) identifies the KL anchor as the key stabiliser,
and text-to-image alignment studies report the resulting diversity loss
(Lee et al., 2023). These observations belong to the reward-side
regime: diversity erodes because the reward is pursued too far past its
design envelope, the classical over-optimisation scaling of
Gao et al. (2023). Our subject is a different, upstream regime:
even with a well-designed reward and a generous KL anchor, the collapse
boundary is set by the prior’s geometry — the two failure modes are
complementary, not competing, and neither subsumes the other.
Poole et al. (2022) introduced stochastic gradient methods
for diffusion fine-tuning with KL anchors, and Dhariwal et al. (2023)
showed that reward-weighted diffusion produces mode collapse at
sufficiently large $\beta$ . Lu et al. (2024) identified a
phase transition in reverse-KL fine-tuning and called for theoretical
understanding of the critical $\beta_{c}$ — our work answers this call
by connecting $\beta_{c}$ to prior geometry.

## 3 Theory

We now connect the experimental findings to a closed-form analysis of
reverse-KL RL fine-tuning. The key insight is that prior geometry
— specifically the VAE’s latent-space mode width $\sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}$ —
is the first-order determinant of the critical $\beta_{c}$ below which the
model collapses toward the RL target.

## 3.1 Setup and exact reverse-KL optimum

Consider a parametric model $\pi_{\theta}(z)$ fine-tuned from a frozen
Gaussian-mixture reference $p_{0}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}(z;\mu_{k},\sigma_{0}^{2}I)$ under the reverse-KL RL objective:

 $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi_{\theta}}[R(z)]+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}\|p_{0}\bigr).$ 

(RL-KL)

Reward is quadratic toward a target mode $z_{t}$ : $R(z)=-\|z-z_{t}\|^{2}$ .

The first-order optimality condition gives the Gibbs tilt
 $\pi^{*}(z)\propto p_{0}(z)\exp(-\lambda\|z-z_{t}\|^{2}/\beta)$ . Since the
product of two Gaussians is a Gaussian, the tilted optimum is also a GMM:

 $\displaystyle\sigma_{\beta}^{2}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}\,\tau^{2}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\tau^{2}},\quad\mu^{\prime}_{k,\beta}=\frac{\mu_{k}\,\tau^{2}+z_{t}\,\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\sigma_{0}^{2}+\tau^{2}},\quad\tau^{2}=\frac{\beta}{2\lambda}.$ 

(width-center)

Equations (width-center) give the exact reverse-KL optimum
(a special case of the theory derived in theory.py, which also
evaluates forward-KL on a 1D grid).

## 3.2 The two limits: rigid vs collapsible priors

The component width $\sigma_{\beta}$ in (width-center) has two clean
limits:

Theorem 1 (Rigid vs collapsible priors).

Under reverse KL with quadratic reward:

1. 

Narrow prior $\sigma_{0}\ll\tau$ :
 $\sigma_{\beta}\to\sigma_{0}$ (constant!), $\mu^{\prime}_{k,\beta}\to\mu_{k}$ 
(centers rigid).

2. 

Wide prior $\sigma_{0}\gg\tau$ :
 $\sigma_{\beta}\to\tau$ (grows with $\sqrt{\beta}$ ),
 $\mu^{\prime}_{k,\beta}\to z_{t}$ (all centers collapse toward $z_{t}$ ).

Proof.

 $\sigma_{\beta}^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2}/(1+\sigma_{0}^{2}/\tau^{2})$ .
(1) When $\sigma_{0}^{2}\ll\tau^{2}$ , expand in $\sigma_{0}^{2}/\tau^{2}$ :
 $\sigma_{\beta}^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2}(1-\sigma_{0}^{2}/\tau^{2}+O(\sigma_{0}^{4}/\tau^{4}))$ .
The center shift is $\mu^{\prime}_{k,\beta}-\mu_{k}=(\mu_{k}-z_{t})\sigma_{0}^{2}/(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\tau^{2})=O(\sigma_{0}^{2}/\tau^{2})$ . (2) When $\sigma_{0}^{2}\gg\tau^{2}$ ,
 $\sigma_{\beta}^{2}=\tau^{2}/(1+\tau^{2}/\sigma_{0}^{2})\to\tau^{2}$ , and
 $\mu^{\prime}_{k,\beta}-z_{t}=(\mu_{k}-z_{t})\tau^{2}/(\sigma_{0}^{2}+\tau^{2})\to 0$ .
∎

The two regimes cross at $\beta_{\mathrm{cross}}=2\lambda\sigma_{0}^{2}$ 
where $\tau(\beta_{\mathrm{cross}})=\sigma_{0}$ .

This crossover scale is
the key order-of-magnitude predictor for the RL collapse boundary.

The KL term of the standard VAE objective pulls every encoder posterior
toward the unit Gaussian, forcing $\sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}\approx 1$ . When
the data are multimodal, the encoder must therefore pack distinct modes
into a single broad envelope: the latent modes overlap, and the
separation-to-width ratio $d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})$ — the smallest
inter-mode distance measured in units of the mode diameter — drops
below $1$ . This compression is not a training failure but the optimum
of the Gaussian-ELBO objective itself: the KL term does not merely
ignore mode structure — separation and tightness are exactly what it
charges for (the KL pricing structure is quantified by
Propositions 2 and 3 in §3;
Figure 2 shows the compression forming during training).

The narrative of this paper is limitation $\to$ condition $\to$ 
remedy: the Gaussian prior’s structural limitation under RL
fine-tuning (it packs multimodal data into an overlapping latent), the
geometric condition under which the limitation bites

necessary precisely in the overlap regime). The causal

must be before it fires. We fix terminology, state the boundary
condition on the remedy, give three implications, and end with the
genuinely open question.

title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining
abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

4.1 Language modeling and cross-lingual context use
body_start:
Abstract

High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual
transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining.
Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making
parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual
pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations
independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure.
We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve
multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its
translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel
pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training
models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the
benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone
does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT.
Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong
cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information
across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and
single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language
understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following
the pretraining–fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a
cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard
language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings,
the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and
cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched
training budgets.

Figure 1: Sequence construction and the motivation for PPT followed by SPT. (a) SPT samples documents independently; PPT joins translation pairs before sequence packing. Both use the same bilingual corpus. Letters identify content and EN/FR identify languages. (b) Continuing PPT with SPT improves general language understanding and translation over SPT at matched training budgets. The book pages illustrate these tasks using two HellaSwag continuations and an English–French translation excerpt.

## 1 Introduction

Multilingual parallel data has been widely used to improve cross-lingual language understanding (Lample and Conneau, 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Chi et al., 2021). However, high-quality human-translated corpora are typically too small for large-scale multilingual pretraining, and scaling them is costly (Team et al., 2022). Machine translation makes it possible to translate high-quality English web corpora into a wide range of languages at pretraining scale (Doshi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). This reduces the resource gap by providing more high-quality training data for languages with lower-quality web data than English. Standard multilingual pretraining uses translated documents as an additional training source, treating original documents and their translations as independent examples and sampling them independently (Wang et al., 2025).

However, treating these documents independently does not make direct use of their parallel structure. Previous work has used parallel data to improve cross-lingual language modeling and to adapt pretrained models to translation and other multilingual tasks (Lample and Conneau, 2019; Lee et al., 2022; Kondo et al., 2024; Alves et al., 2024). Qorib et al. (2025) study how to incorporate sentence-level parallel data11
 1

 Their experiments use less than 5B tokens of parallel data. into predominantly non-parallel pretraining. These studies show that parallel structure can improve cross-lingual capabilities even with relatively small amounts of parallel data (Lin et al., 2025). With parallel documents available at pretraining scale (Wang et al., 2025; Penedo et al., 2026), it remains unclear how to use their parallel structure effectively for multilingual pretraining.

We investigate this question by introducing parallel pretraining (PPT), which concatenates each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare PPT with standard multilingual pretraining (SPT), which treats the original and translated documents as independent training examples (Figure 1(a)). To avoid uncertainty about what existing open-weight models have already learned from parallel data, we train both models from scratch. We use the same training setup and hyperparameters. The only difference is whether a document and its translation are treated as a single training sequence.

We pretrain 1.3B-parameter dense models with the Llama 2 architecture (Touvron et al., 2023) on TransWebEdu (Wang et al., 2025). Our experiments cover English–French and English–Swahili, representing high-resource and low-resource settings, respectively. We train both SPT and PPT models for approximately 200B tokens and evaluate their performance on general language understanding and translation tasks.

Surprisingly, PPT alone does not consistently improve general language understanding over SPT. Further analysis shows that PPT models benefit more from cross-lingual context than SPT models. However, general language understanding tasks typically use single-language inputs, unlike the parallel sequences used in PPT. This context mismatch may limit how much these tasks benefit from PPT’s cross-lingual capabilities.

This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the
pretraining–fine-tuning paradigm (Howard and Ruder, 2018): PPT develops cross-lingual capabilities, and subsequent SPT adapts the model to standard language modeling (Figure 1(b)). We start the second stage from intermediate pretraining checkpoints and continue with SPT for 20B tokens. We also test SPT followed by PPT. We compare both two-stage approaches with SPT-only and PPT-only training
at the same total training budget.
At a total training budget of 120B tokens, our experimental results show that PPT followed by SPT improves average general language understanding over SPT alone in both language settings. It also achieves the best translation performance among the four training strategies, with relative improvements in BLEU over SPT alone of 77% on English--French and 45% on English--Swahili.22
 2

 BLEU increases from 19.25 to 34.03 on English–French and from 9.07 to 13.18 on English–Swahili.

Our behavioral analyses show that continuing PPT with SPT improves monolingual language modeling. The resulting model also benefits more from cross-lingual context than a model trained with SPT alone.

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

• 

We investigate how to use parallel data at pretraining scale through
controlled comparisons of multilingual models trained from scratch.

• 

Our proposed two-stage pretraining approach, which uses PPT followed
by SPT, shows improvements in both general language understanding and
translation over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

• 

Our behavioral analyses show that continued SPT improves monolingual
language modeling while retaining an advantage over SPT alone in using
cross-lingual context.

## 2 Pretraining with Parallel Data

## 2.1 Independent and paired-document sequences

Following Wang et al. (2025), standard pretraining (SPT) samples
source and translated documents independently. Parallel pretraining (PPT)
concatenates each document with its translation in the same training
sequence (Figure 1(a)). Each document is preceded
by its language name, a colon, and a newline, giving the prefixes
“English:\n” and “French:\n”
in English–French.
We alternate which language comes first across document
pairs, preserving sentence order within each document.

Both methods train on the same bilingual corpus with autoregressive
next-token prediction. Both languages contribute to the loss, and
attention can span preceding documents within each 2,048-token window.
Pairing documents makes corresponding cross-lingual content available
when predicting the later document, alongside its preceding text in the
same language. Alternating document order provides this context in both
directions. Appendix A
describes document matching, separators and training windows.

## 2.2 From parallel to standard pretraining

PPT provides corresponding cross-lingual content during training, whereas
general language-understanding tasks typically use single-language inputs.
We therefore continue PPT with SPT to adapt the model to independently
sampled documents, denoting this approach by PPT→SPT
(Figure 1(b)). In this second stage, the model
continues learning from both languages without systematically receiving
the translation of the document it is predicting.

We compare PPT→SPT with SPT-only and PPT-only training at matched token
budgets. We also evaluate SPT→PPT to examine how the order of paired-document
and independent-document training affects language understanding,
translation, and use of cross-lingual context. Section 3.1
gives the training schedules and language settings.

Figure 2: English–French pretraining with SPT, PPT, and their staged combinations. SPT and PPT curves contain all ten checkpoints from 20B to 200B tokens. Each staged run branches from its initial method at 60B, 100B or 160B and trains for another 20B tokens, with evaluations every 5B tokens in both panels. Each branch is a separate training run. Accuracy averages six tasks and both languages equally. BLEU equally weights FLORES-200 and WMT14, both translation directions and the two prompt formats specified in Section 3.1.

## 3 Experiments

## 3.1 Experimental setup

Data and training. We use English documents from TransWebEdu (Wang et al., 2025)
and their corresponding French or Swahili translations, with approximately
150B available tokens per language. Each model is a 1.3B-parameter
decoder-only Transformer using the TransWebLLM architecture and tokenizer
(Wang et al., 2025). Within each language pair, the SPT and PPT
models train separately from the same initial weights for approximately
200B tokens, saving checkpoints every 20B.

To compare the two training orders at different stages, we continue
English–French models from 60B, 100B and 160B tokens with the other
sequence construction for another 20B tokens. These early-, middle-
and late-stage continuations use the same sampled TransWebEdu data
and end at 80B, 120B and 180B tokens, respectively.
English–Swahili uses the middle-stage comparison, from 100B to 120B.
Both orders use a new optimizer with learning-rate re-warming
(Gupta et al., 2023; Ibrahim et al., 2024) followed by cosine decay.
We compare the resulting models with SPT and PPT at the same total
training budget; these baselines retain their original schedule.
Appendix A gives the model,
optimization and data-construction details.

Evaluation. We assess multilingual language understanding
with tasks in each language and cross-lingual generation with translation.
We evaluate language understanding with lm-evaluation-harness
(Gao et al., 2024). English–French
uses ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag
(Zellers et al., 2019), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022a),
PAWS-X (Yang et al., 2019), XNLI (Conneau et al., 2018) and
XWinograd (Tikhonov and Ryabinin, 2021) in both languages.
English–Swahili uses XNLI, XStoryCloze (Lin et al., 2022b),
COPA/XCOPA (Gordon et al., 2012; Ponti et al., 2020)

body_start:
Abstract

Inference-time scaling is often treated as a token-budget problem, but a failed coding agent can seek qualitatively different resources: computation, information, or feedback. We introduce Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA), a controlled factorial framework that measures each resource’s marginal contribution to repair and its interactions while holding the failed state and revision protocol fixed. We evaluate six models on 194 function-level failures from MBPP+ and HumanEval+ and 126 repository-level failures from SWE-bench Verified. Task-relevant specifications consistently improve repair, whereas public-test feedback provides small gains and retrieved code little to none. The value of additional computation declines with model capability, while information remains useful; resource channels largely exhibit diminishing returns, although complementary information can reinforce itself. Yet three of four frontier models select feedback in $95$ – $100\%$ of cases and obtain lower gains than uniform random resource selection. BRA thus exposes a gap between the resources agents prefer and those that measurably improve repair.

## 1 Introduction

Language models improve when given more to work with at inference time. Longer chains of thought [43, 36, 19], repeated sampling with a verifier [9, 29, 3], and compute-optimal allocation between revision and search [40, 45] all trade tokens for accuracy along a single axis, the generation budget. For agents, however, inference-time resources differ in kind as well as in quantity. When a coding agent is stuck, its next tokens can buy three different things: more computation (deliberating without new observations), more information (documentation, retrieved code, a specification of what the program must do), or more feedback (executing the artifact and reading what failed) [48, 28, 8, 39, 47]. Each channel has its own literature, evaluated by comparing end-to-end pipelines. Such comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the channel itself.

End-to-end comparisons cannot say which resource binds at a failed step, or whether a second still helps once the first is present, for three reasons. Along a trajectory the resource, the state, and the next revision vary together, so a verifier call that seems to help may only have triggered another edit. One-at-a-time ablations cannot tell sufficiency from necessity: rescuing a failure is not the same as being its bottleneck. And with bounded outcomes, an apparent interaction may be substitution, complementarity, or a ceiling unless every combination is observed.

These obstacles call for a controlled comparison of resources at fixed failed states. A resource-choice probe in coding tasks highlights why this comparison matters: when asked to choose a single resource before revising, three of the four frontier models we evaluate request execution feedback in $95$ – $100\%$ of cases (§5.5).
Whether it is justified depends on how feedback compares with the other resources, alone and combined, at the same state. This leads to the central question of the paper: at a fixed failed state, how much does each inference-time resource contribute to a repair, how do the contributions combine, and how does the answer change with model capability?

To answer it we treat the three resources as players in a cooperative game whose worth is the utility an agent attains when a given bundle of them is supplied at the failed state. Asked this way, “what is computation worth here?” has no single answer: its marginal contribution depends on whether information and feedback are already present, and the natural summary is the average of that contribution over all bundles of the other resources, which is the resource’s Banzhaf value [2]; the departures of the bundles’ worths from additivity are the pairwise and three-way synergies of the game [21, 18]. Trajectories never reveal these quantities because an agent visits one bundle per state.
We therefore introduce Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA): a framework for measuring how inference time resources contribute to repair at a fixed failed state. BRA first replicates this checkpoint across a full $2^{n}$ factorial design, with $n=3$ resource channels: computation ( $C$ ), information ( $I$ ), and feedback ( $F$ ).
Each replica receives exactly the resources of its cell and then one final revision call under a common protocol: the same model, prompt template, and output budget. Artifacts are scored on held-out tests disjoint from the public tests used for feedback. Because every bundle’s worth is observed, Banzhaf values, interactions, and the Möbius decomposition of the full-resource gain are computed exactly per checkpoint and model, instead of estimated from samples.

We run BRA on 194 frozen function-level failures from MBPP+ and HumanEval+ [1, 7, 30] and 126 repository-level failures from SWE-bench Verified [24], with six repair models spanning an order of magnitude of capability (Qwen3-4B/14B/32B, DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5). Three findings recur. 1 Information is the binding resource, and only the right information. An audited specification raises held-out utility for every model, by $0.06$ – $0.14$ at function level and $0.05$ – $0.10$ at repository level. A length-matched irrelevant packet is worth nothing, and so is retrieved repository code. Public-test feedback is worth at most $0.03$ . 2 More capable models gain less from computation, but still benefit from information. Along the ladder, the value of computation falls from $0.131$ to $0.007$ ; the value of information stays between $0.06$ and $0.14$ . 3 Resource channels show diminishing returns, while information components complement one another. All pairwise interactions among $C$ , $I$ , and $F$ are negative or null. Knowing where to change code is worth nothing alone; knowing what to change is worth about half the full effect; both together are worth the whole. These measurements also reveal a mismatch in resource selection: models exhibiting feedback fixation obtain lower average repair gains from their choices than from uniform random selection among the same resource options.

Our main contributions are: 1 BRA, a controlled counterfactual design with pre-registered estimands, leakage audits, a placebo, and dose ladders, released with the frozen checkpoints and per-cell outcomes (§3). 2 Evidence across two task families and six models that inference resources are non-fungible and substitutable, that information rather than feedback binds, and that scaling migrates the bottleneck from computation to information (§5). 3 A decision-theoretic use of the surface that quantifies the misallocation of current agents. Using the same surfaces to score the agents’ own resource choices, we find that three of four frontier models almost always request feedback, the least valuable resource, and realise less than a random choice would (§5.5).

Figure 1: BRA overview.
A frozen failed checkpoint $s=(x,y,h)$ is the unit of analysis. Computation, information, and feedback enter as separate interventions, each through its own channel, and every bundle of the three is assigned to the same $s$ ; a common final revision and held-out scoring identify the response surface, the eight cell means $q_{cif}$ . A resource’s value is its marginal contribution averaged over every bundle of the other two, its Banzhaf value; the interactions tell substitutes from complements. The fingerprint compares models on the same states and scores the agent’s own resource choice by its regret.

## 2 Preliminaries

A checkpoint $s=(x,y,h)$ records a task, the artifact an agent has produced for it, and the context the agent saw; we consider checkpoints whose artifact fails the held-out evaluator, $U(y)<1$ , and ask what would happen if the agent were granted a set of resources before revising once. Let $N=\{C,I,F\}$ be the three resources and, for a bundle $T\subseteq N$ , let $Y_{s}(T)$ be the utility $s$ would attain if exactly the resources in $T$ were supplied and a fixed revision by a repair model $M$ ; its expectation over the revision’s randomness is $v_{s}(T)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{s}(T)]$ . In a trajectory one of the eight potential outcomes is realised, chosen by the agent, so differences between trajectories are not causal effects.
Because a checkpoint is frozen we can assign every bundle to the same $s$ and observe all eight up to revision noise: a $2^{3}$ full factorial with the checkpoint as block [13], in which every interaction is estimable without assumptions.

The resource game.
The expected outcomes $v_{s}(T)$ define a cooperative game on the player set $N$ , in which a bundle’s worth is the utility obtained when exactly its resources are supplied; $g_{s}(T)=v_{s}(T)-v_{s}(\emptyset)$ is the corresponding gain game with $g_{s}(\emptyset)=0$ . The marginal contribution of $X\notin T$ is $\mathrm{MV}_{X}(T)=v_{s}(T\cup\{X\})-v_{s}(T)$ . Three classical objects summarise the game. The Banzhaf value [2, 10] and the Shapley value [38] of resource $X$ are weighted averages of its marginal contributions over the bundles $T\subseteq N\setminus\{X\}$ ,

 $\beta_{X}(v_{s})=\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{T}\mathrm{MV}_{X}(T),\qquad\phi_{X}(v_{s})=\sum_{T}\frac{|T|!\,(n-1-|T|)!}{n!}\,\mathrm{MV}_{X}(T);$ 

(1)

the Harsanyi dividends are the Möbius coefficients $m(T)=\sum_{S\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|S|}v_{s}(S)$ , which attribute every unit of $g_{s}(N)=\sum_{T\neq\emptyset}m(T)$ exactly once to a single resource or to the synergy of a set [21, 18]; and the interaction index of a pair is the average over bundles $T$ of the others of the second difference $\Delta_{XY}v_{s}(T)=v_{s}(T\cup\{X,Y\})-v_{s}(T\cup\{X\})-v_{s}(T\cup\{Y\})+v_{s}(T)$ [17]. A positive pairwise dividend marks complements, a negative one substitutes; since a ceiling on $U$ also produces substitution, interactions are read against the distance of $v_{s}(\emptyset)$ from the ceiling. The pre-registered estimands are exactly these objects (§3.3).
For readability we index a bundle by its indicator vector $(c,i,f)\in\{0,1\}^{3}$ and write $q_{cif}=v_{s}(T)$ , so that $q_{000}=v_{s}(\emptyset)$ , $q_{010}=v_{s}(\{I\})$ , and $q_{111}=v_{s}(N)$ ; when the model matters we write $q_{M}(s;c,i,f)$ . Tables and figures label the eight cells by $cif$ . The two notations denote the same eight numbers: $v_{s}$ is used when a formula ranges over bundles, $q$ when it names a cell.

Costs and allocation.
With a cost $\kappa_{X}>0$ per resource, additive over bundles, the return of $X$ given $T$ is $\rho_{X}(T)=\mathrm{MV}_{X}(T)/\kappa_{X}$ ; an allocation policy chooses a bundle maximising $v_{s}(T)$ subject to $\kappa(T)\leq B$ , or one next resource $\pi(s)\in N\cup\{\varnothing\}$ , whose realised gain $G(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{s}[\mathrm{MV}_{\pi(s)}(\emptyset)]$ falls short of the oracle gain $G^{\star}=\mathbb{E}_{s}[\max_{X}\mathrm{MV}_{X}(\emptyset)]$ by the regret $R(\pi)$ . $v_{s}$ is submodular exactly when $m(\{X,Y\})\leq 0$ and $m(\{X,Y\})+m(N)\leq 0$ for every pair, in which case greedy allocation by return is provably near-optimal [33, 27] (Appendix C).

[Problem] Inference-bottleneck attribution.

Given: a population of frozen failed checkpoints, a held-out utility $U$ , a set of repair models, and resource interventions with specified definitions and doses, with outcomes defined under a fixed final revision.
Estimate: for each checkpoint $s$ and repair model $M$ , the response surface $v^{M}_{s}(T)$ over bundles $T\subseteq\{C,I,F\}$ , where $v^{M}_{s}(T)$ is the expected held-out utility after assigning $T$ ; from it, each resource’s Banzhaf value and its interactions with the others (the fingerprint $z_{s}$ ). Across checkpoints, characterise their population averages and heterogeneity; across models, compare them on the same failed states.
Use: evaluate a resource-allocation policy $\pi(s)$ by comparing the gain of its selected resource with that of a checkpoint-wise oracle over the same feasible choices, i.e. its allocation regret.

## 3 Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA)

Above problem asks for a surface that trajectories never reveal, because in a trajectory the resource, the state, and the revision move together. BRA makes it identifiable as illustrated in Figure 1: clone the frozen state into every resource combination and follow each clone with one identical revision (§3.1); define each resource so that it is supplied only through its own channel, at a controlled dose (§3.2); reduce the eight cell means to pre-registered contrasts with checkpoint-level uncertainty (§3.3); and use the same surfaces to compare models and to score the agent’s own allocation (§3.4).

## 3.1 Checkpoint-conditioned counterfactual forks

A checkpoint is cloned into the eight cells of the full factorial over $(c,i,f)$ ; in each cell the model receives $s$ with exactly the indicated resources and then makes one common final revision, a single call with the same model, template, and maximum output length and no tools, whose output $y^{\prime}$ replaces the artifact and is scored. Because the revision is identical across cells, any difference between cells is attributable to what preceded it, and because the intervention is assigned rather than chosen, $q_{M}(s;c,i,f)$ is identified by the cell mean, estimated from $k$ rollouts. Ablations from the empty cell identify only the simple effects $\Delta^{00}_{X}$ ; whether $X$ still has value once another resource is present is an interaction question, and the full factorial is the smallest design in which every interaction is estimable, at $8k$ revision and $4k$ planning calls per checkpoint and model (Appendix G).

## 3.2 Three resources, orthogonal as interventions and graded as doses

Computation, information, and feedback are not orthogonal in nature: a failing test is also information, and deliberation may reconstruct what a document would supply. They can be made orthogonal as interventions by fixing where each may come from. The definitions were frozen before any outcome was inspected and used unchanged for both task families.

Computation ( $c=1$ ) is one analysis-only call by $M$ with a fixed output budget ( $2048$ tokens in the main runs; $256$ – $4096$ in the dose curve) that reads the task, the artifact, and the cell’s other packets and returns a diagnosis and repair plan in prose, appended to the revision context; it may not execute, test, retrieve, or edit. All models run without hidden reasoning, so this call is the only extra computation in the design.

Information ( $i=1$ ) is a packet that depends on the task but not on the artifact: generated once per task, identical across checkpoints and cells. Artifact independence is what separates information from feedback. Information is graded on a ladder of artifact-independent rungs: retrieval, deterministic BM25 retrieval over the repository at the base commit queried with the issue text; location, the files and enclosing functions the reference fix changes, extracted mechanically from the reference patch; behaviour, an account of the root cause and required behaviour written from the reference fix by a fixed writer model that may not name any file, function, or variable; and specification, both halves together (at function level, the input–output contract and edge cases). Written packets pass an automated audit against code, reference-solution lines, test literals and identifiers, and, for the behaviour rung, paths and symbols of the reference patch. A placebo arm supplies a length-matched neutral text, so the information effect reads as the value of content rather than presence; rungs above retrieval are instruments that establish what information would do, not what a system can obtain.

Feedback ( $f=1$ ) is a report from executing the current artifact against a public evaluator, appended to the context; the artifact is never modified. Public tests are disjoint from the held-out tests defining $U$ . Levels increase in detail: pass counts (F1), failing inputs (F2), with expected outputs (F3, the main level), with observed outputs (F4). On repositories, where public tests are the benchmark’s own, a split-test protocol designates one of at least two failing target tests as observed, reports its outcome and failure excerpt, and scores $U$ on the rest; otherwise only outcome counts are reported.

Cells thus differ only in the presence of a packet; because $C$ may read the $I$ and $F$ packets, an interaction between computation and another resource measures whether deliberation makes that resource more productive; and $M$ is a technology, not a fourth resource, so the same intervention under two models yields two surfaces whose difference is their differential ability to convert resources into success.

title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

Abstract

As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches.
