3.2 Search, fresh rescoring, and plan acceptance
body_start:
Abstract

World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent
must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should
replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI(Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference.
SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated
rollouts of the actor’s own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior.
This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides
an exploration signal, and a proposed plan’s predicted advantage, which governs
action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds
the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor.
SDI reuses the base agent’s world model, actor, and critic without requiring an
additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data
collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across
Meta-World, Adroit, and
DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed
task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or
exceeds the strongest baseline’s performance on $15$ of $18$ tasks.
Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of
exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from
identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor
failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning,
while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support
comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach
to exploring and planning with world models.11
 1

 Code and configurations are available in the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sdi-EEDA.

Figure 1: Overview of SDI.
Imagine: candidate action sequences (siblings, blue) and repeated rollouts
of the actor’s fixed sequence (dashed gray) start at the same latent state $z_{t}$ .
Compare: fresh plan and actor rollouts provide the mean return gap $\hat{g}$ 
and actor-return standard deviation $s$ ; dots represent candidate mean returns,
whose spread is measured by $\mathrm{sib}$ .
Act/explore: the upper branch selects the planned action $\mu_{0}$ or actor
fallback $a^{\pi}$ ; dark cells indicate the executed action. The lower branch normalizes,
clips, and weights the exploration bonus $b$ to augment the first imagined reward
 $\tilde{r}$ . The bonus anneals after the first training success. Exploration and gating
use separate rollout settings; evaluation uses the actor alone.

## 1 Introduction

Learned world models support two complementary ways to improve control. Agents such as
Dreamer train a fast actor on imagined experience (Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2025),
whereas PlaNet and TD-MPC2 search through predicted futures when an action is needed
(Hafner et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2024). Hybrid approaches use a learned actor or
value function to guide online search (Sikchi et al., 2022). These approaches make
imagination useful both for learning a policy and for revising its decisions. An actor
acts quickly, whereas a planner searches at each step. During online learning, planned
actions also change the actor’s training data. When learning stalls, when should a
searched action replace the actor’s choice?

A planner optimizes predictions from an imperfect model. Its highest-scoring sequence
can therefore exploit errors in those predictions rather than improve the real outcome
(Talvitie, 2017; Lambert et al., 2020; Sims et al., 2024).
Searching many alternatives can favor prediction errors, and even an accurately
predicted high return offers little reason to intervene if the actor would do as well.
Probabilistic ensembles and short model rollouts limit some forms of this risk
(Chua et al., 2018; Janner et al., 2019), but a decision still requires comparing a proposed
plan with the action the agent would otherwise take. During training, that choice also
changes the experience from which the actor learns. It is thus important to distinguish
the effect of planning on the eventual policy from the effect of a particular
intervention (Hamrick et al., 2021).

Exploration poses a related problem. Prediction error, novelty, and model disagreement
can direct an agent toward unfamiliar experience
(Pathak et al., 2017; Burda et al., 2019; Pathak et al., 2019; Sekar et al., 2020).
These signals are valuable for learning the environment, but familiarity with the
dynamics and progress on a particular task are different properties. Even a predictable
state may offer actions with very different task outcomes.
When a task reward is specified, the agent may therefore seek
actions with meaningfully different predicted returns. A large spread across imagined
actions is hard to interpret on its own, however: stochastic rollouts can also disagree
about the return of one fixed action sequence. A useful comparison needs to account for
that variation while remaining relevant to the actor’s current behavior.

We introduce SDI(Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which compares imagined
action sequences with repeated rollouts of the actor’s fixed sequence from the same
model state. This actor-based reference guides exploration and plan acceptance during
data collection; evaluation uses the actor alone. SDI reuses the existing world model
and search optimizer. Across Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020a), Adroit (Rajeswaran et al., 2018), and
DM-Control (Tassa et al., 2018), SDI matches or exceeds the strongest compared
baseline on $15$ of $18$ tasks. In a replicated, matched-occupancy ablation, it raises
mean precision-manipulation success from $32\%$ with ungated planning to $53\%$ .

Our contributions are:

• 

A task-directed measure of imagined disagreement. We define sibling
disagreement as variation in predicted task returns across action sequences imagined
from the same latent state, measured relative to repeated rollouts of the actor’s
fixed sequence. This comparison separates action-dependent return variation from
stochastic variation under fixed behavior.

• 

A unified rule for exploration and selective planning. We introduce
SDI, which uses the same actor-repeat reference to reward informative imagined
alternatives and to accept a planned action only when its predicted advantage exceeds
local actor variability. SDI requires no additional disagreement ensemble, guides
data collection during training, and retains actor-only evaluation.

• 

Broad and intervention-level empirical evidence. We demonstrate that
SDI achieves the highest observed task-average score among compared methods in each
of three benchmark suites and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline mean on
 $15$ of $18$ tasks. Matched-occupancy ablations and paired-state executions further
show improved actor learning, recovery, success preservation, and return retention
relative to ungated planning.

## 2 Related work

World-model learning and planning. Dreamer trains an actor in imagined rollouts and executes it without further search
(Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2025); R2-Dreamer provides the primary base agent in our experiments (Morihira et al., 2026). Decision-time planners instead search through model-based imagination (Hafner et al., 2019; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2022; Hansen et al., 2024; Nagabandi et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2025),
while hybrid methods combine search with learned policies or values
(Sikchi et al., 2022; Anthony et al., 2017). LOOP combines finite-horizon model lookahead with
an off-policy terminal value and constrains search relative to an actor
(Sikchi et al., 2022). SDI adds an explicit post-search comparison against repeated
actor rollouts and uses that same reference construction for exploration. This targets
the acceptance of a proposal as well as the experience collected through planning
(Hamrick et al., 2021).

Model error and uncertainty.
Model error can compound over a rollout (Talvitie, 2017), prediction objectives
need not align with control (Lambert et al., 2020), and planning can exploit poorly
covered regions (Sims et al., 2024). Short rollouts, ensembles, and uncertainty-aware
updates address these problems in different ways
(Janner et al., 2019; Chua et al., 2018; Buckman et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020b; Pan et al., 2020; Frauenknecht et al., 2024).
PETS propagates uncertainty through probabilistic ensembles and trajectory sampling
(Chua et al., 2018). SDI obtains its reference from stochastic repeats within the
base world model. This estimates rollout variability for a fixed actor sequence;
model bias remains possible (Berger et al., 2026). Our paired-state experiments
test whether a margin scaled by that reference identifies executed improvements.

Exploration and action comparisons.
Intrinsic rewards use prediction error, novelty, information gain, or ensemble disagreement
to encourage exploration
(Pathak et al., 2017; Pathak et al., 2019; Burda et al., 2019; Houthooft et al., 2016; Sekar et al., 2020; Kauvar et al., 2023).
Other signals measure action influence or reward disagreement
(Seitzer et al., 2021; Bierling et al., 2025). Adaptive mechanisms switch exploration
modes or balance intrinsic and extrinsic rewards (Pîslar et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022),
while dormant-representation diagnostics provide a different basis for adapting training
interventions (Sokar et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024).
Plan2Explore rewards disagreement among predictions of the next observation embedding
to seek expected information gain (Sekar et al., 2020). SDI instead compares
task-return predictions across action sequences, relative to actor-repeat variability.
This makes the signal task-directed and ties it to the reference used for plan acceptance.
The construction relates to interventional advantage, counterfactual credit assignment,
and twin models (Pan et al., 2022; Pan and Schölkopf, 2024; Mesnard et al., 2021; Balke and Pearl, 1994; Vlontzos et al., 2023);
interventional causal representation learning likewise studies information obtained
under interventions (Ahuja et al., 2023). We therefore evaluate SDI’s predictions using executed alternatives.

## 3 Method

SDI augments a world-model actor–critic during training while leaving the
base learning objectives unchanged. At each latent state, it constructs a local actor
reference from repeated imagined rollouts of a fixed actor sequence. The same reference
scales a task-directed exploration bonus and the advantage required to execute a planned
action. Planning changes the experience collected for learning; evaluation executes the
learned actor’s mode without planning. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete
training-time interaction.

rollouts, their returns are not reused as evidence for acceptance. Instead, SDI
re-evaluates the selected plan and the actor’s fixed mode sequence from the same latent

title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

body_start:
Abstract

RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt.
Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO’s credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.11
 1

 All code to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/Nghi-Dao/ReAPO.

## 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective approach for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) without requiring human-written reasoning traces
(Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025; Lambert et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025).
Given a problem with an easily verifiable answer (e.g., formalized mathematics or compilable code), RLVR samples multiple responses from a policy, evaluates each response, and reinforces responses that receive higher rewards. Most contemporary approaches to RLVR are based on the seminal algorithm Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the quality of individual responses by comparing verified rewards within the group of sampled responses.
Despite the success of GRPO, the algorithm is limited by its reliance on policy stochasticity to explore semantically distinct reasoning trajectories. Indeed, like many policy gradient methods, GRPO does not explicitly encourage exploration, the process by which a model actively seeks out novel reasoning strategies; moreover, this deficiency has been noted in prior work that questions the ability of RL methods to drive genuine reasoning improvements beyond the capabilities of the base model (Yue et al., 2025; Karan and Du, 2025; Huang et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a).

Figure 1: 
Overview of ReAPO. Each rollout begins with an independent response; failed responses receive a verifier-conditioned retry, while successful rollouts terminate. Advantages are computed for each attempt separately, ensuring that credit is assigned appropriately to both initial and retry attempts, before applying a policy update with the GRPO loss.

Critically, GRPO relies on independently sampled rollouts to explore different reasoning trajectories, which can result in repeated exploration of the same incorrect paths and inefficient use of computational resources. Indeed, if a model is unlikely to solve a given problem, it may well be the case that independent rollouts make the same mistake again and again, leading to no useful training signal for the model to learn from its mistakes and wasting valuable computational resources in generating redundant and uninformative tokens.
Recent work has demonstrated that introducing dependence into the generation process can help improve coverage and potentially improve RLVR (Snell et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2023; Sprague et al., 2026; Kumar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026), but the best way to do so remains unclear. We thus ask: How can we introduce structured dependence in the sampling process to improve exploration, and how should we assign credit to each attempt?

In this work, we propose Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO) (Algorithm 1), a simple yet effective modification to GRPO that explicitly encourages exploration by allowing the model to generate retries after failed attempts and assigning credit to each attempt in a theoretically principled manner. ReAPO is compatible with any verifier-based reward function and does not require additional supervision or auxiliary objectives; moreover, ReAPO can be easily integrated into existing training pipelines, requiring minimal changes to existing code.

In more detail, our motivating question breaks into two parts whose combination yields ReAPO: (i) introducing beneficial dependence into generation and (ii) correctly assigning credit to individual attempts. Prior work has demonstrated the efficacy of keeping information in context to encourage language models to reflect on prior mistakes and correct themselves (Kumar et al., 2024; He et al., 2026; Bensal et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). We build on this idea and propose failure-conditioned repeated attempts: given a prompt and response, we grade the answer and, if the answer is incorrect, append an instruction to the model to try again. This process can then be repeated either until a correct answer is generated or until some maximum budget of attempts (or tokens) is reached. Critically, unlike GRPO, where each attempt is fully independent, future attempts can learn from prior incorrect solutions, thereby achieving better coverage than mere independent sampling (Snell et al., 2024). While taking this idea to the extreme would entirely replace the parallel sampling of GRPO with serial sampling, in practice, the system’s benefits of parallelization lead us to instead rollout multiple sequences of attempts independently, thereby introducing dependence within but not among distinct rollouts.
Failure-conditioning has additional benefits beyond exploration: serial sampling
can be viewed as a way to dynamically assign additional compute (measured in generated tokens) to more difficult problems where early attempts are less likely to achieve success. Differentially allocating compute based on problem difficulty has been observed to lead to significant improvements in token and wall-clock efficiency (Yu et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Microsoft AI Team, 2024), and is likely partially responsible for ReAPO’s efficiency.

Given a group of sequences of attempts as described above, it is not obvious how to assign credit to a given sub-attempt within a larger sequence. We propose to minimize the expected number of incorrect attempts before a correct solution is provided, which is an instance of a stochastic shortest path problem from the classical RL literature (Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, 1991). Under natural simplifying assumptions, the resulting policy gradient computes response-level advantages, i.e., we treat each attempt within a sequence independently and assign each attempt’s advantage only to the tokens relevant to that attempt, thereby allowing different attempts within a single sequence to receive different advantages. This approach encourages the model to produce correct solutions quickly while at the same time allowing the RL process to retain the benefits of conditioned sampling. The resulting algorithm is represented visually in Figure 1, demonstrating how failed responses are incorporated into context and how correct and incorrect responses are scored.

We now summarize the remainder of the paper. In Section 2 we introduce the prerequisite notions to our derivation of ReAPO. Then, in Section 3, we formally derive ReAPO’s objective under natural simplifying assumptions on the generation process. In Section 4, we investigate ReAPO empirically across four models from two families (0.6B to 4B parameters) and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, comparing against GRPO, compute-matched GRPO variants and other recent baselines, and ablating each component. We briefly discuss related work in Section 5, and defer further discussion, additional experiments and all proofs to the appendix.

## 2 Preliminaries

We now provide a brief overview of RLVR as well as the popular Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm.
As is common in RL for language models, we consider a language model to be a policy $\pi_{\theta}$ that maps a prompt $x$ to a distribution over responses $y$ . In this work, we always assume that the model is autoregressive, i.e., the response is generated one token at a time so that for each time step $t$ , the model produces a token $y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{<t})$ conditioned on the prompt and all previously generated tokens. To train the model, we assume that there is a verifier $r$ that can determine whether a given response $y$ is correct for a given prompt $x$ , and our goal is to optimize the model to maximize the probability of generating correct responses.
More precisely, we let $\mathcal{D}=\{x\}$ be a dataset of problems $x$ . Given a problem $x$ , the model generates a response $y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)$ , and the verifier $r$ produces a binary reward $r(x,y)\in\{0,1\}$ indicating whether the response is correct, with the goal of maximizing $\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(\cdot|x)}}\left[r(x,y)\right]$ .

## GRPO.

The most popular approach to RLVR is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Shao et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2025). For a given prompt $x$ , GRPO samples a group $\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x)$ of $G$ responses from the current policy and obtains rewards $r_{i}=r(x,y_{i})$ for each response. The rewards are then centered and normalized within the group to produce the response-level advantages

 $\displaystyle\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\varepsilon},\qquad\mu_{r}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}r_{i},\qquad\sigma_{r}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}(r_{i}-\mu_{r})^{2}},$ 

(2)

where $\varepsilon>0$ provides numerical stability.
GRPO maximizes the PPO objective Schulman et al. (2017)

## 3 ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization

In this section we introduce our algorithm Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO), summarized in Algorithm 1.
ReAPO has two key components on top of the standard GRPO pipeline: (1) verifier-conditioned exploration, which allows the model to generate retries after failed attempts, and (2) attempt-level credit assignment, which correctly assigns credit to each attempt based on its relative performance within the group. We describe each component in detail below.

## 3.1 Verifier-Conditioned Exploration

In GRPO, each model rollout is sampled independently and thus can repeatedly explore the same (incorrect and useless) reasoning trajectories, wasting compute and failing to learn from its mistakes. Motivated by prior work (Sprague et al., 2026; Kumar et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2025), we instead propose verifier-conditioned exploration.
More precisely, for each problem $x$ , ReAPO begins with the same initial group of $G$ rollouts as standard GRPO. Each rollout first generates an independent response $y_{g,1}$ . If the verifier marks this response as correct, the rollout terminates. If it is incorrect, however, the response is appended to the context together with a retry prompt, that explicitly instructs the model to reconsider its previous answer and attempt a different reasoning strategy. Our ablations demonstrate that the exact wording of the retry prompt is not critical, and we use “Your answer is wrong. Reflect on your previous answer and try something else.” for most of our experiments.
The model then generates a second response $y_{g,2}$ conditioned on the problem, its previous response, and the verifier feedback. This process can continue until the model produces a correct response or reaches the maximum number of (per-problem) attempts $K$ , or hits its token budget.

Because retries are generated only after failures, ReAPO dynamically expands the training group according to the observed difficulty of the problem under the current policy, which is known to help improve efficiency in modern RL for language modeling (Zhang et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Problems for which most initial responses are correct receive few additional generations, whereas problems with many incorrect responses receive more retries. This conditioned sampling allows for greater exploration of the model’s reasoning space; for example in Figure 15 in the appendix, we observe a substantial reduction in the required number of attempts in order to achieve a target pass@ $k$ accuracy relative to naïve independent sampling, even for just the base model.

## 3.2 Assigning Credit with Multiple attempts

Verifier-conditioned exploration helps solve the problem of repeated incorrect reasoning by allowing the model to condition its retries on previous failures, but it raises the question of how to properly assign credit to individual attempts within a multi-attempt trajectory. We propose minimizing the expected number of failed attempts to reach a correct solution as a natural objective. Note that in so doing, we are encouraging the model to produce correct solutions earlier, including on the first attempt, which is the desideratum during evaluation.

More formally, fix a problem $x$ and let $y_{k}$ denote the $k$ -th attempt generated for this problem, with $r_{k}=r(x,y_{k})$ the binary reward; letting $\tau=\inf\left\{k\geq 1\mid r_{k}=1\right\}$ denote the index of the first successful attempt, we aim to minimize $\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\left[\tau-1\right]$ . This is an example of a Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem, where the terminal state is a correct answer and the cost is constant per action Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis (1991). title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

Abstract

Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score.
This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets.
To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis.
The framework integrates advances from two areas:
(1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and
(2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs.
We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval).
Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items.
We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks:
(1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and
(2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM.
Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

## 1 Introduction

Benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) have rapidly proliferated in recent years. While this creates new opportunities, it also raises a key challenge: how to effectively leverage a large collection of benchmarks for comprehensive LLM evaluation?
Current evaluation practices remain quite raw.
The common approach is to evaluate a model on all items in a benchmark and then report the average score.
This naive statistical way collapses performance across items into a single number, which obscures fine-grained capability differences (Cui et al., 2026a).
For example, two LLMs with similar overall accuracy on a math benchmark (0.63 vs. 0.65) may exhibit very different profiles across sub-skills such as algebra and geometry.
This leads to a natural question: Given a set of test items, how can we go beyond a scalar score to a more informative, human-understandable capability estimate?

To answer this, we develop a new evaluation framework that aims to assess the latent abilities underlying observed item scores, and represents them as fine-grained skill profiles of LLMs.
This problem has long been studied in psychometrics and the education community using various latent variable models.
A representative family of approaches is Item Response Theory (Lord and Novick, 1968, IRT;), which jointly models test-taker traits (e.g., ability) and item traits (e.g., difficulty and discrimination).
IRT models are also increasingly used in machine learning, but typically for data-centric tasks such as dataset analysis or distillation (Kipnis et al., 2025; Maia Polo et al., 2024; Zouhar et al., 2025; Rodriguez et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2026b), and less often for LLM evaluation as it still produces a scalar overall ability score that suffers from capability collapse.
Some recent work explores multidimensional-IRT (Reckase, 2006) and its neural variants that learn ability vectors (Chen et al., 2025; Cui and Sachan, 2025; Song et al., 2025; Gor et al., 2024).
However, these multidimensional models are known to suffer from poor interpretability and non-identifiability, making them less suitable for reliable evaluation.

In this study, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that identifies latent skills and estimates LLM abilities at the skill level.
The framework consists of a skill discovery module, which extracts shared skills from problems, and a neural cognitive diagnosis model (Wang et al., 2020, CDM;), which estimates per-skill abilities based on model performance on skill-associated items.
We evaluate SkillEval on a large-scale dataset of 36M model–item response records, covering 3,811 models and 9,523 items across five benchmarks from various domains, including MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), GPQA (Rein et al., 2024), MuSR (Sprague et al., 2024), and IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023).
We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate the superiority of SkillEval from various aspects:

• 

Compared to MIRT-style methods, SkillEval extracts high-quality, human-understandable skills and produces stable ability estimates across runs, ensuring reproducible and robust evaluation.

• 

SkillEval accurately predicts model performance at both the item (with ${\rm AUC}=81.73$ ) and benchmark (with Pearson $r=0.989$ ) levels, outperforming strong baselines. In a downstream routing task where the goal is to assign queries to a cheap yet capable model, SkillEval matches the strongest LLM at $25\%$ of the cost ( $\tau{=}0.80$ , $99.9\%$ of strongest accuracy), and exceeds it by $3.7$ points at $37\%$ of the cost ( $\tau{=}0.95$ ). It also profiles previously unseen LLMs efficiently without retraining the shared network: $20$ adaptively chosen answers yield a mean benchmark-score error comparable to $100$ randomly chosen answers.

• 

In addition, SkillEval serves as a useful tool for analyzing dataset structure and model behavior, such as skill coverage across benchmarks, co-mastery patterns among skills, and skill-level differences between base and instruction-tuned models, offering useful insights into data curation and model training.

## 2 Profiling LLMs’ Skills with Cognitive Diagnostic Models

## 2.1 Problem Statement

Given a set of models to be evaluated $\{\mathcal{M}_{1},...,\mathcal{M}_{M}\}$ and a collection of test items $\{x_{1},...,x_{N}\}$ from one or multiple benchmarks, we represent their performance using a matrix $\mathcal{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}$ , where each entry $\mathcal{S}_{ij}$ denotes the score of the $i$ -th model on the $j$ -th item.
We formulate LLM profiling as a function $\mathcal{F}$ that takes $\mathcal{S}$ as input and outputs some estimates for each model’s capabilities, i.e., $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{S})\rightarrow\{\theta_{1},...,\theta_{M}\}$ , where $\theta_{i}$ is a quantitative measurement of the capabilities of model $i$ .

The common practice in evaluation is to model $\mathcal{F}$ as a simple average over individual items, i.e., $\theta_{i}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}S_{ij}$ .
While this provides a concise summary of model performance, it suffers from two key limitations. First, it compresses the model’s performance into a single scalar metric, failing to capture variations across fine-grained skills.
Second, the naive average can be affected by bias induced by the difficulty distribution of the test items, and may not faithfully reflect the model’s true ability. Indeed, this type of ability modeling assumes that all items in a given benchmark contribute equally to the estimation of a single ability dimension, which is typically an implausible assumption.

To address these limitations, we propose a new paradigm for profiling LLMs.
We assume that the items in the benchmark are associated with a set of underlying latent skills $\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}\}$ .
Inspired by psychometric approaches for assessing latent traits, we use Cognitive Diagnosis Models (CDMs) to construct the profiling function $\mathcal{F}_{\rm CD}(\mathcal{S})\rightarrow\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K}$ , where the profile $\theta_{i}$ for each model is a $k$ -dimensional vector representing its proficiency over the set of skills.
An overview of our method is shown in Figure 1.

## 2.2 Q-Matrix Construction

We use a binary Q-matrix $\mathcal{Q}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}$ to denote the mapping between $N$ items and $K$ skills, where each entry $\mathcal{Q}_{ij}=1$ indicates the $i$ -th item is associated with the $j$ -th skill and 0 otherwise.
Manually defining and annotating skills is challenging, costly, and difficult to scale.
Recent work shows that LLMs can automatically identify meaningful skills from problem content (Didolkar et al., 2024; He et al., 2026).
We adapt this approach to our setting, consisting of two main steps: skill labeling and skill clustering.

## Skill labeling.

For each item $j$ , we prompt GPT-4o-mini with the question stem and ask
for (i) a single primary skill and (ii) the full list of skills
required for the solution (exact prompt in Appendix D).
We use the full list rather than only the primary skill: primary-skill assignments produce Q-matrix rows
of mean row-sum $1.0$ , which under-constrains NCDM.
Full-list extraction yields a mean of $2.9$ skills per item and $13{,}276$ unique skill strings
across $9{,}523$ items.

## Skill clustering.

Because skills are extracted independently from different problems, they may contain redundancy and noise.
To obtain a more compact and coherent skill set, we cluster similar skills and merge them accordingly.
Didolkar et al. (2024) employ an LLM to perform this grouping process; however, such approaches may not scale well to a large number of skills. Therefore, we adopt an embedding-based clustering method, which is more efficient and scalable.
Each unique skill string is first encoded by the pretrained SBERT
all-mpnet-base-v2 (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) into
 $\mathbb{R}^{768}$ .
Then, we use the hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) algorithm with cosine distance and average linkage, specifying the number of final clusters as $K$ .

## Q-matrix assembly.

We set $\mathcal{Q}_{jk}=1$ iff at least one of item $j$ ’s extracted skills falls
into cluster $k$ . This multi-skill assignment reduces the fraction of
clusters with fewer than ten items from $43\%$ under primary-skill assignment to $36\%$ at

## 2.3 Neural CDM

We adopt the Neural Cognitive Diagnosis Model
(Wang et al., 2020). The probability that LLM $s$ answers item $j$ correctly
is estimated as:

 $p(\mathcal{S}_{ij}=1)\;=\;{\rm sigmoid}\!\Big(f\!\big(\,\alpha_{j}\,({\bm{\theta}}_{i}-\bm{d}_{j})\odot\bm{q}_{j}\,\big)\Big),$ 

(1)

where $\bm{\theta}_{i}\in[0,1]^{K}$ represents the learned skill mastery of model $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ , $\alpha_{j}\in[0,1]$ is the discrimination parameter of item $j$ , $\bm{d}_{j}\in[0,1]^{K}$ is its per-skill difficulty vector, and $\bm{q}_{j}\in\{0,1\}^{K}$ is the corresponding Q-matrix row.
The scalar $\alpha_{j}$ scales all skill dimensions equally. The function $f$ is a three-layer MLP with ${\rm PosLinear}$ layers. Each ${\rm PosLinear}$ layer uses non-negative weights, $\mathbf{W}^{+}=\max(\mathbf{W},0)$ .
Together with the non-decreasing sigmoid activations, this ensures that increasing any mastery component cannot decrease the predicted probability, holding all other inputs fixed.

## 2.4 Learning Item Parameters from Text

The original NCDM treats item discrimination $\alpha_{j}$ and difficulty $\bm{d}_{j}$ as model parameters learned during training, preventing predictions on unseen items.
To overcome this limitation, we follow previous context-aware approaches (Gor et al., 2024; Cui and Sachan, 2025) to use a lightweight neural network to learn item parameters based on their text features.
Specifically, for a given item $x_{j}$ , we first use a pretrained encoder to obtain its embedding $\bm{e}_{j}$ .
Then, we compute $\alpha_{j}$ and $\bm{d}_{j}$ via:

 $\alpha_{j}=\sigma\!\big(\mathbf{w}_{\alpha}^{\top}\bm{e}_{j}+b_{\alpha}\big),\qquad\bm{d}_{j}=\sigma\!\big(\mathbf{W}_{d}\,\bm{e}_{j}+{b}_{d}\big).$ 

(2)

To maintain computational efficiency, we freeze the pretrained encoder and only optimize the projection parameters $\mathbf{w}_{\alpha},\mathbf{W}_{d}$ and $b_{\alpha},{b}_{d}$ .

## 3 Evaluation of Skill Profiles

## Experiment Setup.

We train our text-conditioned NCDM on a subset of the RouterEval dataset (Huang et al., 2025), including 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items from five benchmarks: MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, and IFEval.
For the number of skills, we set $K{=}100$ as the main experimental configuration, as it achieves a better balance between interpretability and performance. We provide comparisons with other values of $K$ in Appendix F.

## 3.1 Quality of Discovered Skills

Since our evaluation is centered around skills, it is crucial to assess the quality of these LLM-discovered skills.
We consider the following three criteria:
(1) Semantic clarity, which measures whether a skill description is clear, unambiguous, and self-contained;
(2) Level of abstraction, which captures the granularity of a skill, where a good skill should be neither overly broad nor overly specific to particular questions;
(3) Diversity, which evaluates whether different skills are non-redundant and capture distinct aspects.
For the first two criteria, we adopt LLM-as-a-judge.
For the last one, we use intra-list diversity defined as averaged pair-wise dissimilarities, which is widely used in recommendation systems.

As a reference, we compare our skills with the Common Core State Standards22

Our skills achieve a similar level of semantic clarity to the Common Core.
In terms of granularity, they are slightly more fine-grained.
They also show lower variance ( ${\rm std}$ . 0.29 vs. 0.55), indicating more consistent granularity across skills, which is desirable.
In addition, our skills are more diverse ( ${\rm avg}$ . 0.83 vs. 0.76), likely because they cover more domains and reduce redundancy through clustering.
Overall, our automatically extracted skills are competitive with manually designed ones along key dimensions.

## Human validation of skill–question assignments.

Clear skill descriptions do not by themselves establish that the skills are relevant to their assigned questions. We therefore evaluate the skill–question assignments through human annotation. Three annotators, each holding an MSc in engineering, evaluated $780$ skill–question pairs covering all $100$ skills. We sampled up to $10$ questions uniformly at random from each skill’s assigned items, retaining all items for smaller clusters. Annotators were shown revised descriptive skill names and question text, and judged whether answering each question required the named skill. Majority voting accepted $652$ of $780$ assignments ( $83.6\%$ ), with an acceptance rate of $81.7\%$ when averaged equally across skills. Inter-annotator agreement was $0.715$ in mean pairwise Cohen’s kappa and $0.714$ in Krippendorff’s nominal alpha; both measures equal $1$ for perfect agreement and $0$ for agreement expected by chance. These judgments provide evidence for the semantic relevance of the sampled assignments.

## 3.2 Stability

For an evaluation method, the stability of its results is essential.
However, multidimensional latent ability models commonly suffer from non-identifiability: the $\theta$ vectors learned in repeated training runs are inconsistent, as they are affected by rotation, permutation, and random initialization.
This prevents such models from serving as a reliable and reproducible means of evaluation.
SkillEval instead ties each dimension of $\theta$ to a named skill through a fixed Q-matrix, which anchors the coordinate system across runs.

We test whether ability profiles remain consistent across retraining, and compare SkillEval with IRTNet (Chen et al., 2025), a high-dimensional neural IRT model that represents each LLM with a $d$ -dimensional latent ability vector.
We train SkillEval with five random seeds and IRTNet with different dimensionalities.
We compute Pearson correlations across learned $\mathbf{\Theta}$ across different runs in Table 2.
Averaged over dimensions and run pairs, the correlation is $0.96$ for SkillEval and $\approx 0.00$ for each IRTNet configuration.
To rule out differences that arise merely from different coordinate systems, we also compare runs after Procrustes alignment, which finds the rotation that best maps one run’s $\theta$ vectors onto another’s.
Despite this, IRTNet’s mean correlations rise only to $0.10$ – $0.43$ .
Thus, SkillEval supports more reliable and consistent evaluation of LLMs.

title: GPU-Accelerated Construction of the Gabriel Graph: Parallelization Strategies and Applications to Large-Margin Classification and Graph-Based Clustering
abstract: The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph widely used in computational geometry and geometric machine learning, underlying large-margin classifiers and, as we show in this work, density-aware clustering methods. Its construction, however, has cubic time complexity $O(N^3)$ in the naive formulation, which severely limits its use on datasets beyond a few thousand samples. This paper presents a set of GPU parallelization strategies, implemented in CUDA, that make Gabriel graph construction practical at scale. We introduce (i) an implicit closed-form mapping from a linear thread index to the corresponding vertex pair $(i,j)$, which removes the need for an explicit $O(N^2)$ adjacency structure and lets every thread locate its pair in constant time and constant memory; (ii) a two-pass, bitmask-based, atomically-compacted edge-list construction that produces a dense edge array proportional only to the number of edges actually found; and (iii) a thread-coarsening strategy in which each thread evaluates several candidate pairs, trading launch and scheduling overhead against load balance. We evaluate these strategies on the acceleration of a Gabriel-graph-based large-margin classifier (NN-clas) and on a novel Gabriel-graph clustering algorithm that identifies connected components on a residual graph and performs GPU-parallel Union-Find with hierarchical edge-based merging. On 14 public benchmark datasets, the GPU implementation reduces Gabriel graph construction time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude relative to a sequential CPU baseline (up to 8484x), without loss of classification accuracy, and the proposed clustering method is statistically competitive with DBSCAN on the topological validity index Dunn while eliminating the need for an explicit density radius parameter.

## GPU-Accelerated Construction of the Gabriel Graph:

Parallelization Strategies and Applications to

Large-Margin Classification

and Graph-Based Clustering

Diego Sanches Nere dos Santos

4.1 Naive Parallelization and the Indexing Problem
body_start:
Abstract

The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph widely used in computational geometry and geometric machine learning, underlying large-margin classifiers and, as we show in this work, density-aware clustering methods. Its construction, however, has cubic time complexity $O(N^{3})$ in the naive formulation, which severely limits its use on datasets beyond a few thousand samples. This paper presents a set of GPU parallelization strategies, implemented in CUDA, that make Gabriel graph construction practical at scale. We introduce (i) an implicit closed-form mapping from a linear thread index to the corresponding vertex pair $(i,j)$ , which removes the need for an explicit $O(N^{2})$ adjacency structure and lets every thread locate its pair in constant time and constant memory; (ii) a two-pass, bitmask-based, atomically-compacted edge-list construction that produces a dense edge array proportional only to the number of edges actually found; and (iii) a thread-coarsening strategy in which each thread evaluates several candidate pairs, trading launch and scheduling overhead against load balance. We evaluate these strategies on the acceleration of a Gabriel-graph-based large-margin classifier (NN-clas) and on a novel Gabriel-graph clustering algorithm that identifies connected components on a residual graph and performs GPU-parallel Union–Find with hierarchical edge-based merging. On 14 public benchmark datasets, the GPU implementation reduces Gabriel graph construction time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude relative to a sequential CPU baseline (up to $8484\times$ ), without loss of classification accuracy, and the proposed clustering method is statistically competitive with DBSCAN on the topological validity index Dunn while eliminating the need for an explicit density radius parameter.

Keywords: Gabriel graph, GPU, CUDA, parallel computing, proximity graphs, large-margin classification, clustering, computational geometry.

## 1 Introduction

Proximity graphs occupy a central role in geometric approaches to machine learning: they turn a set of feature vectors into a combinatorial structure whose edges encode a notion of “closeness” that can be exploited for classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction, or anomaly detection. Among proximity graphs, the Gabriel graph, introduced by Gabriel and Sokal (1969) in the context of geographic variation analysis, is particularly attractive because it depends on nothing but pairwise Euclidean distances, requires no free parameters (unlike $k$ -nearest-neighbor or $\varepsilon$ -radius graphs), and is a subgraph of the Delaunay triangulation, which guarantees several useful connectivity and locality properties (Matula and Sokal, 1980).

A vertex pair $(x_{i},x_{j})$ is connected by an edge in the Gabriel graph if and only if the open hypersphere having the segment $\overline{x_{i}x_{j}}$ as diameter contains no other point of the dataset. This purely geometric criterion has made the Gabriel graph a popular structural backbone for large-margin classifiers (Garcia et al., 2015; Arias-Garcia and others, 2024; Hanriot et al., 2024), where edges connecting samples of different classes – the support edges – approximate the decision margin between classes without solving any optimization problem.

The price of this elegance is computational: verifying the empty-hypersphere condition for every candidate pair against every other point costs $O(N^{3})$ in the number of samples $N$ , since there are $O(N^{2})$ candidate pairs and each check is itself $O(N)$ . This cost quickly becomes the dominant bottleneck of any Gabriel-graph-based pipeline once $N$ grows into the thousands, which is precisely the regime in which real-time or large-scale applications – medical diagnosis, network intrusion detection, industrial monitoring – would most benefit from these classifiers.

Because the empty-hypersphere test for a pair $(i,j)$ is completely independent of the test for any other pair $(k,l)$ , Gabriel graph construction is an embarrassingly parallel problem, and is therefore a natural candidate for acceleration on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), whose Single-Instruction-Multiple-Threads (SIMT) architecture is designed precisely to exploit this kind of massive, independent, data-parallel work (Owens et al., 2008; Nickolls et al., 2008).

## Contributions.

This paper isolates and details the GPU parallelization of Gabriel graph construction – the computational core shared by every Gabriel-graph-based algorithm – and studies it as a problem in its own right. Concretely, we contribute:

1. 

A closed-form, $O(1)$ -time and $O(1)$ -memory mapping from a one-dimensional CUDA thread index $k$ to the pair of vertex indices $(i,j)$ that it must evaluate, which avoids materializing an $O(N^{2})$ index table (Section 4);

2. 

A two-pass, bitmask-based edge construction scheme that uses atomic operations to compact the sparse set of valid Gabriel edges into a dense array proportional to the true edge count, keeping GPU memory usage close to $O(|E|)$ rather than $O(N^{2})$ (Section 4.3);

3. 

An empirical study of thread coarsening – assigning multiple candidate pairs to each thread – showing that the best coarsening factor is dataset-dependent: it reduces execution time on one dataset but not on another (Section 4.4);

4. 

Two downstream applications that validate the approach: an accelerated re-implementation of the NN-clas large-margin classifier (Arias-Garcia and others, 2024), and a new GPU-native clustering algorithm that uses connected components of a distance-filtered Gabriel graph, with an automatic elbow-based cut and a GPU parallel Union–Find with hierarchical merging (Section 5);

5. 

An experimental evaluation on 14 public datasets (synthetic and real), reporting speedups of up to $8484\times$ over a sequential CPU baseline and a statistical comparison of the resulting clustering quality against $K$ -means and DBSCAN (Section 6).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the Gabriel graph and the relevant CUDA/SIMT background. Section 4 presents the parallelization strategies in detail. Section 5 describes the two applications used to validate the approach. Section 6 reports the experimental results, Section 7 discusses limitations, and Section 8 concludes with directions for future work.

## 2 Related Work

## Gabriel-graph-based classification.

Gabriel and Sokal (1969) originally proposed the Gabriel graph for geographic variation analysis; Matula and Sokal (1980) later characterized its geometric properties. In machine learning, the graph has been used to build hyperparameter-free, geometry-driven large-margin classifiers: edges connecting samples of opposite classes (support edges) delineate the separating margin without an explicit optimization procedure. Garcia et al. (2015) studied the effect of label noise on such classifiers and proposed a quality-based filtering step, which we reuse as a pre-processing stage. Arias-Garcia and others (2024) proposed a hardware (FPGA) implementation of a Gabriel-graph classifier to reduce its computational cost, confirming that acceleration of this family of methods is an open and relevant problem, while Hanriot et al. (2024) extended Gabriel-graph classifiers to the multiclass setting and connected them to neural architectures, and The GGClassification Contributors (2020) provide a reference software implementation. None of these works targets general-purpose GPU acceleration of the underlying graph construction, which is the focus of the present paper.

## GPU-accelerated machine learning.

The suitability of GPUs for data-parallel machine learning workloads is well documented (Owens et al., 2008; Eon and others, 2021; Zhang and others, 2023; Çolhak and others, 2025). Çolhak and others (2025) benchmark GPU versus CPU execution of machine learning libraries and report substantial throughput gains; Zhang and others (2023) present a GPU framework that couples neural simulation and AI at scale. These works motivate GPU acceleration in general but do not address the specific combinatorial structure of proximity-graph construction.

## Thread granularity and coarsening.

Magni et al. (2014) show that automatically tuning the amount of work assigned to each GPU thread – thread coarsening – is essential, because a naive one-thread-per-element mapping can be dominated by scheduling overhead. We adopt this principle for Gabriel graph construction and quantify its effect empirically in Section 6.

## Graph-based clustering.

Clustering by connected components of a proximity graph is a classical idea (Cormen et al., 2001; Jain, 2010); the difficulty lies in choosing which edges to keep. We adopt an elbow-based automatic threshold (Thorndike, 1953) on the sorted Gabriel edge weights, following the general taxonomy of internal cluster validity indices surveyed by Ezugwu and others (2022), which we use throughout for quantitative evaluation.

## 3 The Gabriel Graph

## 3.1 Definition and Basic Properties

Let $S=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a finite point set. The Gabriel graph of $S$ is the undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{1,\dots,N\}$ (one vertex per sample) and

Definition 1 (Gabriel edge).

An edge $(i,j)\in E$ exists if and only if no other point $x_{k}\in S$ , $k\neq i,j$ , lies strictly inside the open hypersphere having $\overline{x_{i}x_{j}}$ as diameter. Equivalently,

 $\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\|x_{i}-x_{k}\|^{2}+\|x_{j}-x_{k}\|^{2},\qquad\forall\,x_{k}\in S\setminus\{x_{i},x_{j}\}.$ 

(1)

Figure 1 illustrates the construction: for the highlighted pair, the dashed circle (the two-dimensional analogue of the empty hypersphere) contains no other data point, so the edge is admitted. In a labeled binary classification setting $S=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}$ with $y_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}$ , we call support edges the subset $E_{S}\subseteq E$ of edges whose endpoints have different labels; under mild assumptions on class overlap, $E_{S}$ localizes the decision boundary between classes (Gabriel and Sokal, 1969; Arias-Garcia and others, 2024).

Figure 1: A Gabriel graph built on a synthetic two-class point set. Grey edges connect same-class neighbors; red edges are support edges joining points of different classes. The dashed circle illustrates the empty-hypersphere test of Eq. (1) for one admitted edge: no other point falls inside it.

Property 1 (Complexity).

Checking Eq. (1) for a single candidate pair costs $O(N)$ (one pass over all other points). Since there are $\binom{N}{2}=O(N^{2})$ candidate pairs, the naive construction costs $O(N^{3})$ in time. The graph itself is sparse: it is known to be a subgraph of the Delaunay triangulation, so $|E|=O(N)$ in the planar case and generally $|E|\ll N^{2}$ in higher dimensions for non-adversarial data.

The gap between the $O(N^{3})$ construction cost and the $O(N)$ – $O(N^{2})$ size of the resulting graph is precisely what motivates a parallel, memory-conscious construction strategy: work is heavily redundant across candidate pairs (each requiring an independent scan of $N-2$ points) but the eventual output is small and sparse.

## 3.2 The SIMT Execution Model

CUDA organizes computation into a grid of thread blocks; each block contains threads grouped into warps of 32 threads that execute the same instruction stream in lock-step (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads, SIMT) (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025). Performance is maximized when threads within a warp follow the same control-flow path (avoiding warp divergence) and when global memory accesses are coalesced. Concurrent writes to shared memory locations are protected with atomic operations (e.g., atomicAdd, atomicOr, atomicMin), which guarantee indivisible read-modify-write semantics at the cost of potential serialization when many threads contend for the same address (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025).

Gabriel graph construction maps naturally onto this model: each candidate pair $(i,j)$ can, in principle, be assigned to an independent thread, with no data dependency between threads other than read-only access to the (immutable) point set. The remainder of this paper addresses how to organize that mapping efficiently.

## 4 Parallel Construction Strategies

## 4.1 Naive Parallelization and the Indexing Problem

A direct GPU translation of Gabriel graph construction launches one thread per candidate pair $(i,j)$ , $i<j$ , and has each thread evaluate Eq. (1). The number of candidate pairs is

 $T=\binom{N}{2}=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}.$ 

(2)

The immediate difficulty is indexing: CUDA launches a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) grid of threads, each receiving a linear global index $k\in[0,T-1]$ ; the thread must recover the pair $(i,j)$ that $k$ represents. Materializing a lookup table of size $T=O(N^{2})$ defeats the purpose of an efficient implementation, since it alone can exceed available GPU global memory for large $N$ (e.g., $N=30{,}000$ already gives $T\approx 4.5\times 10^{8}$ pairs).

## 4.2 Implicit Index Mapping $k\mapsto(i,j)$ 

We derive a closed-form inverse of the standard row-major enumeration of the strict upper triangle of the $N\times N$ pair matrix,

 $(0,1),(0,2),\dots,(0,N-1),\;(1,2),(1,3),\dots,(1,N-1),\;\dots,\;(N-2,N-1),$ 

so that every thread can compute its own $(i,j)$ in constant time and constant memory, using only $N$ and its own index $k$ .

Row $i$ contains $L_{i}=N-i-1$ valid pairs. The number of pairs enumerated strictly before row $i$ is

 $P(i)=\sum_{r=0}^{i-1}(N-r-1)=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}-\frac{(N-i)(N-i-1)}{2}.$ 

(3)

Index $k$ belongs to the (unique) row $i$ satisfying $P(i)\leq k<P(i+1)$ . Solving this quadratic inequality for $i$ in closed form gives

 $i=N-2-\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{-8k+4N(N-1)-7}}{2}-0.5\right\rfloor.$ 

(4)

The column index then follows directly from the offset within row $i$ :

 $j=k-\left(\frac{N(N-1)}{2}-\frac{(N-i)(N-i-1)}{2}\right)+i+1.$ 

(5)

Equations (4)–(5) let every thread invert its linear index $k$ into a vertex pair $(i,j)$ using a handful of arithmetic operations and one square root – no auxiliary memory, and no per-thread branching that would introduce warp divergence.

Example 1.

For $N=5$ , $T=10$ and the enumeration is

 $\begin{array}[]{c|ccccc}&0&1&2&3&4\\
\hline\cr 0&-&(0,1)_{0}&(0,2)_{1}&(0,3)_{2}&(0,4)_{3}\\
1&&-&(1,2)_{4}&(1,3)_{5}&(1,4)_{6}\\
2&&&-&(2,3)_{7}&(2,4)_{8}\\
3&&&&-&(3,4)_{9}\\
4&&&&&-\end{array}$ 

For $k=5$ , Eq. (4) gives $i=3-\lfloor\sqrt{33}/2-0.5\rfloor=3-\lfloor 2.37\rfloor=1$ , then $P(1)=4$ and Eq. (5) gives $j=1+1+(5-4)=3$ , correctly recovering the pair $(1,3)$ .

To guard against 64-bit overflow when $N$ is large, all index arithmetic (grid sizing, $T$ , and the intermediate terms of Eqs. (4)–(5)) is carried out using 64-bit integer/floating-point types.

## 4.3 Two-Pass Construction with Bitmask Compaction

Even without materializing an index table, naively allocating one flag per candidate pair still costs $O(N^{2})$ memory if a full byte (or worse, a 32-bit int) is used per flag. We instead use a two-pass, bitmask-compacted scheme:

1. 

Pass 1 – Marking. Each thread evaluates Eq. (1) for its pair $(i,j)$ (recovered via Eqs. (4)–(5)). If the pair satisfies the Gabriel condition, the thread sets a single bit in a global bitmask using atomicOr, reducing flag storage by a factor of 32 relative to one int per pair, and increments a global counter with atomicAdd to determine the exact number of valid edges.

2. 

Intermediate allocation. The host reads the counter and allocates exactly the memory required for the dense edge list (and, if needed, the associated edge weights).

3. 

Pass 2 – Compaction. Threads re-scan the bitmask; for every set bit, an atomic increment on a write-cursor determines that edge’s position in the dense output array, which is then populated.

This scheme keeps peak GPU memory proportional to the number of candidate pairs only during the (cheap, bit-packed) marking pass, and proportional to $|E|$ thereafter – the true asymptotic footprint of the graph. All device vectors are managed through the Thrust library (thrust::device_vector), and intermediate buffers are explicitly released (shrink_to_fit) as soon as they are no longer needed, which is important because subsequent stages (noise filtering, classification, or clustering) may need to allocate further structures on the same device.

## 4.4 Thread Coarsening

Mapping exactly one candidate pair to one thread maximizes available parallelism but also maximizes the number of threads that must be created, scheduled and retired, which introduces overhead that is not always amortized by useful work – especially for the many pairs, per warp, that fail the Gabriel test early. We therefore evaluate thread coarsening (Magni et al., 2014): each thread is assigned a contiguous block of $c$ candidate pairs (indices $k,k+1,\dots,k+c-1$ under the mapping of Eqs. (4)–(5)), amortizing per-thread overhead and improving data locality, at the cost of a coarser and potentially less balanced distribution of work across the device. Figure 2 sketches the expected trade-off: execution time can fall as $c$ grows (overhead amortization dominates), reach a minimum, and rise again as load imbalance across threads dominates. Section 6.3 measures whether this holds in practice.

Figure 2: Schematic illustration of the thread-coarsening trade-off in Gabriel graph construction: very fine granularity is dominated by kernel-launch and scheduling overhead, while very coarse granularity is dominated by load imbalance across threads. An intermediate “sweet spot” minimizes total execution time; measurements on two datasets, where the optimum turns out to be dataset-dependent, are reported in Section 6.3.

## 4.5 Summary of the Construction Pipeline

Algorithm 1 summarizes the full GPU construction pipeline combining implicit indexing, coarsening and two-pass compaction.

limitations:
The results support two related claims. First, the $O(N^{3})$ cost that has historically limited Gabriel-graph methods to small or medium datasets is not an intrinsic obstacle but an artifact of sequential execution: because the empty-hypersphere test is independent across candidate pairs, a GPU implementation combining implicit pair indexing and bitmask-compacted two-pass construction reduces execution time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude with no loss of downstream accuracy (Table 1, measured with $c=1$ ); thread coarsening can reduce it further on some datasets, but not on all. Second, once construction is fast, the Gabriel graph becomes a practical building block not only for classification (as in NN-clas) but also for density-aware clustering, where it is competitive with DBSCAN on the Dunn index while avoiding an explicit density-radius parameter.

Several limitations should be noted. The reported speedups compare a single-threaded CPU baseline to a single-GPU implementation on hardware with a substantial theoretical performance gap between host and device, which the community’s convention (and our stated intent to isolate parallel-kernel efficiency) accepts but which should be kept in mind when transferring absolute speedup numbers to other hardware pairings; a multi-threaded CPU baseline (e.g., OpenMP) would narrow the reported gap while leaving the qualitative conclusions unchanged. The clustering method’s hierarchical merge stage relies on a global minimum-weight-edge search per merge step, which, while GPU-parallel, adds sequential dependency across merge iterations and could itself be a target for further optimization (e.g., a parallel priority structure). Finally, the largest datasets used for the coarsening study ( $N\approx 10^{5}$ ) already produce several billion candidate pairs ( $T\approx 5\times 10^{9}$ for $N=10^{5}$ ); scaling further, into the range where the bitmask itself exceeds single-GPU memory, would require a multi-GPU or out-of-core extension of the pipeline described here.
conclusion:
The results support two related claims. First, the $O(N^{3})$ cost that has historically limited Gabriel-graph methods to small or medium datasets is not an intrinsic obstacle but an artifact of sequential execution: because the empty-hypersphere test is independent across candidate pairs, a GPU implementation combining implicit pair indexing and bitmask-compacted two-pass construction reduces execution time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude with no loss of downstream accuracy (Table 1, measured with $c=1$ ); thread coarsening can reduce it further on some datasets, but not on all. Second, once construction is fast, the Gabriel graph becomes a practical building block not only for classification (as in NN-clas) but also for density-aware clustering, where it is competitive with DBSCAN on the Dunn index while avoiding an explicit density-radius parameter.

Several limitations should be noted. The reported speedups compare a single-threaded CPU baseline to a single-GPU implementation on hardware with a substantial theoretical performance gap between host and device, which the community’s convention (and our stated intent to isolate parallel-kernel efficiency) accepts but which should be kept in mind when transferring absolute speedup numbers to other hardware pairings; a multi-threaded CPU baseline (e.g., OpenMP) would narrow the reported gap while leaving the qualitative conclusions unchanged. The clustering method’s hierarchical merge stage relies on a global minimum-weight-edge search per merge step, which, while GPU-parallel, adds sequential dependency across merge iterations and could itself be a target for further optimization (e.g., a parallel priority structure). Finally, the largest datasets used for the coarsening study ( $N\approx 10^{5}$ ) already produce several billion candidate pairs ( $T\approx 5\times 10^{9}$ for $N=10^{5}$ ); scaling further, into the range where the bitmask itself exceeds single-GPU memory, would require a multi-GPU or out-of-core extension of the pipeline described here.

Apprenticeship Learning (AL) infers policies directly from expert demonstrations by recovering the underlying reward structure, enabling strictly offline learning without environment interaction. Abstract

Effective decision-making in human-centric environments such as Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) and clinical healthcare requires policies that are adaptive, data-efficient, and ethically deployable. Apprenticeship Learning (AL) offers a principled path: rather than engineering reward functions, AL infers policies directly from expert demonstrations by recovering the underlying reward structure, enabling strictly offline learning without environment interaction. This dissertation develops a progression of offline AL frameworks addressing increasingly realistic complexities of human demonstration data, organized around two central challenges: reward modeling and demonstration quality.

On the reward modeling front, we first relax the standard assumption that all demonstrations share a single, homogeneous reward function. We apply EM-EDM, an Expectation-Maximization framework built upon Energy-based Distribution Matching (EDM), which simultaneously clusters demonstrations by their latent reward functions and induces cluster-specific policies over large continuous state spaces. We show that EM-EDM outperforms AL baselines and two DRL induced policies on student pedagogical decision prediction, demonstrating that heterogeneous reward modeling is both feasible and effective from a small number of expert demonstrations. We then address the further assumption that reward functions remain fixed within a trajectory. We leverage THEMES (Time-aware Hierarchical EM Energy-based Subtrajectory AL), which partitions trajectories into temporally coherent sub-trajectories and induces policies over each partition guided by a hierarchically learned reward regulator. Validated across one educational and three real-world clinical healthcare datasets, THEMES consistently outperforms all flat and hierarchical AL baselines, establishing that modeling temporally evolving reward functions substantially improves policy induction in human-centric domains.

On the demonstration quality front, we first challenge the assumption that demonstrations are uniformly optimal. We introduce HALIDE (Hierarchical Apprenticeship Learning from Imperfect Demonstrations with Evolving Rewards), which integrates continuous demonstration quality signals directly into the hierarchical policy induction process. HALIDE establishes that incorporating suboptimal trajectories without quality-aware ranking degrades performance, whereas ranked hierarchical learning enables principled reuse of mixed-quality data, yielding consistent gains under cross-semester distribution shift. We then go further and jointly attribute demonstration quality to individual decisions via CCHAL (Critical Contrast Hierarchical Apprenticeship Learning). Rather than weighting entire trajectories uniformly, CCHAL distributes trajectory-level demonstration ranks to per-decision weights via Bayesian credit assignment, separately scores each decision’s criticality by contrasting expert against non-expert behavior in a dual-arm design, and sharpens reward learning with a Bradley-Terry pairwise contrastive IRL objective over observed failure trajectories. Evaluated across three clinical EHR datasets and a student ITS dataset, CCHAL outperforms flat and hierarchical AL baselines, including its direct predecessor HALIDE, establishing that decision-level outcome attribution and behavioral criticality are both necessary to fully exploit demonstration quality signals.

Finally, the dissertation is grounded by a real-world classroom evaluation of StuEDM, an EDM-induced policy that lets students make their own decisions about how to engage with each problem and intervenes only when it disagrees with the student’s choice, trained on a substantially smaller and shorter-span demonstration corpus than a comparable Conservative-Q-Learning-induced policy. StuEDM significantly improves posttest performance and normalized learning gain over a pretest-equivalent Expert baseline that assigns among the same domain-expert-designed presentation modes with no adaptive guidance, and significantly improves the pretest-adjusted posttest score over the CQL-induced policy trained on a much larger historical corpus, while overriding students’ own decisions less than half as often; together these results provide empirical evidence that offline AL from a substantially smaller, agency-preserving demonstration corpus can rival reward-optimizing DRL trained on far larger corpora in live educational deployments.

Taken together, this dissertation establishes offline AL as a practical, data-efficient, and ethically viable paradigm for human-centric environments, tracing a principled path from reward modeling to quality-aware demonstration learning, and from retrospective evaluation to real-world classroom deployment.
